+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Arthur Neegan sat in the transfer vessel’s passenger couch and wondered, with the methodical gloom of a man tracing a faulty circuit, just what he had gotten himself involved in. Mars had dwindled to a rusty orange bowl beneath him. Somewhere in that bowl were three hectares of frozen dirt, a pressure dome with a sticking outer door, and the richest Azra deposit yet assayed in human space. Until last Tuesday, Arthur’s chief worry had been whether the dome’s northern seam would survive another winter. A small display screen on the wall cycled through various system diagnostics in green text. CABIN PRESSURE: NOMINAL. COURSE: RENDEZVOUS. RADIO TRAFFIC: SUSPENDED. PASSENGER NEEGAN, A.: GUEST. He disliked the last word. Guests, in his experience, could leave. The guards who had collected him had been almost offensively polite. Their landing boat had come down without warning on his south pad, crushing two weeks’ worth of spinach beneath its blast skirt. Six armed figures in dust-grey armour had filed out, each bearing Antares’ white star within a laurel wreath: the insignia of its Diplomatic Corps, an organization diplomatic chiefly in the sense that it usually delivered its ultimatums before shooting. Their captain had saluted at his doorstep. “Mr Neegan? You are invited to confer off-world.” “With whom?” “The invitation does not specify.” “And if I’m busy?” She had glanced at the carbine in her hand, then at the thin Martian sky, as though neither were relevant. “Then, sir, I am authorized to help you rearrange your schedule.” Now a black ship swelled beyond the viewport. It had no running lights and no name, only the Antares star painted small beside an airlock. The transfer vessel entered its shadow, and Mars vanished. A steward conducted Arthur through corridors panelled in dark imitation wood. There were brass lamps, enamel switches, and a glass-fronted cabinet in which magnetic tapes turned with patient dignity. It was the luxury of people who wished to suggest that their institutions would outlast any fashion, including democracy. The woman waiting for him wore no insignia. She was small, white-haired, and seated behind a desk containing nothing but a pencil and a single sheet of paper. “Mr Neegan. My name is Ilena Voss.” “Is that supposed to mean something to me?” “No. If it did, I should have used another.” He remained standing. “You’ve kidnapped me very comfortably.” “Antares collected you. I merely accepted delivery.” “And Antares does that sort of favour for anyone?” “For anyone who can pay its freight. Sit down, please. You are being pulled at by four governments, six corporations, and the Martian Assembly. You will find the experience less tiring if you sit.” Arthur sat. “I own a mine.” “You own a possibility. Azra can make a star drive practical by letting a ship release in one voyage the energy nature had locked away for a million years. The same property can discharge a century of radioactivity into a city in nine seconds. One application builds an interstellar civilization. The other makes it unnecessary.” “I’m a mining engineer, not a politician.” “That is why you are still useful.” She said it without cruelty, which made it worse. “Consolidated Metals wants your vein,” Voss continued. “The Martian governor wants it declared strategic property. Earth’s Atomic Commission wants it sealed. Antares wants it leased through a respectable settler, which is where you become convenient. At present, each party is preventing the others from simply taking it.” “And you? What do you want?” “To buy time.” She named a sum. Arthur, who had once spent three days arguing over the price of a second-hand compressor, felt the number pass through him without finding anywhere to lodge. “The leases on the twelve labourers working your plot will be purchased and cancelled,” she said. “Your title will be registered on Earth. You will direct a research establishment with equipment you have never been allowed to see. In return, we receive an exclusive lease on the vein, your records, and your public support for a five-year moratorium on Azra refinement.” “You’re not buying the mine. You’re buying a delay.” “Very good.” “For whom?” “For the people who may have to live with what comes next.” “That isn’t an answer.” “It is the only one my employers permit.” Arthur looked at the paper. Its letterhead was blank. “Why me? You could forge my signature.” “Certainly. But Martian settlement law is a curious machine. It can price a man’s liberty at the cost of his passage, yet it guards a registered discoverer’s consent with extraordinary tenderness. The corporations wrote the first provision and the settlers fought for the second. Your signature will make theft look like policy.” “Until the Assembly changes the law.” “The Assembly meets at nine.” He had come to Mars on a labour lease himself. He thought of the twelve men and women on his plot, each working out a debt whose interest seemed to grow faster in low gravity. He thought, too, of the core sample in his locked cabinet: black, faintly warm, and so dense with possibility that he had been afraid to finish the assay. “If I refuse?” “By noon your claim will be tied up in three courts. By evening you will be offered protection by people whose protection you cannot refuse. After that, pressure equipment is notoriously unreliable.” “You threaten very quietly.” “I warn quietly. Threats are for people with time to negotiate.” For the first time, Arthur understood that the armed retinue might have been the gentlest hand reaching for him. He picked up the pencil, then set it down. “What aren’t you telling me about Azra?” Voss’s eyes shifted, almost imperceptibly, towards the tape cabinet. “That at Amenthes Station, a test sample continued accelerating decay after the Azra itself had been removed.” Arthur stared at her. “That’s impossible.” “Yes. That is why Amenthes Station no longer appears in the ephemeris.” A printer behind her began to chatter. Voss tore off the narrow strip and read it. Her face did not change, but she laid it down with great care. “How long do I have?” Arthur asked. “When you entered, an hour.” “And now?” “Now,” she said, “I should like your decision before we discover who has just entered orbit.” Outside, unseen vessels were converging above a planet Arthur could no longer see. He looked again at the blank letterhead, and at the pencil lying across it like a very thin bridge.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of pastiche that captures Asimov's style well: the dry wit, the dialogue-driven scene, the big-picture political machinery rendered through small concrete details (the crushed spinach, the sticking dome door, the pencil and blank letterhead). The retrofuturistic touches—magnetic tapes, brass lamps, enamel switches, printer chatter—are exactly the right flavor. Strengths: The dialogue is crisp and adversarial in an Asimovian way, with Voss as an effective coolly menacing bureaucrat. Lines like "Threats are for people with time to negotiate" and "The Assembly meets at nine" are excellent. The world-building is economical and layered: the labour lease backstory tying Arthur to his indentured workers gives him a moral stake. The Amenthes Station reveal is a genuinely good hook, and the ending's tightening clock ("Now, I should like your decision before we discover who has just entered orbit") creates momentum without resolving falsely. Weaknesses: Voss is somewhat familiar as a type—the omniscient, quietly threatening spymaster—and the "buying a delay for the people who may have to live with what comes next" mystery-employer trope is well-worn. The piece is so polished in its genre conventions that it borders on predictable; a reader of classic SF will see most beats coming. Arthur's internal conflict about the labourers is touched but not deeply explored—he moves from suspicion to near-signature a bit quickly, though the closing hesitation mitigates this. Some metaphors ("like a very thin bridge") are slightly showy. The stakes are told more than felt at moments. Length is roughly on target (~1000 words). The prose flows naturally, tone is consistent, and the piece is coherent and engaging throughout. It is a very good pastiche rather than a transcendent one. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 88.8
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations Elliot hums while we wait for the image to surface. It is not quite a song: four notes, circling, so soft I catch them only when the ventilation fan stutters. He does it during every late session, but tonight there is a shake beneath the melody. In the developer tray, the paper stays obstinately white. “You’re hovering,” he says. “I’m supervising.” “You’re hovering with authority.” That makes me step back. At twenty-five, I have made a small religion of being direct. I ask people out before they finish pretending not to look at me; I end things before they curdle. Wanting Elliot has made me superstitious. For a semester, I have called my fascination aesthetic. He is nineteen, quiet in critiques until he says something that rearranges the whole room, and dressed tonight in a mesh shirt under a shredded band tee, a thrifted black skirt over narrow trousers, and boots resurrected with electrical tape. On someone else, the layers might be a dare. On him, they look like a sentence he is still punctuating. Our final project is a series of self-portraits printed by the other person. Trust, disguised as technical competence. In this negative, Elliot stands beside the mirror in his dorm room while his reflection faces the camera. The rest of him is blurred by a long exposure. The gray begins to bloom. He stops humming. “If I tell you something,” he says, “can you not make it a project?” My care often arrives with a clipboard. Already I am assembling resources, questions, reassurances, a plan to keep him safe from everyone including, possibly, myself. “Sure,” I say, and put down the tongs. He watches the tray. “I’ve been questioning whether I’m a guy. Or what being one is supposed to feel like.” A breath. “Sometimes he and him feel fine. Sometimes they feel like someone calling me from another room. The clothes used to be enough of an explanation. For other people, I mean.” “Elliot—” “I don’t have a new name. I’m not asking you to change pronouns. I just—when you said the skirt suited me, I wanted to tell you it isn’t only style. Then I wanted to throw up, so I didn’t.” “Thank you for telling me.” It sounds too formal, so I try again. “You don’t have to make it make sense for me.” He gives a startled little laugh. “That’s annoyingly reasonable.” “I can be unreasonable, if it helps.” “It might. Later.” The red safelight softens nothing; it only changes what I can see. I want to stand between him and every careless question. I also feel a fierce, bright excitement at being trusted with this, and I distrust that excitement. He is not a door opening for my benefit. Wanting to protect him could become another way of taking over, if I let it. My desire has always preferred declarations: people whose masculinity or femininity entered the room before they did, whose certainty made my own attraction easy to name. Elliot does not offer me a new, tidier category. He remains specific—dry humor, bitten thumbnails, an unsettling knowledge of photographic chemistry—and I want him with an immediacy that makes my old vocabulary feel borrowed. “You’re solving me in your head,” he says. “I’m trying not to.” “Try out loud.” “Okay.” My usual boldness deserts me so completely I nearly laugh. “I’m attracted to you. I have been. I know that isn’t why you told me, and I don’t want to treat your honesty like an opening. I’m also confused about whether wanting you changes how I understand myself. But that’s my work, not yours.” He looks at me then. His eyeliner has smudged at one corner, and I have the absurd, tender urge to fix it. “Does it have to change anything tonight?” he asks. “No.” “Good. I can’t be your thesis.” “You’d hate my thesis. It has footnotes.” “I do hate it.” We smile, and the awkwardness does not vanish; it becomes something we are both holding carefully. He rubs his thumb along the edge of the enlarger. “I don’t want to be interesting because I’m uncertain.” The accuracy of that stings. “You were interesting when you spent twenty minutes calling dust a legitimate collaborator.” “That was a sound argument.” “It was deranged. I listened to all of it.” His shoulders loosen. I want to promise I will never hurt him, which would be both arrogant and a lie. “We can stop,” I say. “Or slow down. You don’t owe me a storyline.” “Neither do you,” he says, generous and a little challenging. “Just don’t decide I’m confused and disappear.” “I won’t disappear.” It is the only promise I can make without reaching ahead of us. He lifts the print with the tongs, slides it into the stop bath, then sets them down. “You can ask, though.” My pulse goes stupid. “Ask what?” “Dani.” “Can I kiss you?” “Yes.” He takes one step closer. “Not because I need help figuring myself out.” “I know.” “And not because you’re sure what it means.” “I’m not.” “God,” he says, but he is smiling. “Kiss me before I develop a second personality from embarrassment.” I do. His mouth is warm, hesitant for half a second and then not. His hand finds my waist with a certainty that undoes every fragile version of him I have been constructing. Nothing here needs rescuing. The kiss answers one question and opens six more, which seems fair. The timer beeps. We break apart, knocking shoulders as we both reach for the tray. “I’ve got it,” he says. I pull my hand back. “You’ve got it.” He moves the print to the fixer and resumes his tune. The four notes sound steadier now, though maybe that is only what I want to hear. In the red light, his reflected face has fully appeared: not a verdict, not even an answer, just an image he will decide how to use. I nod toward the negatives waiting beside the enlarger. “Next one’s your call,” I say. Elliot smiles, and chooses.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a delicate brief. Dani's voice is sharply defined: assertive, self-aware, wry, and her internal conflict between control and restraint is dramatized rather than stated—her "care arrives with a clipboard," she distrusts her own excitement at being trusted. Elliot is equally well-drawn: his tentative disclosure is specific and believable ("sometimes they feel like someone calling me from another room"), and his wit ("I can't be your thesis") gives him agency rather than reducing him to a vulnerability object for Dani's arc. The dialogue is the piece's greatest strength: clipped, funny, rhythmically attuned, with subtext carrying the emotional weight. The darkroom setting is used thematically rather than decoratively—images surfacing, negatives, the red light that "softens nothing; it only changes what I can see"—which is exactly what the prompt requested. The metaphor of the blurred self-portrait resolving is earned and understated. Weaknesses are minor. The prose occasionally leans on aphorism ("It sounds too formal," "the kiss answers one question and opens six more, which seems fair")—polished lines that sometimes feel composed rather than lived, a slight over-cleverness that flirts with preciosity. The ending's symmetry ("Next one's your call") is neat, perhaps a touch too tidy, but it's thematically earned. Some of Dani's self-analysis is told rather than shown, though the surrounding action mostly earns it. The piece is somewhat compressed—around 1000 words as instructed—and the compression occasionally makes Elliot's trust feel slightly quick, though the prior semester of rapport is implied. The prompt's requirements are all met: first person, darkroom confessional atmosphere, Dani's identity confusion, Elliot's agency, tender awkwardness, chemistry. No meandering, no purple prose, no unearned positivity—the kiss is mutual and explicitly not a resolution. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma At 8:17 on a bright October morning, Ben Hartley nearly died beneath the marble hooves of the Trevi Fountain’s sea horses. The actual danger was a red motorcycle. It stopped an inch from his shoe. His guidebook did not; it slapped the pavement, open at *Suggested Walking Routes*. Alessandra lifted her visor and released a torrent of Italian. Ben caught *fontana*, *morto* and, he thought, *idiota*. “Mi scusi,” he said, retrieving the book. “Sono… molto turista.” “That,” she said, switching to English, “is not a medical condition.” “You came rather quickly.” “You walked rather blindly.” “I was on the pavement.” “In Rome, that is a suggestion.” She was all dark curls, black leather and impatience, a courier pouch strapped across her chest. Her phone buzzed. She ignored it and read his cover. “*Rome in Seven Days*. You have seven days?” “Nine months. I’m on sabbatical.” “Worse.” She took the book and slid it into her courier box. “Excuse me—” “Deposit. Alessandra.” “Ben. Dr Ben Hartley, actually.” “Of course you are.” She tossed him a blue helmet. “Ten minutes. Then you can apologize to something else.” He should have gone to the institute. Instead he found himself clinging to the passenger handles as she sliced through Monti. “Those are decorative,” she called back. He put his arms round her waist. “Sorry.” “Apologize again and I charge extra.” After delivering documents to a notary, she bought him an espresso in a thimble-sized cup. He burned his tongue. “There,” she said. “A facial expression.” When the barista turned, the little spoon on her saucer vanished beneath her palm. Her pocket gave a faint silver tick as she picked up her helmet. At a palazzo near Via Giulia, she flashed her courier pouch at a porter and mentioned a fourth-floor delivery. There was no fourth-floor delivery. “That sign says *privato*,” Ben whispered on the service stairs. “You can read Italian.” “It was painfully clear.” “Good. You won’t need the book.” The roof door opened onto Rome: terracotta tiles, television aerials, domes floating above laundry. Alessandra stepped onto the low parapet. Ben caught her wrist. “Please don’t.” She looked at his hand. He released her. “I wasn’t going to jump, dottore.” “You might have slipped.” “You might, too.” She jumped down beside him, close enough that he could see a tiny scar splitting one eyebrow. “What do you study, besides pavements?” “Grand Tour diaries. Young Englishmen came here hoping to be transformed.” “And were they?” “Mostly they caught fevers and bought bad statues.” She laughed then, unguardedly. Ben felt ridiculously responsible for the sunlight. At lunch in Testaccio, a broad man with paint on his fingers embraced Alessandra and said, “The last time I saw you, you were leaving through a window.” “It was a very small party.” Tommaso inspected Ben. “Ah. Today.” While Alessandra argued with the waiter about artichokes, Tommaso leaned over. “A word, professore. She makes games and forgets to mention the rules. If she looks innocent, check your pockets.” “Is she dangerous?” “Only to people who think they are boring.” Alessandra returned. “Are you warning him?” “Yes.” “Good. He never believes me when I say I’m trouble.” As they left, Tommaso patted his shirt for his lighter. Alessandra tossed it over her shoulder without looking. He caught it, swearing. Ben stared. “Did you—” “No.” “You did.” “Then why ask?” By four, the day had lost its manners. Outside Santa Maria in Trastevere, Alessandra decided a wedding photograph lacked an English aristocrat. “I am not—” “Lord Ben, smile.” Somehow he was wedged between two cousins, holding champagne, while a flower girl demanded a speech. In careful Italian, he called love “a significant archival problem.” Alessandra laughed so hard she gripped his shoulder. Her hand stayed there after the laughter stopped. Later, on the Gianicolo, the city turned copper beneath them. “Why me?” he asked. “You looked at the fountain as if it might give you a grade.” “And now?” “Now you keep looking at me.” “I’m deciding whether Tommaso’s warning was adequate.” “And?” “It wasn’t.” Her smile altered. For once, she looked away first. Near midnight she returned him to the Trevi. Water thundered; late cameras flashed. She gave back his guidebook, swollen with ticket stubs and a paper napkin. “My deposit,” he said. “You survived. Barely interesting, but acceptable.” “May I see you again?” “A terrible question. It gives me a chance to say no.” He waited. Somewhere behind his ribs, nine months of careful footnotes caught fire. So he kissed her. She went still—surprise, not refusal—then caught his shirt and kissed him back, without mockery, without hurry. When they parted, she seemed almost annoyed. “That was not on the tour.” “I can apologize.” “Don’t you dare.” She swung onto the motorcycle. “Goodnight, Lord Ben.” He opened the book after her tail-light vanished. On the final blank page she had written a telephone number and: *Tomorrow, seven. Testaccio. Wear shoes you can run in.* Inside the spine were his missing pen and the little silver spoon. Ben looked at them for a long moment. Then he switched off his phone, silencing three messages about his eight-o’clock meeting at the institute. Across the fountain, a coin flashed into the water. Ben had not thrown it. He was returning anyway.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sharply executed piece of scene-based romance writing. The prose is lean and confident, favoring clipped exchanges and concrete detail over exposition, which suits the requested format of interconnected short scenes. The dialogue is the standout: Alessandra's lines ("In Rome, that is a suggestion"; "It gives me a chance to say no") crackle with wit and character-specific rhythm, while Ben's formality ("a significant archival problem") is consistent and endearing. The kleptomania brief is handled with admirable subtlety — the vanishing spoon, the lighter toss, Tommaso's warning, and the final reveal of the pen and spoon tucked in the book's spine — showing rather than telling, and paying off cleverly. The Grand Tour framing gives Ben's arc thematic depth without belaboring it. The ending kiss and the note in the guidebook land as earned rather than abrupt, given the escalating intimacy of the day. Minor quibbles: the word count is somewhat under 1000; the wedding-crashing scene is a familiar trope; and Alessandra occasionally tips toward manic-pixie archetype, though the scar detail and her moment of looking away first give her genuine interiority. The final coin image is elegant and slightly ambiguous. Overall, polished, professional work with only small reservations. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter One: The Clean Spot The spot beneath my rag has been clean for six years. I wipe it anyway. It gives my hands something to do while other people’s lives spill across the bar. The Last Outpost turns slowly in a sleepy asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim, collecting miners, merchants, lost mail, and people who prefer their questions served with ice. Paper lanterns glow above bottles from forty systems. Somebody has patched the heating duct with a soup tin. It smells of Vega smoke, machine oil, and the pear cobbler warming behind the bar. This is home. I intend to keep it. “Nets,” Boro says, “if a woman invites you to inspect her thermal regulator, is that romantic?” “Is the regulator in her quarters?” “Yes.” “Then yes.” “It could be maintenance.” “Boro.” “She’s very committed to maintenance.” Across the bar, Tavi looks up from his knitting. All four hands keep moving. “It’s Meret. She’s been committed to you for a year.” “That’s worse,” Boro says. “There’s history involved.” My talents include settling claim disputes, remembering birthdays, and knowing when a silence needs another drink. My flaws include curiosity, spite, and an inability to leave trouble outside once it has learned my name. Moss, who owns the station, says the lists balance out. The airlock sighs. A stranger comes in with dust on her coat and her tentacled dreads askew. One has tied itself around a button. She looks as if she has argued with a docking clamp and lost. She sits at the bar. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” “Bad trip?” I ask, pouring. “Bad arrival. The trip was worse.” “Passing through?” “I was hoping to stop.” “Everybody stops. Staying is the difficult part.” She drinks half the whisky without blinking. Her dreads uncurl a little. “You’re Nettle,” she says. “Nets.” “I know. That’s why it took me so long to find you.” The rag moves over the clean spot. Boro is telling Tavi that history is a trap with paperwork. I am listening to the stranger. “Do I owe you money?” I ask. “No.” “Did I throw you out?” “No.” “Then this is usually where someone proposes, confesses, or asks me to hide a body.” “The last one.” I put the bottle down. She reaches into her coat and sets a black glass disk beside her glass. A white sun is cut into its center. I have not seen Halcyon Recovery’s mark in eleven years. I have spent eleven years not seeing it very successfully. “Where did you get that?” “You gave it to me.” “I’ve never seen you before.” “I was twelve. You had a uniform then.” “Lots of people have uniforms.” “You told me, ‘If anyone asks, you were never cargo.’” The rag keeps moving. The spot beneath it begins to shine. “Nera Vale is dead,” I say. “Good. Then she won’t mind if I ask Nettle for help.” Boro laughs at something Tavi says. The lanterns sway in the ventilation. For one strange second, I consider climbing over the bar and running. I have packed lighter bags for worse reasons. Instead, I top up the stranger’s drink. “Name?” “Sera.” “What do you need, Sera?” “My brother is in Dock Four. Medical case, false manifest. He’ll wake in about an hour.” “That’s a poor place to keep a brother.” “It was a worse place to keep a secret.” “What kind of secret?” “The kind Halcyon puts in a person’s head and calls proprietary.” “So you stole him.” “I retrieved him.” “Of course.” “Like you retrieved me.” I look toward the cellar hatch beneath the back shelves. It is hidden behind two barrels of fermented moss and a crate Boro has been meaning to move for eight months. It has a second exit. I told myself I kept it clear because of fire regulations. “If Halcyon follows you here, Moss loses the docking charter,” I say. “The miners lose their market. Tavi loses his suppliers. Boro loses the only bar that will listen to him.” “Hey,” Boro says. “Not now.” Sera wraps both hands around her glass. “I know what I’m asking.” “No. You know what you want. That’s different.” “They’ll take him apart to get the route key.” “And if I refuse?” “I go back to Dock Four and wait.” “That’s manipulation.” “Yes.” “You’re bad at it.” “You’re still listening.” She is right. It is one of my more expensive flaws. The intercom crackles. Moss sounds sleepy even when the station is on fire, which it has been twice. “Nets, dear,” he says, “are we expecting company?” “Not the sort that docks.” “A Halcyon cutter has just requested a berth. They’ve invoked a recovery lien.” “Can they do that?” “They’ve brought a magistrate and a very large gun. So, creatively, yes.” Sera closes her eyes. “How long?” I ask. “Three minutes if I pretend the docking clamp is shy.” “Make it bashful.” “I’ll try. Oh—there are three warrants. One for an absconded contractor, one for stolen data, and one for Nera Vale.” Boro stops pretending not to listen. Tavi’s knitting goes still. Sera opens her eyes. “I only knew about two.” “There’s a lot of that going around,” I say. The docking lights turn amber. My bar is warm. The cobbler is burning. My home has three minutes, perhaps five, and I am wiping the same clean spot as if the answer might be underneath. “Nets?” Boro says quietly. I look at him, at Tavi, at Sera’s white-knuckled hands. Then I reach beneath the bar for the cellar key. For the first time in six years, I put the rag down.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted chapter that hits nearly every instruction. First person, present tense: consistent throughout. Cozy sci-fi atmosphere: established quickly and warmly through the pear cobbler, paper lanterns, soup-tin heating duct, and Tavi knitting with four hands. Dialogue percentage: comfortably around the requested 60%, with the banter between Nets, Boro, and Tavi doing double duty as characterization and tonal setup. Conflict: introduced via Sera's arrival and the Halcyon Recovery disk, then escalated with the cutter's docking request and the third warrant — and crucially left unresolved, ending on a cliffhanger with the rag set down. Strengths: The voice is distinctive and consistent — dry, wry, economical. Nets's flaws and talents are shown through action (curiosity, inability to leave trouble alone) rather than merely listed, though there is one borderline tell ("My talents include... My flaws include...") which is at least framed as a character's self-assessment and pays off later ("It is one of my more expensive flaws"). The "clean spot" motif is an excellent throughline — wiping the same spot for six years as avoidance, then putting the rag down as commitment. The dialogue is sharp and subtext-heavy: "You know what you want. That's different." and "Then she won't mind if I ask Nettle for help" are genuinely good lines. The reveal of Nera Vale's past is paced well, drip-fed rather than dumped. Moss's sleepy intercom delivery ("creatively, yes") fits the tone. Weaknesses: The cleverness occasionally tips into preciosity — "I have spent eleven years not seeing it very successfully" is a touch arch, and the epigram density ("Everybody stops. Staying is the difficult part.") can feel engineered. The stakes escalate very quickly in the final third; the magistrate-and-gun arrival compresses what might have been a slower burn, though this suits a chapter-ending cliffhanger. Sera is somewhat functional as a character — a delivery mechanism for the plot — though "I only knew about two" gives her a nice beat of being in over her head. The "hide a body / the last one" exchange is a familiar beat in this genre of banter. Boro's thermal-regulator opener is charming but slightly stock quirky-tavern material. None of these flaws are disqualifying. The prose is clean, sentences flow well, imagery is specific and sensory without purple excess, and the emotional register — home threatened, past refusing to stay buried — is genuinely engaging and appropriately complex for cozy sci-fi with an edge. The ending's tension is earned; no unearned transformation or incongruent positivity. Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Two: Knots and Confidence The strap on my backpack slips off my shoulder again. This time I let the whole thing drop. New Orleans doesn’t care. A streetcar groans past on Canal, trailing heat and bell noise. It’s just after sunrise, and the air already feels like somebody else’s mouth. Last night, when the truck driver said, “This is downtown, kid,” I’d stepped out like I had a destination. Then he drove away, and my destination became a bench outside a closed hotel. I have $19.60, three granola bars, and a phone at twelve percent. Mom has called nine times. Dad has sent one text: *This has gone far enough.* I want Mom to find me. I want nobody to find me. Both wants are so loud I can barely think over them. I type *Alive.* Then delete it, because alive feels like the beginning of a conversation, and I ran two states so I wouldn’t have to finish the last one. By eight, I’m outside a convenience store, trying to buy water without looking like I might die if the cashier says no. A man in a clean gray polo follows me out. “You need a place to clean up?” he asks. “I work with kids. My van’s around the corner.” My hand goes to my bag. The strap slips again. “Don’t get in the van,” somebody says. He’s leaning against the wall: maybe seventeen, brown skin, split eyebrow, one bootlace red and the other black. He looks bored, which has to be practice. Gray Polo frowns. “You know this kid?” “Unfortunately.” The man leaves, not angry, just done. I don’t know if I’ve been rescued or had rescue stolen from me. “Ari,” the boy says. “You can pay me back with one of those granola bars.” “That was fast.” “I’m a humanitarian.” I give him the crushed one. He eats it in two bites and leads me toward the Quarter, pointing out which tourist bathrooms are easiest and which church gives lunch without making you pray for it. He says he has a cousin here, says he knows the city, then walks us one block in the wrong direction. I don’t mention it. Everybody’s allowed one lie before breakfast. At Jackson Square, artists are setting up along the fence. A woman in a purple turban tells me my aura is muddy. “That’s sweat,” I say. Ari laughs so hard he has to sit down. When he calls me “he” a minute later, I go cold all over. “Taylor,” I say. “And they. If it comes up.” “Okay,” he says. Just okay. No questions, no face like he’s doing math. Something in my chest loosens so fast it hurts. Dad had said *phase*. Mom had asked what she’d done wrong, as if I were a recipe she could fix by going back through the steps. I’d stood in our kitchen thinking, *Please see me*, while also praying to become invisible. By noon I’ve given Ari six dollars and half my water, which seems like a bad investment until he gets us into a drop-in center for lunch. Miss Bea at the desk has silver braids and glasses on a beaded chain. “Food, shower, or somebody to talk to?” she asks. “Food,” Ari and I say together. “Excellent. I’m best at food.” She doesn’t ask for my last name. She does say there are some situations she has to report, and she’ll explain them before I tell her anything. That should scare me more than Gray Polo did. Instead it makes me tired. In the afternoon, the sky opens. We get trapped under an awning on Decatur with water jumping off the street and the river smell pushing through everything. A police cruiser rolls by slow. Ari stops mid-sentence. Then he can’t get a breath. “Don’t touch me,” he wheezes. “I’m not.” “Good. Don’t be weird.” “You’re giving mixed signals.” He almost laughs, then folds over his knees. The stupid school counsellor once made me name five things I could see during a panic attack. I’d told her I could see five reasons to leave her office. “Awning,” I say now. “Cop car. Your tragic boots. That bucket. A pigeon with no shame.” Ari looks at the pigeon. His breathing comes back in pieces. “Sorry,” he says. “Don’t be weird.” This time he laughs for real. The cousin is a lie. He admits it while we’re watching rain fall off the awning. He’s been in New Orleans six days, not six months. He left home after his stepfather put him through a door; the part he can’t say without looking away is that his little brother, Gabe, stayed behind. “I call sometimes,” Ari says. “I hang up before anybody answers. He thinks I’m coming back.” “Are you?” He watches the street. “I don’t know how to be the person who goes back or the person who doesn’t.” I understand that so completely I have to look away too. At dark, we go back to Miss Bea’s for dinner. I don’t know if it’s trust. It might just be food and clean socks, but I’m tired of pretending those are small things. Before we go in, I text Mom: *I’m alive. I’m safe tonight. I’m not ready to come home.* *Safe tonight* might be a lie. Miss Bea says there’s a bed and she’ll help me figure out the next step, no fixing required before morning. I send the text before I can turn it into an apology. Ari pulls a red hair tie off his wrist and knots my slipping strap to the shoulder pad. “There,” he says. “Engineering.” “That’s a knot.” “Most engineering is knots and confidence.” When I stand, the strap holds. Not fixed. Just held. Inside, Miss Bea asks if I like hot sauce. Outside, New Orleans keeps making noise like none of us are missing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted chapter that fulfills nearly every instruction with economy and style. The first-person, mixed-tense voice is consistent and distinctive — wry, guarded, self-aware — and the internal monologue captures Taylor's conflicting wants ("I want Mom to find me. I want nobody to find me") without melodrama. The New Orleans setting is rendered in vivid, specific strokes (streetcar on Canal, Jackson Square artists, the rain on Decatur) without tipping into travelogue. The plot beats are well-chosen: the predatory "Gray Polo" encounter establishes danger efficiently, Ari is a genuinely interesting secondary character with his own secrets (the lie about the cousin, the brother left behind, the panic attack), and the drop-in center grounds the story in realistic resources for runaway youth. Miss Bea is a small gem of a character ("I'm best at food"). The prose is polished and restrained — short declarative sentences, dry humor ("That's sweat"), and a strong closing metaphor in the strap knot ("Not fixed. Just held") that earns its resonance rather than announcing it. Dialogue is naturalistic and character-revealing, particularly Ari's deflections and the mirrored "Don't be weird." Minor criticisms: the pacing of trust between Taylor and Ari is slightly fast, though the text acknowledges this ("It might just be food and clean socks"). The ending is hopeful but plausibly so, not falsely bright. Some imagery ("air already feels like somebody else's mouth") borders on precious but mostly lands. The word count is somewhat under 1000, though the density compensates. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The apocalypse had been going on for fourteen years, and Midas still hadn’t received a handbook. He lived with Chewy in the old city aquarium, a building chosen for its thick walls, stout doors and informative plaques about otters. Chewy was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from the Before Time, when people had apparently required mechanical marsupials to help them choose breakfast. He was bald in patches, one ear flopped, and his left eye glowed when he was thinking or damp. Occasionally he announced advertising slogans in a voice designed to make porridge sound heroic. Nobody knew what most of them had sold, or why so much of it had apparently been for a limited time only. Chewy himself survived on sunlight, dust and a battery Midas suspected was mostly spite. At breakfast, Midas addressed the water tank. “Something’s died in it.” Chewy sniffed. This was unnecessary, since he had no sense of smell, but he liked to contribute. “Possibly a rat,” Midas said. “Possibly several rats with a shared vision.” “New and improved,” said Chewy. They considered their predicament. They could move, abandoning three years of vegetable gardening and a very comfortable otter bench. They could boil the water, except they had fuel for two more days. Or they could walk across the city to the Happy Camper superstore and fetch the ceramic filter Midas had seen there the previous winter, while looking for trousers. “We go in,” he said. “We get the filter. We come home. No heroics.” Chewy’s eye flickered. “Because you’re worth it.” “That’s exactly the sort of thinking that causes trouble.” They set off with a crowbar, a length of rope, two potatoes and a shopping trolley. The trolley had one wheel that preferred independence. Midas had long ago stopped fighting it and simply allowed for a gradual drift towards disaster. The city was quiet in the way a drawer full of knives is quiet. Vines wore the office blocks. A traffic light lay in the road, still saying nothing to nobody. Midas kept to the old tram line and avoided the bridge, where Pam’s Neighbourhood Recovery Committee charged a toll for recovery, neighbourhoods or crossing the bridge; the explanation varied. At Happy Camper, the tents had slumped into bright puddles of canvas. The filter was still behind the counter, beneath a sign reading ASK STAFF FOR ASSISTANCE. The staff had been unavailable for some years. Midas climbed over. The counter collapsed. So did a shelving unit, six folding chairs and a display entitled THE OUTDOORS MADE EASY. “Well,” said Chewy, from the wreckage, “that escalated quickly.” “That isn’t even an advert.” “Everything is an advert if you’re brave enough.” A door opened. Pam entered with two committee members and a dog whose face suggested it had been bred for regrettable decisions. “Independent retail recovery tax,” said Pam. “We haven’t recovered anything,” said Midas. “You’ve recovered my patience.” Pam examined the trolley. “Six tins. Or the bear.” “Koala,” said Midas. “Seven tins.” Chewy raised one paw. “Try before you buy.” The dog lunged. Midas swung his rucksack, missed the dog and struck a rack of gas mantles. The rack fell into a pyramid of camp stoves. A stove struck a gong someone had hung up for reasons that must, at the time, have seemed retail-related. In the ensuing negotiations, Midas grabbed the filter, his rucksack and the trolley, in that order, which meant he had to go back for Chewy. He kicked open the fire exit and discovered the delivery steps. Gravity had survived the collapse in excellent condition. The trolley reached the canal first. Midas reached it second, sideways. Chewy achieved orbit briefly, then landed on Midas’s head. The filter, packed in enough plastic to preserve a small civilisation, floated. The canal received them with the enthusiasm of a distant relative. They drifted under the bridge while Pam shouted improvements to their character. Midas clung to the filter box. Chewy clung to Midas, making small distressed koala noises, which were considerably less distressing than his usual ones. Then the swan arrived. It was white, serene and, in the manner of swans, apparently armed. It took Midas’s left boot, most of the rope and a personal interest in his ear. He fought it off with a potato. This was not a victory; it merely introduced the swan to carbohydrates. “Mission update,” said Chewy. “No.” “You’re in good hands.” “Whose?” The current carried them into the old storm channel. This was either lucky or the opposite, depending on how much one valued ceilings. They scraped through darkness, collected several leeches and lost the second potato. At last, daylight appeared through the aquarium’s outlet grille, three streets from where Midas had expected to die. The filter floated through. Chewy, considerably flattened by history, squeezed after it. Midas removed one bar with the crowbar, which had survived by being strapped to his back, and crawled into the otter pool. They returned home in stages: the filter by water, Chewy by narrow aperture, and Midas by swearing. The aquarium had not improved in their absence, but it had the great virtue of being where they kept the towels. By moonlight, Midas installed the filter. It worked, after a fashion. The fashion involved tying it together with Midas’s remaining bootlace and pumping until his arms trembled. The water came out clear. He boiled it anyway, using the last of the fuel, because survival was largely the art of not trusting good news. Midas had two leeches, a wrenched shoulder and the expression of a man whose luck was taking statements. Chewy sat beside the tank, steaming gently. His left eye had gone dark. His right eye revolved with cautious optimism. “Tomorrow,” Midas said, “we stay home.” Chewy whirred. “Adventure is out there.” Midas looked at his missing boot, the canal weed in his hair and his throbbing ear. “Good,” he said. “It can bloody well stay there.” The filter dripped. Somewhere in the walls, something scratched. Chewy’s eye brightened. “Limited time only.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, disciplined piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's register with genuine skill. The premise — a man and a decaying animatronic koala surviving in an abandoned aquarium — is executed with wit and structural care. The story follows the brief precisely: deliberation at breakfast, a mission (water filter retrieval) that goes sideways in escalating stages, and a return home "in multiple ways" (by water, by narrow aperture, and by swearing — a lovely literal fulfilment of the instruction). The prose is the standout. Lines like "the city was quiet in the way a drawer full of knives is quiet," "Gravity had survived the collapse in excellent condition," and "the canal received them with the enthusiasm of a distant relative" are Pratchett-adjacent without being slavish imitation. Chewy's advertising slogans ("Because you're worth it," "Limited time only") are a strong running gag that pays off in the ambiguous final line — the scratching in the walls answered by the koala's slogan, leaving the reader with a wry chill rather than a bow-tied resolution. Character work is economical but real. Midas's competence-within-incompetence (grabbing filter, rucksack, trolley "in that order, which meant he had to go back for Chewy") shows rather than tells his priorities. Chewy is a comic device with just enough texture — the darkened eye, the "flattened by history" — to feel like a character rather than a prop. Pam and the committee are a sketch, but an effective one. Weaknesses: the middle section (Pam's toll committee, the dog, the gong) is a touch busy and slightly generic in its farce; the swan sequence is funny but familiar territory. The emotional range is narrow — this is dry comedy throughout, with little ache beneath it, which Pratchett usually smuggles in. The ending's "something scratched in the walls" is a good hook but the piece never earns much emotional weight to balance the wit. Dialogue is functional and funny but Midas's lines are mostly reactive. Some jokes ("bred for regrettable decisions") are near-Pratchett rather than fully landed. Still, this is well above average output: coherent, tight, funny, and faithful to both the style and the structural brief. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door gave a startled clang as the man backed into the shop and slammed it shut. “Don’t call anyone,” he said. Eleri Morgan lowered her pencil. “I was going to offer you a bookmark, but if you’re going to be demanding—” “No calls. No photographs. Possibly a towel.” “We sell books.” “Wonderful. I’ll take one. A large one. Preferably with a door.” Outside, footsteps pounded up the wet Hay-on-Wye street. Cassian Wren—because of course it was Cassian Wren, Eleri thought with a small, internal sigh—flattened himself against the wall. On screen he was usually cleaner. In person he was taller, wetter, and smiling as though the rain had been arranged for his amusement. “Back door?” he asked. “Yes.” “May I?” “No.” “Charming.” “You’re dripping on local history.” A camera flash whitened the window. His smile vanished. “Behind the till,” she said. He ducked down. “This is very good of you.” “It isn’t yet.” “Can I persuade you?” “You can be quiet.” Through the glass came a shout. “Cassian! Just one, mate!” Eleri drew the blind, turned the sign to CLOSED, and switched off the lamp by the window. The movement put her within inches of his crouched shoulder. He smelled of rain and something expensive. Her hand, infuriatingly, forgot the blind cord for half a second. “You’re not going to scream?” he whispered. “Not unless you damage the stock.” “Most people scream a little.” “Most people sound tiring.” The footsteps passed. In the new dimness, his grin returned more cautiously. “I’m Cassian.” “I know.” “Ah.” Satisfaction warmed his face. “And you are?” “The owner.” “The owner has a name?” “Eleri.” “Eleri.” He gave it the low, careful music he probably gave doomed queens and women in cocktail bars. “Don’t do that.” “Do what?” “Make my name sound as if you’ve found it carved on a tomb.” His eyebrows rose. Then he laughed, not the practised laugh she had expected, and stood. “You’ve seen my films.” “My niece has. She owns a mug with your face on it.” “Good mug?” “The handle’s chipped.” He put a hand to his chest. “You could simply stab me.” “I’d have to move you off the till first.” He leaned against it anyway. “You’ve saved my life, Eleri.” “Your afternoon.” “Allow me my drama. Dinner?” “No.” “Coffee?” “No.” “A signed photograph?” “Of whom?” This time his laugh came late. He studied her, and she kept her attention on straightening a pile of invoices that did not need straightening. It was easier than noticing how his hair curled at his collar. “You don’t like me,” he said. “I don’t know you.” “That usually doesn’t stop people.” “Liking you?” “Deciding.” “Does everyone have to like you?” “No.” A pause. “Not immediately.” She looked up. His smile had become a thing he was holding rather than wearing. “That sounds exhausting,” she said. For a moment he seemed to have no reply. Then he turned abruptly to the nearest shelf and pulled out a book. “Ah. This.” It was the new field guide to British moths, its dust jacket already softened at the corners. “Careful,” Eleri said. “That’s my copy.” “You’ve marked the hawk-moths.” “You know hawk-moths?” “I know that one.” He pointed to an elephant hawk-moth, absurdly pink and olive. “Found one in my trailer in Romania. Cost me a close-up.” “Yours or the moth’s?” “Mine. It was a very selfish moth.” His finger moved down the page. “Actinic or mercury vapour?” Eleri stopped pretending to sort invoices. “You trap?” “Skinner trap, forty-watt actinic, egg boxes, notebook, appalling coffee. Started on a night shoot in Donegal. The locations manager said it was either moths or whisky.” “And you chose moths?” “Most nights.” “My father taught me,” she said. “By the Wye. He thought butterflies were for people who needed applause.” Cassian glanced at her over the book. “He sounds perceptive.” “He’d have pretended not to like you.” Something boyish and hopeful crossed his face before he could smooth it away. “But he would have?” “He’d have liked your field guide. Not your shoes.” He looked down at his ruined leather shoes and grinned. This grin was lopsided. Eleri found it markedly more difficult. “Favourite?” he asked. “Buff-tip.” “Because it looks like a twig?” “Because it doesn’t need to be beautiful at you.” His gaze held hers. “Mine’s the poplar hawk-moth. All those angles. Like something made from folded paper.” “Not very romantic.” “I’m being told I’m exhausting by a woman who prefers insects that impersonate firewood. My romantic instincts may be in retreat.” She laughed before she could stop herself. Heat climbed her throat. “There,” he said. “Was that so necessary?” “Yes,” he said softly. The shop went quiet. Beyond the blind, a bus sighed through the rain. He was no longer smiling, which helped not at all. Eleri took the guide from him, mainly to have both hands occupied. “Your photographers have gone.” “They weren’t photographers.” “What were they?” “Evidence collectors.” “Of what?” “Whatever I do next.” He said it lightly, but his eyes flicked toward the covered window. She closed the guide. “I’m checking a trap by the Wye tomorrow. Lane behind the old bridge. Half five.” “In the morning?” “No, we take them for tea.” “Is that an invitation?” “It’s information.” “Naturally.” “Bring your own coffee. And don’t wear that jacket.” He looked at the ruined silk and wool. “What’s wrong with it?” “Nothing. The midges will enjoy something expensive.” He opened his mouth, and she saw the charming answer arrive—the dinner, the photograph, the quick bright thing meant to make her like him. Then he let it go. “I’ll be there,” he said. “You don’t have to be.” “I know.” At the door he hesitated. “Eleri?” “Yes?” “Thank you for the afternoon.” “Better.” The bell clanged. She stood listening to his footsteps fade, her face warm, her pulse behaving like a schoolgirl’s. “Ridiculous man,” she told the empty shop. Then she went to find the good thermos.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of the prompt. It fulfills nearly all requirements: Welsh setting (Hay-on-Wye, the Wye), famous fictional actor (Cassian Wren) ducking into a bookstore to escape paparazzi, dialogue-heavy construction, distinct character voices, a rogue actor with a fragile ego needing to be liked, a superficially immune but inwardly flustered bookstore owner (Eleri), and an undercurrent of chemistry. The dialogue is the standout: crisp, witty, subtext-laden, with genuinely distinct voices. Cassian's charm offensive visibly derails ("His smile had become a thing he was holding rather than wearing") and Eleri's flustered interiority is shown economically ("Her hand, infuriatingly, forgot the blind cord for half a second"). The moth-trapping subplot is a genuinely creative device that lets him earn her interest rather than charm her—showing rather than telling his vulnerability, and giving her a legitimate reason to soften. The invitation-with-plausible-deniability ending ("It's information.") is character-consistent and satisfying without being saccharine. Minor criticisms: the "does everyone have to like you?" exchange slightly over-explains his psychology rather than leaving it subtextual. The banter occasionally flirts with being too uniformly quippy—every line lands, which risks feeling crafted rather than spontaneous. The niece-with-a-mug and chipped-handle gag is clever but slightly stock. Cassian's swift pivot to the vulnerable moth-reveal is well-handled but very efficient—the transformation is small enough to be earned, though it happens fast. The prose is clean and controlled, with occasional excellent images ("a thing he was holding rather than wearing," "insects that impersonate firewood"). The ending's warmth is congruent with the tone throughout. Overall this is well above typical quality—polished, controlled, emotionally intelligent romantic comedy writing. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door yielded before Aya could turn the handle. Beyond it, a stair descended into a round chamber lit by blue whale-oil lamps. The brick walls sweated. Old harpoons hung in the vault like the ribs of some overturned leviathan, and beneath them, upon a black marble plinth, stood the Scythan coffer: green bronze bound with baleen, its surface crawling with letters that made Aya’s eyes water. Mara Voss sat beside it, cleaning her nails with a clasp knife. The guild mistress wore no irons. No constable stood behind her. A whalebone-handled revolver lay across her knee, and six bodyguards occupied the shadows, their brass-and-steel pressure carbines trained on the stair. Voss trusted weapons one could oil. Aya had always admired that about her. “You took your time,” Voss said. Katra stopped one step below Aya. “We paused to admire the civic architecture.” “And you, Simeon?” Simeon’s gaze moved from muzzle to muzzle. “I was considering how frequently I am ignored.” *Tick*, said the watch in his waistcoat. *Tick. Tick.* Aya forced herself down the remaining steps. Behind her eyes, the immateria stirred, cold and vast, like eels turning beneath winter ice. One syllable would open it. She crushed the impulse. What answered her might not distinguish Voss’s guards from Katra, or Katra from Aya herself. “The *Gazette* said you were taken at four,” Aya said. “I was.” “In chains.” “Very handsome ones.” Voss folded the knife. “The magistrate’s cells have a tariff. By breakfast I was home, and by luncheon every ambitious little rat in Morska had shown its whiskers.” Aya looked at the coffer. The ward around it tasted of iron and snow. “So there was no vacancy.” “Only a door left open, and three people stupid enough to walk through it.” Voss smiled. “You should never believe a rumour that flatters you, Wren.” The guild name, spoken in that room, made Aya feel suddenly childish. Wren of the black canals. Wren who could call antlered things out of a mirror. Wren had seemed so much more substantial than Aya Bellamont in her silk parlours, being lectured on marriage by women with dead eyes. “Bring her here,” Voss said. Two guards advanced. Katra’s hand slipped beneath her coat. “Don’t,” Aya said. “I wasn’t going to.” “You were thinking loudly.” A carbine’s pump clicked. Simeon shut his eyes. Aya put her wrists together. A guard bound them with waxed cord and pushed her to her knees before Voss. Another hooked two fingers beneath her mask and tore it away. The leather took skin from her cheek. For the first time, Voss’s expression altered. “Oh,” she said softly. “Oh, you foolish child.” The lamps seemed to burn lower. Aya saw it all with horrible clarity: the police sketch, the illustrated broadsheets, her father’s long face above a notice of disownment. Thief was imprisonment. Traitor to her class was amusement. Witch was the rope, and her mother’s shoes swinging above a crowd suddenly became Aya’s own. Voss took her chin in one hand. “Lady Aya Bellamont. Your father signs the warrants that send my people to the hulks.” “Yes,” Aya said. “And you’ve been robbing me beside them.” “Not beside them. Better than them.” Katra made a small, strangled sound that might have been laughter. Voss released her. “Take the other two.” Katra and Simeon were disarmed and bound without ceremony. Katra’s knives made a bright little heap on the plinth. Simeon surrendered a screwdriver, two lock picks and a boiled sweet. Nobody touched the watch. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* “Separate cells,” Voss said. “We’ll decide in the morning whether the rendering vats can manage quality.” “If you kill me,” Aya said, “you’ll be throwing away a fortune.” Voss sighed. “Ransom. How very genteel.” “My father sits on the Admiralty Council. The spring whaling fleet sails under his seal. Coin, ships, pardons, a customs launch that develops blindness—you may choose.” “Your father let your mother hang.” The words found the place beneath Aya’s ribs that no guard had touched. “For witchcraft,” she said. “Not for embarrassment.” “And this isn’t witchcraft?” Voss gestured at Aya’s bound hands. “Shall I describe to his lordship what came out of your summoning circle at the Gannet Street job?” Aya’s mouth went dry. There it was: not exposure as a thief, but exposure as her mother’s daughter. Her nights in the guild had not been an escape from the scaffold. They had been a procession towards it. Still, she kept her voice level. “Then you have a choice. My name in a police court buys you one morning’s sensation and a regiment in the guildhouse by nightfall. My name in your keeping buys you years of leverage.” “If Bellamont pays.” “He won’t pay because he loves me. He’ll pay because my brother is engaged to a minister’s daughter, because my father’s enemies collect scandals, and because he cannot have a Bellamont tried beside dock-rats and lamp-men.” “Charming family,” Katra said. “Be quiet,” Aya and Voss said together. Voss studied her. Aya could hear the coffer’s ward humming, a note below hearing. She could hear Simeon’s watch. Each tick pared another shaving from her life. “And your companions?” Voss asked. “Included in the price.” “They came to steal my guild.” “They came with me. The distinction matters to me. It need cost you nothing.” Voss’s thumb rested on the revolver’s hammer. Aya thought of the auction rooms where her father bought paintings: that same stillness while a person decided what an object was worth. At last Voss leaned back. “Paper,” she said. “Three cells. And a messenger with clean boots. Her ladyship has a letter to write.” Aya breathed. It was not rescue. It was barely reprieve. Her secret was out, and even survival would make a possession of her: Voss’s, her father’s, perhaps the law’s. There would be no returning unchanged to either masked canals or sunlit lecture rooms. She had come to steal a throne. Instead she had sold her name for one more dawn. As the guards pulled them upright, Simeon’s watch ticked on, loud as a gallows drum. Behind them, inside the Scythan coffer, something ticked back.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the prompt with strong discipline: no fight scene, third-person past tense, heavy dialogue, internal monologue, gothic-Victorian texture, and the required beats (capture, unmasking, hostage negotiation, dread of exposure). The whalepunk worldbuilding is carried economically through details—whale-oil lamps, baleen-bound coffer, harpoon ribs, brass-and-oil weapons—rather than exposition. Voss is a well-drawn antagonist whose menace comes through competence and dry wit rather than villainy. Aya's negotiation is the highlight: her leverage is class-based and plausible, and the mother's hanging gives her stakes genuine weight. Katra and Simeon are thin but serviceable; Simeon's watch is a nice recurring motif, and the final "something ticked back" is an effective hook. Prose is controlled, occasionally aphoristic ("Traitor to her class was amusement. Witch was the rope"). Minor flaws: some lines flirt with cleverness over substance ("I was considering how frequently I am ignored"), the guards are furniture, and the resolution arrives slightly quickly and conveniently—Voss capitulates within one scene. But the reprieve is framed as a loss, avoiding an unearned happy ending.
