+ Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By supper, JT had almost talked himself out of it. That was the useful thing about the lodge: it gave a person jobs. There was firewood to stack, rifles to wipe down, the propane refrigerator to coax into lighting. Ordinary work made ordinary thoughts. By the time the potatoes were frying, the clearing had begun to seem like something he might have invented between one bootlace and the next. Eli Boucher, their guide, did not help with the work. Usually Eli talked as if silence cost him money. He told stories about hunters who got turned around half a mile from camp, about bear in the dump, about winters so cold the lake ice boomed like cannon fire. Now he stood beside the woodpile with his hands in his jacket pockets, watching the trees. “You going to wear a hole in my yard?” Dad called. Eli looked over. “You get that meat hung?” “Like always.” Eli’s gaze moved toward the meat shed, then quickly away. “Good.” He came to the door when Dad called him for supper, but he wouldn’t sit down. He wouldn’t take coffee, either. “You should make it a short trip this year,” he said. Dad lowered his fork. “That so?” “Be gone before the moon’s full.” Mike glanced at Dad, waiting to see whether this was a joke. “Full moon’s Friday,” Dad said. Eli’s eyes shifted to JT. For one alarming second, JT was certain he knew about the clearing—knew what Dad had almost done, or what JT had only imagined him doing. “All right,” Eli said. “What happens Friday?” Dad asked. “Nothing, if you’re gone.” Then he went out, letting the screen door slap behind him. JT found him by the generator shed, unlocking his truck. “What did you mean in there?” JT asked. Eli kept his back turned. “You heard me.” “Dad’s not going to leave. We just got here.” “No,” Eli said. “They generally don’t.” A gust moved through the spruce tops. From the meat shed came a small, sticky sound, as though something hanging inside had shifted on its hook. JT swallowed. “Did something happen to that caribou we shot?” Eli finally looked at him. “Did it run?” JT shook his head. Something passed across the guide’s face. Not surprise. Resignation, maybe. “You stay inside after dark,” Eli said. “And if you hear somebody calling you, make sure you see them before you answer.” “Who would be calling?” Eli got into the truck. “That’s what I mean.” His taillights jolted down the lane and vanished among the trees. Dad took the news of his departure badly, then decided not to take it seriously at all. “Man spends enough winters alone, every sound starts meaning something,” he said. “He’ll be back in the morning.” “And if he isn’t?” Mike asked. “Then I save myself some money.” JT said nothing. He could have told them about the clearing then. He could have asked whether either of them remembered standing there, empty-handed, while the animal breathed. Instead he pushed a cold potato around his plate and listened to the refrigerator tick. He woke at 2:13 with the strange conviction that he had slept for several days. Mike was snoring in the other bed. Beyond him, the window was filled with moonlight so white it looked photographic. JT lay still, trying to identify what had woken him. The generator had stopped. It never stopped before five. Somewhere below, wood knocked gently against wood. Once. Again. He went downstairs in his socks. The kitchen smelled of cold grease and rifle oil. On the wall calendar, Friday’s little printed moon was a perfect white circle. He crossed to the window without deciding to. His father stood in the yard. He wore long underwear and wool socks. His hair was flattened on one side, and his shoulders were bare to the moonlight. In front of him, close enough to touch, stood the animal from the clearing. There was no reason JT should have known it was the same one. He knew anyway. Its chest rose and fell. Each breath smoked briefly around its muzzle. Dad lifted one hand toward it, slowly, exactly as he had before. His lips were parted. He might have been praying. JT raised his fist to strike the window. From the bedroom off the kitchen came his father’s snore: a clogged, familiar rumble, followed by the hitch and snort that always preceded him turning over. JT’s fist stopped an inch from the glass. He looked toward the dark hallway. Then back into the yard. The man out there was still standing with the caribou, but the animal had turned its head toward the lodge. Its eyes caught no light. They were only two smooth, dark places in its face. Bedsprings creaked behind JT. “JT?” his father called sleepily. “That you?” In the yard, the other man lowered his hand. Then he beckoned. JT felt the cold brass of the dead bolt against his palm. He looked down and saw his fingers curled around it. He did not remember reaching for the door.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This continuation succeeds at nearly everything it attempts. The prose is disciplined and King-like: short declarative sentences, concrete physical detail (the propane refrigerator, the meat shed, the dead bolt's cold brass), and dread built through omission rather than declaration. The introduction of Eli Boucher as a warning-figure is a classic but well-executed move; his dialogue is clipped and evasive in a way that feels authentic to a taciturn guide rather than expository. "No. They generally don't" is an excellent line—economical, chilling, and character-revealing. The second half escalates well. The 2:13 a.m. waking, the stopped generator, the knocking wood, the calendar's printed moon—all accumulate convincingly. The doppelgänger reveal (the father snoring inside while a second father stands in the yard) is the story's payoff, and it lands: the detail that JT "shouldn't" know it's the same caribou but knows anyway deepens the unreliability of his perception, exactly as the prompt requested. The final image—his hand on the dead bolt without remembering reaching for it—is a strong, earned ending that pays off the earlier clearing scene and Eli's warning about answering when called. Weaknesses are minor. Eli's abrupt departure is slightly convenient as a plot device, a stock "superstitious local flees" beat. The doppelgänger is a familiar trope, and readers of horror will see the shape of the ending coming, though the execution keeps it fresh. A few sentences ("moonlight so white it looked photographic") flirt with overreach without quite crossing into purple. The mother's absence is unaddressed, though the original text doesn't establish one, so this is forgivable. Dialogue is functional and mostly strong, though Dad's dismissal of Eli ("I save myself some money") is a touch stock. The piece maintains the unreliable-narrator ambiguity perfectly: we never learn whether anything supernatural occurred, whether JT is hallucinating, or what the thing in the yard wants. The isolation of JT's perspective—unable to confide in his family—is preserved and deepened. Word count is roughly on target. Tone is consistent with the seed chapter. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hell is Other Demons At seven in the morning—an affectation, since Hell had no mornings and refused to import them—Lucifer Morningstar made two cups of coffee. He drank one at his window. Below, the infernal city smoked in an orderly fashion. The damned queued for judgment with the patient irritation of people who suspected there would be forms. The second cup cooled on his desk. At nine, his steward, Vax, entered with the schedule and a fresh hole in his sleeve. “Petitions at ten. Inspection of the lakes at eleven. The Furies are threatening industrial action. And Lady Lilith is here.” Lucifer turned a page. “Armed?” “Not excessively.” “Show her in.” Lilith entered without being shown. She wore dark green and carried a scorched leather purse smelling of rain, supermarkets, and an old house fire. Among its contents were a saint’s tooth, a blue marble, three buttons, a ticket to Birmingham, and several objects best not asked about. “You look tired,” she said. “I’m immortal.” “Those aren’t opposites.” She put a brass key on his desk. “Your spare.” “Keep it.” “We’re off.” They were. Their arrangement had outlasted kingdoms, plagues, and several sincere attempts at renovation. Last month she had visited to kill him. Last week she had come to return a book she had not borrowed. “We are frequently off,” Lucifer said. “It has never affected the locks.” “It affects mine.” “Your house has teeth.” “Only when I’m upset.” She had also brought a curse for his seal. One of her daughters had cursed a banking executive, and the curse had been stopped at the border for insufficient specificity. “He has four yachts,” Lilith said. “How specific does one need to be?” Lucifer read the paperwork. “You want his mirrors to show him as other people see him?” “Just the bathroom mirror.” “Moderation. How unlike you.” He sent Vax to find the seal. “Slowly,” he added, while Lilith examined the dead fern. At ten, they heard petitions. A duke requested permission to torment his enemies above quota. An angel, misfiled but polite, asked for directions. A damned emperor complained that eternity was disproportionate to three small wars. “Two,” said Lucifer. “Two?” “Small wars. The third was quite ambitious.” Lilith sat near him, correcting clauses, finding a loophole for the angel, and advising the emperor to stop smiling. By eleven, the Furies had occupied Reception. Their demands concerned workload, blood quality, and the increasing use of “stakeholders.” Lucifer offered a committee. Lilith offered better blood. They accepted the blood, agreed to higher productivity, and ate the committee. “That went well,” Lucifer said. “You always say that when no one you like has died.” At noon, they ate above the Lake of Fire. Below, two demons in overalls held a sign reading TEMPORARILY OUT OF ORDER while souls floated with embarrassed expressions. Lilith took an apple pastry from her purse. It was slightly squashed. “You shouldn’t keep food beside a saint’s tooth,” Lucifer said. “He was a glutton. He doesn’t mind.” She divided the pastry exactly. Lucifer noticed; he had once divided an empire and made a worse job of it. “Why keep these things?” he asked, touching the ticket to Birmingham she had set beside her plate. “They were going to be thrown away.” Below them, a sinner discovered the lake was working again. In the afternoon, they inspected Customer Experience, a new department Lucifer wanted closed. Its waiting room contained uncomfortable chairs, old magazines, and a television fixed slightly too high. “This is petty,” he said. “The best things are,” said Lilith. A demon demonstrated the hold music. After forty seconds, Lucifer approved the budget. They did not discuss the empty rooms in his palace, or the rooms in hers that bit visitors. They spoke of drainage, sedition, and whether mint in the fountains had been a mistake. “You liked the mint,” he said. “I liked that you liked it.” He looked at her. She looked at the fountains. Vax returned at dusk with the seal. Lilith stamped the curse and picked up her purse. “There is a dinner,” Lucifer said. “There usually is.” “Belial will attend.” “Then I’ll need a drink.” “He’ll discuss his boat.” “Two drinks.” She came. By dessert, she had persuaded three archdemons to finance their own rebellion and Belial to apologize to his wife. Lucifer laughed once, startling a minor duke into swallowing his fork. At midnight, they returned to his study. The brass key remained on the desk. So did the second coffee, cold and filmed over. Lilith looked at it, then at him. “You could have made tea,” she said. “I wasn’t expecting you.” “No.” She slipped the key into her purse, among the buttons, tooth, and small mortal disasters. Then she tipped the cold coffee into the dead fern. “Make fresh,” she said. Outside, Hell continued with admirable efficiency. Somewhere, other demons screamed. Lucifer went to put the kettle on, which was not reconciliation, exactly, but had the useful advantage of requiring two cups.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of the brief: a day-in-the-life of Lucifer and Lilith during an "off again" phase, with Gaiman-esque understatement, dry wit, and the mundane-bureaucratic Hell juxtaposed against domestic estrangement. The structure is disciplined—a clear chronological day (7 a.m. to midnight), each scene doing double duty as both infernal administration and relationship subtext. The two cups of coffee bookend is a well-managed motif: the second cup made "just in case," cold by the end, and the final kettle line landing the emotional resolution without ever stating it. The prose is deliberately flat and clipped, which suits the irony. Lines like "I'm immortal." / "Those aren't opposites." and "Only when I'm upset" (about the house with teeth) are genuinely funny and characterful. The purse inventory—saint's tooth, blue marble, ticket to Birmingham—is a lovely Gaiman-style detail, and the payoff ("They were going to be thrown away") quietly reveals Lilith's hoarding tenderness. The curse-approval subplot (mirrors showing the banker as others see him, "Just the bathroom mirror") is excellent dark comedy with moderation as a character note. Weaknesses: the piece occasionally over-relies on the one-line-quip rhythm, so a few exchanges feel like a string of jokes rather than conversation (the Belial boat exchange is the most formulaic). The Furies/committee beat is funny but slightly stock. Some images are underdeveloped—the mint-in-fountains thread is charming but the emotional beat ("I liked that you liked it") is the closest the piece comes to telling rather than showing, though it's earned enough by context. The emperor "two small wars" gag is predictable. The ending's warmth is modest and earned; no incongruent positivity. Characters are nuanced within a narrow tonal range—Lilith in particular is well-drawn through objects and choices rather than exposition. Coherence is high, no meandering, voice consistent throughout. Imagery is sparse by design; the piece favors wit over description, which is appropriate but caps its descriptive ceiling slightly. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
Before dawn, my cell smelled of wet plaster and the onions frying in the guardroom. I woke with iron on my tongue, though nothing had bled. Beyond the wall, mallets knocked and winches screamed as sailors worked the ropes of the Flavian amphitheatre’s awnings. Rome was preparing to be comfortable while it decided whether I lived. On the morning before every fight, I took the single grain of barley from the pouch at my neck. It had travelled from Dacia sewn into my belt, and seven years of sweat had polished it black. I touched it to my forehead, my lips, and the floor, then put it back. Aufidius thought it a charm against death. My mother had only said that seed remembers its field. My name was Zoltes. The notices painted beside the wine shops called me DACUS, with eleven victories painted underneath in red. I had seen apprentice boys spit when I passed and grown men mouth that name as though I were a horse whose legs they admired. Breakfast was barley mash and beans, eaten from wooden bowls while the trainer walked between us, tapping his staff against his calf. He called us his barley-men and loved us in the way a man loves good tools. Sabbio pushed his food around and asked whether the arena sand got into a dead man’s eyes. No one answered. Beyond the gate, a seller of cushions was already crying his wares. Aufidius came at sunrise with the physician. He was soft-bellied, perfumed, and forever complaining that gladiators ate better than senators. The Greek pressed my old scars, smelled my breath, and told me to piss into a bronze bowl. While he held it to the light, Aufidius licked his stylus. “Priscus wants you sound,” he said. “Win tomorrow and I will speak to him about the rudis.” The wooden sword of freedom. He had first promised to speak of it two summers before. I watched him write me down as healthy and thought how easily wax took the shape of a lie. At the second hour he led four of us through the streets to Priscus’s house. We wore no chains. Aufidius said dignity encouraged wagers; besides, where could we run that Rome did not reach? Heat already rose from the basalt. Cartwheels battered it, awning cords snapped, and somewhere a knife-seller praised his blades in the voice of a tragic actor. Sausage smoke, fish sauce, sour wine, dung, and the sharp ammonia from a fuller’s jars thickened the air. A beggar shook a cup at my escort. Seeing my scars, he put it away. Near the grain hall, citizens shoved and argued beneath an official’s bored gaze. One waved his token and shouted that Egyptian ships were late; another said the emperor’s wars had made every loaf dearer. Above us, new marble shone. Dacian gold had built Trajan’s forum, Aufidius told me, perhaps expecting gratitude. On the column, little stone Romans burned little stone villages. I searched the prisoners for my father’s face until Aufidius struck my shoulder with his stick. Priscus received us in a garden where water slid over blue glass and a slave waved away flies with a peacock fan. He was financing the games to honour his dead father, though every notice bore his own name larger than the old man’s. He walked around me slowly. “Not the face,” he said. “The crowd likes him as he is.” “The crowd likes blood,” Aufidius replied. “The emperor likes order. And my wife likes shoulders.” They laughed. I looked at a pear tree netted against birds and understood that I was envying fruit. Two clerks nearby discussed Trajan’s coming campaign in Parthia. More legions, one said; more contracts, said the other. Priscus called for wine and observed that victory always returned to Rome, whatever it cost the provinces. Aufidius glanced at me. I kept my face empty. It was the expression that had earned me most of my money. By evening my arms had been measured for new straps and my price agreed upon. Not the price of freeing me: the price of using me. The cena libera took place in the school’s colonnade. Torchlight shook in the dishes. There were roast pork, mullet, honeyed eggs, and wine dark enough to stain the table. Young Sabbio, due to fight for the first time, ate until he wept, then ate again. Spectators leaned between the columns to watch us. A man with rose oil on his fingers wagered twenty denarii that I would not beg. A veiled woman asked whether I understood Latin. “Only when it concerns money,” I said. Aufidius’s smile warned me. Priscus laughed, so I lived unpunished. Later the Greek physician came to rebind my wrist. He smelled of vinegar and rue. His fingers tightened once. “The woman at Ostia,” he murmured. “She remembers a brother named Zoltes.” For seven years I had searched for my sister through slavers’ lists and the memories of dying men. I had made her dead whenever hope became too expensive. Now hope stood in me like a second spine. “What does she cost?” I asked. He looked toward Aufidius. “More than you have. Less than Priscus will win if you please him.” Then he was gone, and a flute player began something thin and Lydian. Beyond the roof, the amphitheatre lifted its pale bulk against the stars. I thought of the rudis, of Ostia’s salt wind, of Priscus’s netted pears. Rome had taken my name and made it useful; it had taken my country and made it ornamental. Perhaps, piece by piece, it would sell me back my life. That night I returned to my cell without touching the barley again. Sabbio vomited in the next room. Somebody sang a song from Syria. I lay listening to the city’s endless grinding and held the pouch through my tunic. Tomorrow the crowd would roar DACUS. Tonight, silently, I said Zoltes, and then my sister’s name. For the first time in seven years, survival was not enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with skill. The scene follows a Dacian gladiator, Zoltes, through the day before a fight—no combat, as instructed—moving from cell to breakfast to a patron's house to the cena libera, giving it a genuine "slice of a larger story" feel with an implied past (his father, his lost sister) and an implied future (tomorrow's fight). The sensory work is excellent and specific: wet plaster and frying onions, basalt heat, sausage smoke and fuller's ammonia, the peacock fan, vinegar and rue on the physician's hands. Rome feels lived-in rather than researched. The political and social texture is woven in naturally—grain shortages, Trajan's Dacian gold and Parthian campaign, the economics of slavery and spectacle, the lanista's hollow promise of the rudis. The detail of Zoltes searching the Column's carved prisoners for his father's face is a standout moment, understated and devastating. The prose is controlled and restrained, with a dry, ironic first-person voice that suits the character ("wax took the shape of a lie," "I was envying fruit"). Dialogue is functional and characterful—Priscus's "my wife likes shoulders" captures elite callousness efficiently. The sister revelation lands well because the narrator admits he "had made her dead whenever hope became too expensive," which is emotionally sophisticated. Minor criticisms: the ending's turn ("survival was not enough") is slightly neat, a touch more resolved than a "slice" strictly requires, though it is earned by the physician's revelation. A few aphoristic lines ("hope stood in me like a second spine") flirt with over-polish. The physician's convenient knowledge of the sister is a small plot contrivance. The word count is somewhat under 1000. But these are quibbles against an otherwise polished, coherent, and moving piece. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 87.5
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper *Sgeir Breac Lighthouse — 12 March 1962* Dear Mum, You can stop picturing me alone on a rock. There are three of us, and the rock is an island at low tide. Esson, the principal, talks chiefly about mince. Jock is twenty and has six jumpers but no toothbrush he will admit to. My room is dry. The post goes when the boat can manage. Every morning I take paraffin up ninety-eight steps. Two five-gallon cans save a journey and skin my palms; one can doubles the climbing. I change my mind daily. Then there is the lens to cover and the brass to do. I have not had time to be lonely. I have put in a postal order for the roof. Alec *Greenock — 30 March* Dear Alec, The roof is holding. The rain at the scullery window is not your department. I have my pension and two mornings at Dunn’s, so send no more orders. Thank you for describing your colleagues. It saves me worrying you have been eaten by seals. I am sending tablet and your father’s wristlets. Don’t use the tablet for sealing parcels. You needn’t keep saying you are all right. It makes you sound like a notice in a shop. Mum *Sgeir Breac — 19 May* Dear Mum, My hands have split at the knuckles. Paraffin gets into the cuts and salt keeps them open. Esson’s salve smells of bicycle tyres and flavours my tea. When the boat cannot land, we carry every bucket and coal bag from the jetty. Yesterday Jock and I did the water: thirty-four buckets up the path, then the stair. The Board’s leaflet shows a keeper polishing the lamp. They should show him with two buckets and his nose running. I have changed my leave to October. Jock wanted the summer, and the extra comes in useful. Alec *Sgeir Breac — 7 August* Dear Mum, The tablet is gone. Jock says he had one piece, which is arithmetically possible. The boat has not landed for five weeks. We have tinned peas, tinned potatoes and a rice pudding Esson is keeping for an occasion. I know the sound Jock makes before he asks for the salt. I go outside to escape them, then come in because my own company is worse. Don’t send another parcel till the boat gets through. Watching is hard enough without wanting something. I did not change my leave for Jock. I could not face everybody at home being kind about the yard. Alec *Greenock — 21 August* Dear Alec, There you are. That was not so difficult. I will not tell you everybody is kind. Some are nosy. You may walk past them; you have practice at stairs. I have told the street you are working. That is all the information they are due. The yard closed on two hundred men, not on your character. Come home in October, not to be inspected and not because I need looking after. I am off to Largs with Cissie Bell, who is poor company but pays for her own tea. I should like to hear your voice where nobody is asking you to do anything. Mum *Sgeir Breac — 19 September* Dear Mum, I am writing because Esson sat beside me until I started. On Sunday the boat came. When MacLeod put your parcel on the jetty I asked him in for tea. He said the tide would not wait. I shouted that he could damn well give me ten minutes. He has a wife and four weans at Mallaig, and I stood there keeping him from them. Afterwards I could not stop shaking. Esson found me on the tower stair with the lens cloth. I had polished the same panel four times. He took it away and I hit the wall, which was at least a change from hurting my hand with buckets. I have not slept properly since Jock was ill and I took his watches. The light never went out. I keep saying that as if it settles the matter. I am frightened of feeling nothing, and then I feel plenty and that is worse. Jock has made tea with three sugars. I am drinking it. Alec *Greenock — 26 September* Dear Alec, I have telephoned the Board from the call box. You can be angry when you are home. Esson had already written, so I am not the only interfering person in the country. I am glad the light stayed lit. I am gladder you wrote. After your father died, I kept my coat on indoors until bedtime. Taking it off meant admitting there was nowhere I had to be. I thought I was sparing you. Perhaps I only taught you that managing was the same as being all right. I am sorry. Do not send money or decide your whole life this week. Drink Jock’s tea. Let the doctor be tiresome. I have been tiresome for sixty-one years and it has done me no harm. Mum *Sgeir Breac — 14 October* Dear Mum, I was angry for half a day. Then the relief man came and I slept fourteen hours, which took the steam out of my principles. The doctor calls it nervous exhaustion. He says the words are for his form; I needn’t wear them. Jock brings his wireless into the kitchen now. Esson says a man can get a fair dinner out of mince and a carrot. I let him tell me. I have asked about the stores depot at Oban. If they will have me, I can paint buoys and be disagreeable in a crowd. If not, I will finish my year and not sign on again. I am coming home first. Alec *Sgeir Breac — 8 January 1963* Dear Mum, The boat comes for me tomorrow. I start at Oban on the fifteenth: less money, a wireless in the workshop, and a landlady who bans wet socks from her range. I think I shall manage. Esson shook my hand and told me I had packed the wrong bag. He was right. Jock gave me his address and underlined it twice. I wrote inside the stores cupboard where the spare washers are, so I left something useful behind. It was not all the bad bits I told you. Some mornings the lens was covered, the stove was drawing, and your tablet was still in the tin, and I was content. I am glad I knew that. I don’t need to stay to prove it. I’ll be home Thursday on the 6.10. Don’t meet the bus. I would like to walk up the street by myself first. Put the soup on. I can tell you the rest when I am sitting down. Your loving son, Alec
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary story is a strong piece of craft. The two voices are distinct and consistent: Alec's letters are clipped, deflective, and dryly humorous ("I have put in a postal order for the roof"), while Mum's are brisk, wry, and quietly perceptive ("It makes you sound like a notice in a shop"). The Scottish working-class register feels authentic without lapsing into phonetic caricature. The plot unfolds gradually and economically: the postal order reveals Alec's guilt over the yard closure and his father's death before he ever names it; the isolation, the boat failures, and Jock's illness accumulate until the crisis on the jetty. The emotional climax — Alec's shaking breakdown and Esson's intervention — is earned through restraint, and Mum's confession about keeping her coat on indoors is a genuinely moving parallel that reframes the whole correspondence. Details are superb and character-revealing: the two-cans-or-one paraffin calculation, the wristlets, the tablet, Jock's underlined address, the washers written inside the cupboard. The show-don't-show discipline is excellent — the yard closure is revealed obliquely, the breakdown rendered through the polished panel and the salt-shaker sound. Minor criticisms: the resolution is perhaps slightly tidy — the Oban depot, the landlady, the soup all arrive a touch conveniently. The doctor's diagnosis is handled with a light touch that mostly avoids cliché but skirts it. Esson and Jock remain functional rather than fully dimensional, seen only through Alec. The final letter's contentment ("I don't need to stay to prove it") is earned, though the closing warmth is a shade more settled than the preceding months might strictly justify. These are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, unsentimental, and quietly powerful. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The hostess leaves her point-of-sale terminal unlocked when she turns to find our menus. The restaurant Wi-Fi is open, the camera above the bar misses the back door, and someone has taped a password beneath the register, its corner curling invitingly toward me. Three findings before my water arrives. I used to collect moments like this. Now companies pay me to find their unlocked doors before someone less scrupulous does. *Reformed*, my lawyer called it. *White hat*, my dating profile says. Both make it sound cleaner than it feels. My objective tonight is not to enumerate weaknesses. It is to have dinner with Mara and determine whether her profile photographs were honest. They were. This is immediately inconvenient. I had prepared for disappointment, not for the small, unguarded smile she gives when she nearly sits at the wrong table. The conversation stalls over drinks. I am composing a harmless question about her work when she frowns at the menu and says fourteen small plates seem “a little light on synergy.” I look up. “Magic?” She looks betrayed by her own vocabulary. Then delighted. By the appetizers, I know her first deck was mono-red. **Lightning Bolt**, because it was beautiful mathematics. **Goblin Guide**, because she liked being fast enough to apologize later. **Monastery Swiftspear**, because once she got ahead, she hated giving the lead back. I file them despite myself. Bolt: directness, efficiency. Guide: speed over secrecy. Swiftspear: momentum, escalation. This is not a personality test, I tell myself, and continue testing her personality. She asks what I play. I admit to control, to too much mana and an unhealthy attachment to saying *not yet*. “Of course,” she says, but she is smiling. Over entrées, she describes her current Commander deck: **Meren of Clan Nel Toth**. **Sakura-Tribe Elder** goes early and willingly. **Grave Pact** makes every loss somebody else’s problem. **Living Death** is her favorite way to spend half the game losing and one terrible turn winning. Meren: patience. Elder: investment through sacrifice. Pact: boundaries enforced at scale. Living Death: faith in recovery. Or she simply likes making her friends sad. There is joy in it, either way. She laughs while describing a six-hour game, and I realize I have not checked the exits in nearly twenty minutes. Then her phone lights up beside her plate. “Sorry,” she says. “Cat sitter.” Her thumb draws a small L across the screen. Four dots. No hesitation. Under the candlelight, the same route shines faintly in the glass. She turns the phone toward me. Her cat is wearing a dinosaur costume. I should say something about the cat. I should ask its name. I should allow one living creature in this restaurant to remain unaudited. “That’s a very trusting unlock pattern,” I say. The warmth leaves her face so quickly I can almost hear a session expire. “Were you watching me unlock my phone?” “No. I mean, yes, but not—” Every explanation in my queue makes it worse. Observation. Shoulder surfing. Pattern complexity. I could turn this date into an incident report without leaving my chair. “I wasn’t trying to invade your privacy,” I offer, which is true and entirely beside the point. “But you did.” The waiter chooses that moment to ask about dessert. We both look at him with such gratitude that he retreats without an answer. I feel the old, stupid impulse to prove the finding. Show her the smudge. Explain the risk. Win the technical point and lose whatever was happening before I opened my mouth. My mouth loads twelve recommendations. I swallow all of them. “You’re right,” I say. “I noticed something and treated that like permission to comment. It wasn’t. I’m sorry.” She turns her phone facedown. “Do you do that with everything?” Yes is the answer. Yes to people whose smiles arrive late, yes to strangers who touch a door before leaning against it, yes to anyone who says *trust me* without understanding what they are requesting. “Yes,” I tell her. “When I was younger, I broke into places because I could. I told myself curiosity was harmless if I didn’t take anything. It took me too long to learn that access itself could be the theft. Now I only do it with permission. Apparently I need the reminder off the clock.” That is more than I planned to disclose on a first date. It is also the first thing I have said all night without rehearsing how it might land. Mara studies me. I resist searching her expression for a decision tree. “For the record,” she says finally, “I’m changing the pattern.” I nod. I do not congratulate her. I do not suggest a passphrase. This may be the most sophisticated security control I have ever implemented. Her mouth twitches. “Also, for the record, that was a very **Thoughtseize** way to flirt.” Thoughtseize: information obtained by reaching where you were not invited. File under *accurate*. Also under *she is joking again*. We order dessert. By the time the check arrives, she has told me about the worst commander game she ever won and the best one she ever lost. I have told her almost nothing about firewalls. The terminal by the hostess stand is still unlocked. The password is still beneath the register. The world remains beautifully, catastrophically full of holes. Outside, Mara asks whether I am free Thursday. I say yes before I can model all the ways it could go wrong. Her smile is not a vulnerability. My hope is not an exploit vector. For once, I let something stay open without calling it a weakness.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly executed piece that hits nearly every prompt requirement with precision. The first-person internal monologue voice is consistent and distinctive: clipped, analytical, filtering romance through security terminology ("session expire," "decision tree," "incident report"). The hacker mindset is established immediately through environmental scanning in the opening, and the MTG fandom is woven in organically as both plot device and characterization tool — the protagonist "files" deck choices as personality data, which is a clever formal conceit that mirrors his compulsive auditing. The phone unlock pattern moment lands as required, and the fallout is handled with genuine emotional intelligence. The protagonist's apology is specific and self-aware rather than generic, and Mara's response ("that was a very Thoughtseize way to flirt") is a standout line — it resolves tension through the shared fandom rather than through easy forgiveness, which feels earned. The closing image ("I let something stay open without calling it a weakness") ties the theme together without over-explaining. Weaknesses: the "file under" device is used a few too many times and edges toward gimmickry. Mara is somewhat thinly sketched — she exists mostly as a mirror for the protagonist's arc, and her quick forgiveness of a genuinely creepy observation is slightly convenient. Some lines ("Her smile is not a vulnerability") flirt with preciousness. The prose occasionally leans on its own cleverness, and the ending is tidier and warmer than the situation might realistically produce — a second date offered minutes after being surveilled strains believability slightly. Still, the transformation is small enough (a moment of restraint, not a personality overhaul) that it mostly holds. Dialogue is sparse but effective; the monologue dominates as instructed. Imagery is functional rather than lush, which suits the voice. The piece is coherent, economical, and never meanders. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It There are six acceptable ways to ask Eli Parker to pass the thermometer, and by the time I rank them, the water has cooled another degree. *Could you hand me the thermometer?* sounds like I’m a hotel concierge. *Thermometer?* sounds like the word is too heavy to lift. *Can I use that?* implies he’s hogging school equipment, which he isn’t. He sets it between us. I could just pick it up. I pick it up. My eighth-grade science group is testing which insulator keeps water warm the longest. Rina is wrapping cups. Marcus is supposed to be timing us, but he has discovered that aluminum foil makes an excellent hat. Eli and I are taking temperature readings every two minutes, which means I have been assigned a recurring event with him. This would be convenient if I were a different person. I like the project. Heat transfer has rules. Warm water loses energy to cooler air; insulation slows it; you change one variable and control the rest. My brain has approximately forty variables and no control group. While Rina explains the rubric, my pencil wanders into the margin of my lab notes. Doodling gives my hands a problem with instructions. I draw Rina as a stopwatch with legs, because she keeps saying “time check” as if she invented time. Marcus becomes a glue stick with its cap missing. Eli takes longer. Finally I draw a paper crane, like the one he folded from scrap paper in September. I don’t know why I remember that. Actually, I do, which is annoying. Eli isn’t doing anything suspiciously wonderful. He’s labeling axes and drying a water spot with his hand. Somehow this is worse. If he were obviously amazing, I could admire him from a distance. Instead, he says “thanks” when I pass him the pencil, and I have to spend the next minute analyzing whether my “mm-hm” sounded rude. Inside my head, I am excellent at conversations. I have timing. I ask follow-up questions. I say, “That’s interesting—what made you think of that?” and people tell me interesting things. Out here, sentences get stuck behind my teeth and come out as “yeah.” I review my options. *Did you see the moon last night?* He has a Saturn sticker on his notebook, so space is a reasonable topic. Except it was cloudy, and I didn’t see the moon. I can’t base a relationship on false astronomical data. *Your handwriting is really neat.* It is. His fours have open tops. But maybe he doesn’t want his handwriting evaluated by someone he has shared forty words with, thirty-two of which were temperatures. *This project is kind of fun.* Then he’ll know wrapping cups is my idea of fun. It sort of is, but he doesn’t need that information yet. I could say nothing. Silence can look calm, bored, shy, annoyed, or secretly plotting something. There’s no way to control the interpretation. I adjust my face. Was I frowning? Now I’m smiling at a thermometer. I stop smiling. Eli’s elbow is four inches from mine. If I move, will he think I’m avoiding him? If I don’t, am I sitting weirdly close? My hand is just lying on the table. What do hands usually do? Desperate is what I call any visible sign that I want something. Weird is anything I do that I haven’t already watched someone else do successfully. Between them, those rules eliminate most available behavior. I’m exhausted, and there are still twelve minutes left. “Two minutes,” Eli says. I jump, then pretend I was reaching for my pencil. My pencil is already in my other hand. “Do you want to read it this time?” he asks. Inside: *Yes, because the bulb should stay submerged and my eyes should be level with the liquid column, and also because you asked, which makes my stomach do something unscientific.* “You can,” I say. He nods. “Sixty-one point eight.” I write it down. Numbers, at least, mean exactly what they say. At the next reading, he holds the thermometer toward me. “Your turn.” “Fifty-nine point seven,” I manage. Quiet, but accurate. He leans over to check my data table, and his gaze stops in the margin. My whole body becomes an eraser. “Is that Rina?” I could say no. I could say it is a stopwatch with legs for unrelated scientific reasons. “Maybe,” I say. He grins. “And that’s definitely Marcus.” Across the table, Marcus’s foil hat slides over one eye. “Unfortunately,” I say, and Eli laughs. Then he points to the crane. “Who’s that?” There are twelve exits from this moment and all of them are on fire. “You,” I say. My voice comes out almost normal. “You folded one in September. It was…a good crane.” For one terrible second, he just looks at me. I prepare to transfer schools. Then he smiles. “Thanks. I’ve been working on my crane technique.” It’s a joke. A small, easy joke, offered like something I’m allowed to pick up. I laugh. It’s one second late and sounds like a hiccup, but he doesn’t appear to file an incident report. “You notice a lot,” he says. I have four possible answers, three of which are alarming. I choose, “I guess.” The timer beeps. Rina asks for data. Marcus announces that his control cup has “no drip,” and nobody knows what he means. Eli turns back to the table as if we just had a conversation. Maybe we did. I could ask about the Saturn sticker now. Instead, I think of something useful: *Do you want to make the graph with me tomorrow?* Relevant. A natural answer. No need to mention his handwriting, the moon, or September. I rehearse it twice. Then I stop. “Do you want to make the graph tomorrow?” It comes out too fast, and *graph* catches in my throat. “Sure,” Eli says. “That’d be good.” Not proof of anything. Just a plan. I can think of seven ways I could have said it better. For once, I don’t choose one. I record the next temperature in my lab notes. My handwriting is shaky, but I leave it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sharply executed piece of internal monologue that hits nearly every requirement of the prompt. The narrator's voice is articulate, wry, and precise in her head while collapsing to "yeah," "maybe," and "you" aloud — exactly the requested gap between internal and external expression. The overthinking is rendered through concrete, escalating micro-decisions (ranking six ways to ask for a thermometer, auditing her own "mm-hm," wondering what hands usually do), which shows the anxiety rather than labeling it. The definitions of "desperate" and "weird" as self-imposed rules are a standout — economical and psychologically true. The science-project setting is used structurally, not just decoratively: the controlled-variable language mirrors her lack of a control group over her own thoughts, and the recurring two-minute readings give the piece a natural rhythm and a reason for repeated proximity. The doodle subplot gives the plot a small engine — the crane drawing creates a moment of exposure that resolves gently and plausibly. Eli is characterized minimally but effectively ("I've been working on my crane technique"), and his low-stakes joke is a believable, appropriately scaled kindness rather than a romantic miracle. The ending is well-calibrated: she still flubs the line, he says "sure," and she declines to rewrite it in her head. This is a small, earned shift, not a transformation — no confession, no sudden confidence. The final shaky handwriting left uncorrected is a tidy closing image that embodies the theme without moralizing. Weaknesses are minor. Some of the one-liners ("My whole body becomes an eraser," "I prepare to transfer schools") are polished to the point of feeling writerly rather than authentically eighth-grade — the narrator occasionally sounds like a professional humorist. The piece runs slightly under the 1000-word seed, though not egregiously. Marcus's foil hat is a stock comic beat. These are quibbles; the prose is clean, the pacing tight, the emotional register specific and honest. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 87.0
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Rehearsing Rejection The black sweater says I don’t care whether she stays. The blue shirt says I care, but could survive being laughed at. I hold both up while, through the wall, the neighbor’s television murmurs a man, a woman, laughter flattened to a cough. If Mara says, “I can’t do this,” I’ll say, “You could have told me before I dressed for it.” If she says, “You’re too much,” I’ll say, “Only when you’re not enough.” Too good. I try indifference: “Sure. Whatever you need.” Its cruelty pleases me until I imagine her looking relieved. At 6:12 she texts: *Might be ten minutes late. Booked the quiet table. Can’t wait to see you.* Ten minutes becomes a door closing slowly. I read “quiet” as private, no scene, somewhere I’ll be too embarrassed to cry. Then “can’t wait” opens me so fast I sit on the bed. There it is, the stupid, sacred warmth. I press the phone to my sternum, helping the words through. Perhaps she means it. Perhaps warmth makes bad news easier. I choose black. My oldest friend, my lover of three weeks, has been distant since Sunday: three unanswered hours, a goodnight without the heart, dinner moved from Tuesday to Friday. Never mind that she called, that she sounded exhausted and asked twice whether Friday would hurt me, that I said no because no sounded lovable. I’ve converted my generosity into evidence against her. She should have known. By 6:30 I’m brilliant in the restaurant I haven’t entered. “You make everything about your fear,” she says. “And you make disappearing a personality trait.” “I never asked you to need me like this.” “I didn’t ask you to let me.” My eyes burn with the injustice of lines I wrote for her. Under the anger, something small begs: don’t say any of it, just sit beside me. I hate that small thing. I give her a colder face. My therapist calls this fortune-telling, as if it’s scarves and coins. “Notice you’re having the thought.” Noticed. There it goes, driving off with my body in the passenger seat. I can identify the pattern once it’s over. Before it happens, I call it preparation. The television swells: “—don’t—” and the rest is swallowed by the wall. I laugh once, because of course. At 6:41 Mara texts again: *Leaving now. I have your sweater. Also: I miss you. Not a complaint. Just miss you.* I read it three times. First, I believe her so completely my mirrored face looks young and frightening. Second, I hear the apology underneath. Third, I wonder whether “not a complaint” means she’s been complaining to someone else. My hands stop shaking, which feels like betrayal. Need should not be so easy to feed. I practice “You’ve seemed distant” in a voice with no hook. Then: “If you want out, be decent enough to say so.” Then: “Actually, I need space.” This fills me with power and desolation. I could send it now, leave her holding my sweater downstairs while I become the person who ended things, the person no one can catch wanting. I delete *Okay*. I delete *Can’t wait either*. I send *See you soon*: a balanced meal of a message. Her knock comes at 6:58. She’s early after warning me she’d be late, hair damp, my sweater over one arm. When she sees me, her whole face changes. Not carefully. That undoes me: it looks like something happening to her. “There you are,” she says. “Can I?” I nod, and she hugs me. “I’ve missed you.” I press my face into her shoulder; if I speak she’ll hear six conversations. Her coat is cold, her hand warm between my shoulder blades. For one clean moment: pressure, rain, lemon soap. I want to climb inside and nail the door shut. Then I think: she is relieved because I made this easy. She pulls back but holds my wrists. “Before we go—I’ve been in my head, and I let it turn into silence. I’m sorry. You didn’t do anything wrong.” She breathes. “I got scared because I love you. Because this matters. I want us to keep going, if you do.” Love lands without a place to go. It hurts. I had been so ready to defend the room that I forgot to furnish it for anyone staying. “Oh,” my mind says, while my mouth says nothing. She loves me. She loves me now, her face still open. She loves me because she feels guilty. She loves me because she has not yet seen the version of me standing behind this one, composed entirely of teeth. Here is where I should notice. I notice. I also start assembling tomorrow: she will replay her own tenderness and find it excessive; I will ask whether she meant it; she will say yes less quickly; I will hear the difference. The prediction arrives with such intelligence, such detailed weather, that dismissing it feels negligent. Mara brushes rain from my sleeve, though there is none. “We don’t have to talk about everything tonight,” she says. “I just didn’t want you sitting across from me wondering.” But I haven’t been sitting across from her. I’ve been sitting across from every way she might leave. The thought is so clear I nearly say it. Then resentment rushes in to save me: how convenient, that she gets to be scared and I get to be reassuring. How dare she make me wait and arrive with exactly the right words. I could punish her for rehearsals she never attended. I could make her prove it again. Instead, when she asks if I still want dinner, I say yes. It comes out small. She hears yes anyway. Through the wall, the neighbor’s television gives one last muffled burst of laughter. In my head, Mara is already saying, “This was a mistake,” and I am already answering, “I knew you’d say that.” I take her hand before I can make her prove she means it. The rehearsal continues. So do we.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong piece of interior-driven fiction. The narrative stays almost entirely inside the protagonist's head as instructed, cycling through imagined confrontations, preemptive resentments, brief moments of felt love, and immediate doubt. The mechanics of BPD cognition—splitting, fortune-telling, converting kindness into evidence against someone—are rendered with precision and without clinical labeling. The imagined dialogues are sharp and genuinely feel rehearsed: "You make everything about your fear" / "And you make disappearing a personality trait" is exactly the kind of polished, cruel repartee a person rehearses. The detail of hating "that small thing" that begs for tenderness captures self-directed resentment beautifully. The therapist reference ("fortune-telling, as if it's scarves and coins") delivers the required limited, selective self-awareness: the narrator can name the pattern only after the fact, and calls it "preparation" beforehand. The actual events counterpoint the fears perfectly: Mara's texts are warm, her apology is direct and loving, and the narrator's inability to receive it ("Love lands without a place to go") is the cognitive dissonance the prompt requested. The three readings of "Not a complaint. Just miss you" is a standout passage. The ending resists false resolution—"The rehearsal continues. So do we"—which is honest and earned. Minor criticisms: the neighbor's television is a slightly over-engineered recurring device; a few lines ("a balanced meal of a message," "composed entirely of teeth") flirt with cleverness that draws attention to the author. The sweater/shirt opening is efficient but a touch mannered. Dialogue is sparse but what exists is believable and natural. The prose is controlled, rhythmic, and largely show-don't-tell, with imagery serving psychology rather than decoration. Emotionally it is both engaging and complex, sustaining tension between hope and sabotage throughout. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The prohibition had acquired the weight of scripture: no Jigen-ryū adept was to meet a Piguaquan fighter outside a sanctioned hall. Kuroda’s master called it wisdom; Liang’s called it survival. Both young men privately called it cowardice. At midnight they entered the ruined temple by different doors. Their schools had feuded for three generations over a killing each side blamed on the other. Kuroda carried that story like an inherited wound; Liang carried Kuroda’s recent insult—“gutter windmilling”—like a splinter. Lamps burned behind broken screens. Twenty spectators ringed the flagged hall: Jigen partisans along the eastern wall, Liang’s companions beneath the western windows. Coins dropped into a bookmaker’s cap. No one wagered on restraint. A spring had split the floor from the northern altar to the southern entrance. Water threaded through it, spreading at the center into a slick ribbon. Kuroda stood east by a leaning pillar, four paces from Liang, who waited west with a fallen bronze bell behind him. Barefoot, as agreed. Empty-handed, as agreed. Everything else belonged to anger. Kuroda bowed with insulting correctness. Liang spat blood from where he had bitten his cheek. Kuroda attacked before Liang’s chin had lifted. Two driving steps brought him to the seam; he cleared it on the third and landed left-foot-forward on the western side, his right fist going straight for Liang’s breastbone. Liang did not retreat. He stepped south with his right foot and turned, letting the fist pass his left side. His left arm lashed upward from the rotation; the back of his hand cracked against Kuroda’s ear. The western watchers howled. Kuroda’s head snapped sideways, but his feet did not tangle. He pivoted toward Liang and lowered his shoulder. Liang, still withdrawing his arm, took the charge high in the chest. He went backward two short steps, angling west, and his heel struck the bell. Its rim gave a dull note. Kuroda’s left fist flicked at Liang’s eyes. Liang slipped it, but the punch was a screen; Kuroda’s right drove into his ribs. Breath burst from him. He dropped beneath Kuroda’s next hook and circled south, toward the doorway. His open left hand swept Kuroda’s reaching wrist aside. Continuing the same circle, he whipped his right forearm across Kuroda’s jaw. Kuroda gave ground eastward, two stumbling paces. His left foot came down in the stream. It slid no farther than a finger’s width. Kuroda bent his knee and caught his balance, but Liang had followed and was already inside his guard. A whipping palm struck his chest; a second, returning along the opposite arc, snapped across his mouth. Kuroda retreated until his heels reached the dry eastern bank. Blood shone on his teeth. “Peasant footwork,” he said. Liang smiled, though his injured ribs made it ugly. “Come inspect it.” Kuroda spat into the water and advanced slowly. The next exchange belonged to him. He stopped chasing Liang’s head. When Liang circled south, Kuroda stepped diagonally to close the arc; when Liang reversed north, Kuroda was there, crowding him with short, punishing fists. A straight left numbed Liang’s lead arm. Kuroda’s shoulder checked him off balance, and a compact punch to the stomach folded him over it. Liang rolled with the impact. His right foot slid back, his hips turned, and his left arm swung so low it nearly brushed the flags. Kuroda, expecting another high backfist, raised his elbow too late. Liang’s forearm hammered into the side of his knee. Kuroda’s leg buckled. He caught himself on one hand, then sprang up before Liang’s follow-up palm could arrive. The palm passed in front of his nose. Kuroda seized that wrist and drove his right fist toward Liang’s throat. Liang twisted with the pull instead of away from it. The fist grazed his collarbone. His forehead struck Kuroda’s cheekbone—an ugly, unadvertised technique—and Kuroda released him. They broke apart, panting. Their shuffling circle had reversed their ground: Kuroda stood west of the stream, a little toward the altar; Liang stood east, toward the doorway, four paces away. Kuroda’s right eye was swelling shut. Liang pressed an elbow to his ribs; deep breaths were no longer available. The bookmaker quietly changed the odds. Liang studied the water, then Kuroda’s damaged leg. He let his shoulders sag. It was only partly pretense. Kuroda saw the opening he wanted. He came west to east in three explosive steps, hiding the weakness in his knee. The first brought him to the seam; the second carried him over. Liang retreated one pace, until his back nearly touched the pillar. On the third step, Kuroda’s left hand feinted high and his right fist began the straight, finishing line he had trusted since childhood. This time Liang did not circle away. He stepped diagonally in, outside Kuroda’s right shoulder. The fist tore past his ear. His near palm guided the wrist outward; his other arm, hanging loose, rose with the turn of his waist. The heel of his palm struck Kuroda beneath the right arm. Kuroda’s momentum carried him onto the blow. At the same instant his rear foot landed in the wet seam and slipped south. His legs split beneath him; the injured knee gave way. He fell sideways, catching the flagstones with one hand. Liang’s return swing stopped a finger above his temple. For several breaths, neither moved. Kuroda’s fingers clawed at the stone. He tried to push himself upright, but his right side would not take air and his knee folded again. Liang’s raised hand trembled. “Do it,” Kuroda whispered. Liang looked around the ring. No one was cheering now. “A debt isn’t paid,” he said, “by giving another old man a grave to visit.” He lowered his arm. Returning to his companions, he crossed the water, slipped, and hopped twice before catching his balance. No one laughed. Kuroda laughed once, painfully, then rolled onto his back. Through the broken roof, rain was erasing the stars. Behind the screens, the bookmaker paid Liang’s people. Kuroda’s supporters blamed the water. Liang did not argue. The old debt had demanded blood; it received only enough to darken the stones.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece fulfills the prompt well: clear third-person narration, both styles depicted authentically (Jigen-ryū's explosive linear offense vs. Piguaquan's circular whipping strikes and angles), the abandoned temple arena with spectators and wagering, and the rivalry backstory. Spatial coherence is a highlight—the stream bisecting the floor, tracked positions east/west, the bell, the pillar, and the climactic slip in the wet seam are all consistently maintained. Fight choreography is legible and mechanically precise. Characterization is economical but effective: Kuroda's arrogance, Liang's earthy pragmatism, the mutual pride. Dialogue is sparse but sharp ("Peasant footwork" / "Come inspect it"), though the final mercy line ("A debt isn't paid by giving another old man a grave to visit") is slightly neat. The ending—mercy without reconciliation, ambiguity preserved (no one cheering, blame deflected to the water)—is earned and tonally consistent. The light ironic touches (the bookmaker changing odds, Liang slipping on the same water) work well. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally leans on fight-narration formula (short declarative sentences, "the exchange belonged to him"), and emotional interiority is thin—mostly conveyed through action, which suits the piece but limits depth. The three-generation feud is told rather than felt. Some phrases ("like an inherited wound") flirt with cliché. Still, this is a disciplined, coherent, and engaging piece with an unusually strong sense of physical logic. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation By my nineteenth day in Seoul, I had learned to bow before I understood why and to hide the glue on my left sneaker beneath the studio’s white tape. Haneul K-pop Academy smelled of disinfectant and new fabric. The other trainees wore shoes that had never been repaired and discussed cafés whose menus I couldn’t afford to read. My scholarship covered tuition, a dorm bed, and one meal daily. It did not cover looking as if I belonged. Back home, on my block, I learned behind a grocery store, on asphalt glittering with bottle glass. In a cypher, you listened until the beat opened a door, then entered with your history: house jack, top-rock, chest pop sharp enough to make somebody shout. Nobody asked you to repeat it. Repetition meant you hadn’t heard anything new. At Haneul, new was another word for wrong. Six of us faced the front mirror in a line, feet on blue tape, two arm lengths apart. Sora stood left of me, Minjun right. Three meters ahead, Instructor Baek watched with her back to the mirror. She had built three generations of idols and was famous for dismantling dancers before deciding which pieces deserved to survive. Her open fan struck her palm: one, two, three, four. The phrase was eight counts. On one, I stepped right with my right foot, arms cutting into a level T. On two, my left foot closed; my right forearm stood vertical before my nose, my left hand pinning that elbow. Three-four repeated the sidestep and close, reversing the frame. Five-six carried me forward—left, then right—into a squat, knees over toes. Seven-eight took me backward the same way. I rose without bouncing and froze with my arms clamped to my ribs. Each repetition ended one meter right of its starting point; then I walked back to my tape. My body considered this an argument. The first time, my arms hit the T, but the impact kept traveling through shoulder, elbow, wrist. A wave. On the *and* after two, my knees supplied a jack. By five, I was moving half a beat early. Sora and Minjun advanced on either side of me like components in one machine; I rolled my chest through the squat. On seven they retreated. Muscle memory crossed my right foot over my left in a top-rock step and carried me forward. Eight found them frozen in a straight line and me half a meter in front of it, my right arm still loose. The fan snapped shut. Its crack stopped the music. Nobody scratched, swallowed loudly, or looked at the clock. Baek crossed the floor and stopped close enough that her fan could have touched my sternum. “You hear the beat before it arrives,” she said in careful English. “That is rare. Your feet are talented.” The fan lifted, pointing at my chest. “Your attitude is not.” “Maybe the beat doesn’t only live where you put it,” I said. Sora stared straight ahead. Minjun’s mouth tightened. I had survived home by refusing to let people mistake quiet for obedience; here, the same reflex made me sound exactly like the arrogant foreigner Baek expected. “I am not asking you to invent another beat,” she said. “I am asking you to stand inside this one without decorating it.” She returned to her place. The fan opened. We walked back to our tape. For the next hour, we repeated the route: one meter right, half a meter forward, half a meter back, then return. On the fifth run, my right heel slid into a heel-toe variation before I knew it had moved. Crack. On the ninth, my chest popped after the frame. Crack. On the twelfth, I reached the squat cleanly, but my eyes sought my reflection instead of the assigned focus above the mirror’s center seam. Crack. “Again.” Sweat darkened the waistband of my practice pants. My thighs shook so violently in the squat that the floor seemed to vibrate. Yet slowly, frighteningly, the phrase entered me. My T stopped waving. My forward steps landed with the bass instead of anticipating it. On the fifteenth run, all six pairs of feet struck the floor together, a single concussion beneath the music. That was when I understood the real danger. Not failure. Failure would send me home with my movement intact and my mother asking about the opportunity. Success was more patient. It could sand off one impulse at a time until I no longer noticed their absence, until every song arranged itself into eight-count cages and every empty floor became a place to await instructions. Near one in the morning, Baek lowered her fan. “Last one,” she said. “Show me you belong in the line.” We reset. Sora to my left, Minjun to my right, Baek three meters ahead. The music began. One: right foot out, arms iron. Two: left foot in, frame exact. Three-four: sidestep, close, reverse. Five-six: left, right, forward into the squat. In the mirror, our six heads descended to the same level. Seven-eight: backward, rise, freeze. I was perfect. For one second, six bodies held one shape, and I could not tell which breath was mine. I could stay there. I could become employable, admirable, safe. Or I could move before stillness became the only language my body trusted. On the silence after eight, I broke formation. My left foot stepped forward into the empty lane between our line and Baek. My right knee softened. The wave I had cut from count one returned through wrist, elbow, shoulder, then spilled into a loose jack. Right foot crossed left; left opened back. Staying on that small patch of floor, I let my shoulders answer the forbidden syncopation. One final chest pop stopped me facing the mirror, half a meter ahead of the others. The fan did not close. Baek looked at me, then at the empty space I had made between precision and whatever came after it. For the first time all night, she waited.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with discipline and craft. The physical choreography is tracked with genuine precision—the eight-count phrase is laid out move by move, spatial displacements are quantified ("one meter right of its starting point"), and the narrator's deviations (the wave through the T, the jack on the "and," the top-rock crossover on seven) are described in terms that a reader can visualize exactly. The collision of street vocabulary (cypher, top-rock, jack, heel-toe, chest pop) with militaristic K-pop training conventions is handled organically rather than as decoration. The class and culture anxiety is economically established early (glue on the sneaker, one meal daily, cafés), and the central thematic tension—success as erasure of authentic movement voice—is articulated in the strongest passage of the piece ("Success was more patient. It could sand off one impulse at a time..."). The instructor Baek is efficiently characterized, and her final silence is a well-judged ambiguous ending that avoids both punishment fantasy and easy vindication. Weaknesses: the dialogue is functional but slightly stiff and on-the-nose ("Your attitude is not" / "Maybe the beat doesn't only live where you put it"). The narrator's back-talk is a familiar beat, and Baek's "dismantling instructor" archetype is well-trodden. The ending's ambiguity—Baek waiting—is earned but flirts with wish-fulfillment; the piece stops just short of it. Some metaphors ("eight-count cages") are apt but the prose occasionally announces its themes rather than letting them emerge. The transformation of the narrator achieving perfect unison by run fifteen is plausible given the hour of drilling, so it doesn't feel unearned. Prose is clean, controlled, largely free of purple excess; sentence rhythm is varied and confident. Emotionally, the piece is more intellectually engaging than viscerally moving, but the fear of self-erasure is genuinely complex.
