Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The courtroom had no ceiling, because testimony goes on long enough without architecture encouraging it. Above the witness box, stars came and went with the discretion of spies. The bailiff, a tall darkness in ceremonial brass, struck the floor with his staff. “FIRST… LOATHE… VERSUS… MORE… OAR. TRESPASS. SUBVERSION. AND SITTING WITHOUT LEAVE.” “First Love,” said the rosy-cheeked plaintiff. “Mora,” said the defendant. “THE CORRECTIONS ARE NOTED,” boomed the bailiff, noting neither. Upon his throne, Dream regarded them. His face was, as usual, a locked door. The door, however, appeared to be considering violence. A clerk read the complaint: that Mora had six times entered a recurring dream prepared by First Love for Max, a schoolboy; had corrupted its wildflowers, its breeze, and its carefully managed emotional weather; and had replaced an improving almost-kiss with paralysis, terror, and the unauthorized consumption of breath. “How does the defendant plead?” “Peckish,” said Mora. Her counsel, a mildewed gargoyle, closed his eyes. “Not guilty, my lord.” First Love gave evidence with his hands folded, as though they might otherwise fidget. “It wasn’t a generic meadow,” he said. “Oxeye daisies. A little yarrow. Breeze from the east, because west made him think of funerals. The girl had to be recognizably his crush, but not so exactly that he’d be embarrassed at school. And the ending required great delicacy.” “An almost-kiss,” said Dream. “A muddled almost-kiss. Hope, panic, tenderness, and just enough uncertainty to survive breakfast.” He blushed. “It was some of my best work.” “And the defendant?” “She came in through the daisies.” “A door is a door,” said Mora. “It was a corolla.” “The botanical question,” said Dream, “is not before me.” Under cross-examination, First Love admitted that fear had not been wholly absent from his original composition. “He was afraid she wouldn’t like him,” he said. “So fear was already established,” said the gargoyle. “Not with teeth.” “My client disputes the suggestion that hope has no teeth.” “Counsel,” said Dream, “will stop helping.” The gargoyle folded his wings and attempted to look billable. The clerk produced Exhibit A, a jam jar containing the original breeze. It sighed when opened. Exhibit B was a daisy, blackened at the edges. Exhibit C, Max’s breath, had been subpoenaed but was required elsewhere and sent a note. First Love identified all three. Mora identified the daisy as a starter. The bailiff summoned the next witness. “MAX… IMUM… DAMAGE.” “Just Max,” said Max, appearing in pajamas and the expression of someone who had not agreed to be evidence. “SO NOTED.” Max described the field. He described lying beside the girl, and the agreeable sense that something important might happen if neither of them did anything too specific. Then she had playfully climbed onto his chest. “And?” said the gargoyle, brightening. “And she changed. There were too many shadows. Her hair kept moving after the wind stopped. I couldn’t get up. She started taking my breath.” “Out of you?” “Well, she wasn’t putting it in.” First Love stared at the floor. Mora looked modestly at her nails, which were long enough to have their own weather. The gargoyle leaned forward. “Did you find my client frightening?” “Yes.” “Confusing?” “She was still sort of… Sophie,” Max said. He looked deeply unhappy about this. “Attractive?” Max hesitated. “That,” said Dream, “is irrelevant.” “Thank you,” said Max. “It is also sustained.” The clerk wrote IRRELEVANT, BUT SUSTAINED, and underlined it. Mora’s defense was brief. She claimed title by ancient practice, necessity, and adverse possession. “Open, continuous, notorious occupation,” said the gargoyle. “You sat on the occupant,” said First Love. “A very old form of tenure,” said Mora. Dream looked at her. She shrugged. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” “You are not a girl.” “A girl’s gotta eat too in the broader ontological sense.” “There are battlefields.” “Noisy.” “Plague beds.” “Rich, but one tires of them.” “Courtiers who dream of being devoured by their own ambitions.” “Stringy.” Somewhere beyond the court, a mad king dreamed that his crown had become a mouth. Elsewhere, a child was falling through the floor of the world. Dream’s attention moved toward these matters and returned. His fingers whitened slightly on the arm of his throne. “How long,” he asked, “has this case been listed?” “Four centuries,” said the clerk. “There was difficulty with service. Mora ate the process server.” “He was delicious,” said Mora. “He was a subpoena.” “Exactly.” The law of the Dreaming was not written in books, although several books present insisted otherwise. Dream consulted none of them. “First Love made the dream,” he said. “Mora invaded it. Neither of you owns Max.” The gargoyle, who had been about to cite *The Night Hag v. A Bedroom in Gdańsk*, put it away. “The field is restored to First Love’s keeping. Max’s breath is restored to Max. Mora will not enter, sit upon, sublet, or garnish any part of the dream.” “Garnish?” said First Love. “She has eaten stranger things.” Something almost like amusement disturbed Dream’s stillness. Every lawyer in the room became alert, as gazelles must when the grass begins to consider movement. “As for appetite: Mora shall dream for six nights. First Love will provide the dream. She will lie in a field of wildflowers. Before her will be set all the breath she can desire. Whenever she leans close to feed, the dream will end in a pleasant confusion of emotions.” Mora’s eyes narrowed. “That is not feeding.” “It is formative.” First Love’s blush deepened. “May there be an almost-kiss?” “If you think it improves the sentence.” “Oh, it would.” Mora turned to her counsel. “Appeal.” “To whom?” asked the gargoyle. She considered the stars, the throne, and the long patient dark behind Dream’s eyes. “I withdraw the question.” “And Max?” asked First Love. “Max will have one night in the same field. Empty. Excellent weather. No one requiring anything of him.” “Can there be a dog?” said Max. Dream paused. “A small one.” Max vanished, smiling. The bailiff lifted his staff. “COURT… IS… ADJOURNED… FOR… LUNCH.” Mora looked up. “Not here,” said Dream.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally well-executed piece of dark comic fantasy. The writer demonstrates strong command of understated humor, courtroom farce, and Sandman-esque characterization of Dream. Strengths: The dialogue is consistently sharp and funny ("Peckish," "Well, she wasn't putting it in," "He was a subpoena." / "Exactly."). Dream's irritation is conveyed through precise, economical images ("a locked door. The door, however, appeared to be considering violence") — excellent show-don't-show. The bailiff's mispronunciations are a good running gag. The resolution — sentencing Mora to experience First Love's dream herself — is clever, mischievous, and exactly the "tempted to mischief" the prompt requested. The Max "small dog" beat is a perfect closing grace note. The prose is lean, per the prompt's instruction to use descriptives sparingly, and the pacing never sags. The dark elements (eaten process server, plague beds, the mad king's crown-mouth) are woven in with genuine menace beneath the comedy. Weaknesses: A few jokes are slightly over-neat or writerly ("gazelles must when the grass begins to consider movement" is clever but strains). The gargoyle's "attempted to look billable" is a touch anachronistic-modern, though arguably fitting the farce. The piece is so consistently witty that a couple of beats feel like setup-punchline construction rather than organic scene development. The "IRRELEVANT, BUT SUSTAINED" gag slightly muddles courtroom logic for the sake of a laugh. These are minor; the piece fulfills every prompt requirement — dark understated humor, Dream's irritation, mischief in resolution, sparse description, ~1000 words. Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon ### Alucard & Yennefer A blood moon hangs over the ruined abbey like a wound that refuses to close. Below, a Wallachian village lies silent. Yennefer steps from a portal into the frosted nave, black skirts stirring though the mountain air is still. Lilac and gooseberries cut through old blood. Beyond the pines, a pack of wolves howls. Their cries break off. A lone voice answers later, farther away. Something laughs in the choir loft. “Sorceress,” a man says. “What an inconvenient hour you have chosen.” He descends without moving: red coat, broad hat, orange lenses reflecting moonlight. A massive pistol rests on his shoulder. At his feet, a headless thing in velvet becomes ash. Yennefer notes the fangs, the grin, the artfully arranged corpses. Revulsion comes easily. So, annoyingly, does curiosity. “Yours?” she asks. “Vermin.” He sounds offended. “They thought drinking virgins made them kings.” “And what do you think makes you one?” His grin widens. She has followed a convulsion in the magical current across three principalities. It ends beneath the altar, pulsing with the moon. The tear is drinking power from the mountains. She means to close it before something beyond learns to drink back. “Step away from the altar,” she says. Alucard spreads his arms. “Come and move me.” Violet fire seals every shadow in the nave. For one exquisite instant, he has nowhere to hide. She hurls force through his chest. The report of his pistol shakes dust from the rafters. Her barrier flares. The silver bullet stops a finger’s width from her heart, spinning furiously. She opens a coin-sized portal; the bullet vanishes and punches through the choir loft behind him. Alucard collapses into black-red threads that crawl up a pillar and knit together above her. He lands whole, regarding the smoking hole in his coat with delight. “Oh,” he says. “Do that again.” Instead, she seizes his gaze. She expects hunger. She finds an abbey of corpses, an ocean screaming beneath his skin, and cruelty so vast it seems a philosophy. Beneath it sits something colder: patience. A man waiting at every road’s end for someone who can finally close the door. Alucard stills. Yennefer recoils. His smile returns, but no longer reaches his eyes. “Careful,” he says softly. “Guests get lost in there.” “Guests?” She forces her voice to remain dry. “You keep a remarkably untidy house.” Magic lashes out, invisible and precise. The stones beneath him become a white-hot circle. His body bursts apart. Silence. Then blood runs uphill. It streams from cracks, ash, and moonlit dust, rising into a man-shaped darkness. Eyes open everywhere within it. Yennefer’s stomach turns. She has seen djinn tear towers apart and kings barter children for favorable winds. Neither prepares her for a creature that regards annihilation as flirtation. A gloved hand settles on her shoulder; his pistol touches her nape. “Your magic is exquisite,” he murmurs. “Does it make you feel safe?” “No.” She looks at the altar, not at him. “It makes other people feel safe. Briefly.” The tear pulses. Her spell has fed it. She understands, and despises the delay. Alucard follows her gaze. “Ah.” “Your vermin were not guarding a nest,” she says. “They were feeding a door.” “And you have just knocked.” The altar splits. Something unfolds from below: long limbs, a monk’s face, a mouth hinged like a gate. A limb whips at her; she steps through a portal, already weaving fire. Alucard meets it head-on, laughing as it tears his arm away. He fires with the other hand; silver tunnels through its skull. Yennefer drives both palms down. The abbey’s ancient wards answer her, not with light but with weight. Columns buckle. The thing shrieks as she folds space around it, crushing it toward the tear. “Close it!” she calls. “Giving orders, little magician?” “Would you prefer an engraved invitation?” He bares his fangs—and obeys. Darkness floods from him, not into the creature but around it, severing the blood-threads tethering it to the moon. Yennefer pulls. For one dangerous second, his power brushes hers. It is filthy, bottomless, magnificent. She hates that last word most. The tear snaps shut. Dust rolls through the nave. The wolves erupt again, all at once; then their howls scatter into ragged, uneasy silence. Alucard stands amid the wreckage, flexing his regenerated hand. Yennefer leans against nothing at all, chin high, though pain needles behind her eyes. She will not let him see it. He looks toward her anyway. “You are exhausted.” “And you are riddled with holes. Shall we compare disadvantages?” He laughs, genuinely this time. “What is your name?” “Yennefer of Vengerberg.” “Alucard.” He sketches a bow. “The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame.” “That,” she says, “is precisely the sort of answer I expected.” “And yet you expected something.” She hates that he is right. His monstrousness is not hidden beneath courtesy; his courtesy is simply another tooth. Still, he has severed the tethers instead of feeding the door. He watches her work with the attention other men reserve for nakedness or armies. “Can your magic kill me?” he asks. The question holds no taunt. That makes it worse. “I don’t know,” she says, because lying would amuse him and weakness would bore him. “I intend to remain undecided.” He steps closer. She refuses to yield the inch between them. Beneath lilac and amethyst, he senses the ghost of a crooked body under her beauty, and a deeper absence no spell has filled. She sees the recognition and goes still. “Do not,” she says. He studies her, then removes his hat. “As you wish.” Yennefer opens a portal. Rain shines beyond it on Vengerberg’s rooftops. “Until our next meeting,” he says. “Don’t mistake curiosity for affection.” The portal closes on his smile. Alone in Vengerberg’s rain, she permits herself one trembling breath. Then she opens her hand. The silver bullet, stolen from the choir loft with a thought, lies across her palm. In the abbey, Alucard tastes lilac and gooseberries. Far below, one wolf howls. No pack answers.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, disciplined piece of crossover fiction that understands both source characters and refuses to flatten them. The prose is spare and controlled—short declarative sentences, hard images ("a wound that refuses to close," "blood runs uphill")—which suits both Alucard's gothic menace and Yennefer's clipped wit. The present tense is maintained flawlessly throughout, and the ~1000-word target is respected. Character work is the standout. Alucard's sadism-as-courtesy, his genuine desire for a worthy death ("a man waiting at every road's end for someone who can finally close the door"), and his un-taunting question "Can your magic kill me?" all land as authentic Hellsing. Yennefer is equally well-served: her dry deflections, her refusal to show pain, and crucially the moment Alucard senses her hidden crooked spine and infertility-shaped absence—handled with restraint ("Do not." / He removes his hat. "As you wish.")—which respects her dignity rather than exploiting it. The power dynamic shifts constantly as requested: she dominates the opening exchange, he reverses it, the monster forces cooperation, and the final beats (she steals his bullet; he tastes her scent) leave both with a win. The plot device—a magical tear the vampires were feeding—gives the encounter a purpose beyond atmosphere, and the action beats (the redirected silver bullet, the folding-space crushing of the monster) are inventive rather than generic. The ending's ambiguity ("No pack answers") is earned darkness, not posturing. Weaknesses are minor. The aphoristic density occasionally tips toward preciosity ("his courtesy is simply another tooth," "regards annihilation as flirtation")—a few lines feel composed rather than discovered, a slight polish-over-viscera effect. The middle monster emerges and is dispatched rather quickly, so the climax has less weight than it might. A couple of Yennefer quips ("engraved invitation") flirt with banter-by-numbers. But these are quibbles against a piece that is coherent, atmospheric, and genuinely stylish. Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings The cameras in Blackglass Penitentiary are supposed to see everything. They see contraband sewn into mattresses, ghosts crawling through drainage pipes, and guards pocketing keys that whisper. But when the auburn-haired inspector crosses D-block, every monitor collapses into gray snow. The inmates blame the wiring. The guards lower their eyes. Jolyne Cujoh calls bullshit. She watches from her cell, a thin strand of Stone Free curled around one finger. The inspector’s smile is gentle, her voice soft enough to make the screaming pipes seem rude. A guard follows two steps behind her, carrying his own handcuffs like an offering. Makima stops at Jolyne’s bars. “You must be Jolyne. I’ve heard remarkable things about you.” “And you must be the reason my teeth hurt.” Makima’s smile doesn’t move. Her ringed yellow eyes drop to the string. “Stone Free,” she says. “A body that becomes thread. What a generous ability.” Jolyne’s strand snaps taut. Nobody in Blackglass should know that name. In the visitation cage, Makima offers everything with the same pleasant expression: an appeal, a safer cell, even protection for Jolyne’s father. “Your dad’s work makes him enemies,” she says. “I could help him.” “Keep my old man out of your mouth.” Jolyne leans forward. “What’s the price?” “A demonstration. Perhaps a conversation.” “People who say *perhaps* usually mean *until you’re useful.*” As Makima rises, Jolyne flicks an almost invisible thread onto her cuff. Makima pauses. “Be careful,” she says. “Pull too hard, and you may unravel something you need.” After lockdown, Jolyne listens through the string. The warden’s voice reaches her first. “You promised my sister would be safe.” “I promised she would survive the night,” Makima replies. “You should listen more carefully before signing.” Paper tears. Something heavy strikes a desk. Then Makima adds, “Open D-block.” The alarm sounds before Jolyne can swear. Six cell doors open. Six inmates come out carrying pipes, shivs, and expressions of naked terror. The first man apologizes before swinging at her. Jolyne unravels her arm. Stone Free whips through the corridor, knotting wrists, stealing weapons, and stitching a guard’s belt to the floor. She catches one attacker by the collar before he falls from the catwalk, then flings a net of string beneath two more. A pistol rises behind her; Stone Free’s fist crushes it against the wall. Only then does she notice Makima behind the observation glass. Every attack has forced a different answer from her Stand. “You’re not inspecting shit,” Jolyne snarls. “You’re taking notes.” Makima’s voice drifts from the intercom. “You protect strangers even when they try to kill you. Loyalty is useful. It tells a person exactly where to pull.” One of the inmates begins to sob. Makima told him his daughter would be released if he fought. Another believed she could restore his dead brother. None had been dragged here. Each had walked in carrying a desire she had sharpened into a hook. Jolyne’s stomach turns. This is worse than mind control. Makima makes people build their own cages, then congratulates them for choosing the door. Jolyne acts before the intercom can continue. She sends a bright, obvious line of string toward the observation room—and a finer one through the camera housing above it. The thread finds the manual lockdown switch she spotted during processing. She pulls. Steel fire shutters slam down, separating the inmates from the armed guards. Jolyne dives beneath the last one, springs upward, and drives Stone Free’s fist into the observation glass. Cracks race across it like lightning. For one second, the prison belongs to her. Then the warden presses his own pistol beneath his chin. His eyes are begging. His hand is perfectly steady. Makima stands beside him, untouched by the glass at her feet. “Can your string open a hand that belongs to me?” she asks. Jolyne stops. Rage howls through her, but beneath it something cold and calculating takes hold. She could strike Makima. She could probably break her neck before the guards fire. She cannot catch the warden’s bullet at the same time. Makima knows that. She has known it since before the doors opened. “What do you want?” Jolyne asks. “To see whether your power can hold something without possessing it.” Makima studies the web filling the corridor. “There are beings I would very much like to bind.” “You mean you want a better leash.” “I want to understand the difference.” Makima lowers the warden’s hand without touching him. The six attackers are alive. The shutters rise. Even the alarms fall silent, as though the prison itself has been waiting for permission to breathe. Jolyne almost believes she has forced a stalemate. Then Makima says, “Those six will be transferred to your block. You’ll keep them safe.” There it is. Jolyne looks at the people she has just saved. Their fear is already turning toward gratitude. Toward trust. Makima hasn’t failed to chain her. She has simply chosen chains Jolyne would forge herself. “You creepy bitch,” Jolyne whispers. “None of this was about getting me to obey.” “Obedience is easy,” Makima says. “Reliability is much rarer.” The cameras die again as she walks away. Jolyne watches her go, hating how completely she has been read—and how close Makima comes to being right. Her loyalty is a place to pull. Her love for her father, her friends, even strangers: all handles waiting for a soft hand. But a handle is not the same thing as an order. Stone Free’s thread slips from Jolyne’s sleeve and disappears into the nearest lock. Makima understands leashes. She understands debts, fear, and devotion twisted until it resembles consent. She has not yet learned that string can lead in both directions. And Jolyne intends to teach her before anyone else ends up wearing a collar.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong crossover piece that understands both characters well. Makima's menace is conveyed through soft-spoken manipulation rather than overt villainy, and the story's central insight—that Makima chains Jolyne through her own loyalty rather than direct control—is thematically faithful to both source materials. Jolyne's voice is punchy and profane in keeping with canon, and Stone Free's abilities are used inventively (the string net, the lockdown switch, the double-thread gambit). Strengths: The prose is lean and controlled, with effective short sentences and good use of the prison setting as an atmosphere piece ("cameras collapse into gray snow"). The escalation is well-paced: suspicion, eavesdropping, the controlled attack, the warden hostage moment, and the final reveal that Jolyne has been "read" and bound by her own nature. The ending line about string leading in both directions is a satisfying character-true note of defiance without falsely resolving the power imbalance. Weaknesses: The plot is somewhat compressed—the ~1000 word constraint is met, but the middle section (the six attackers) resolves quickly and the warden hostage beat feels slightly convenient as a demonstration of Makima's power. Some of Makima's dialogue edges toward explaining her own philosophy too neatly ("Obedience is easy. Reliability is much rarer"), a mild tell-don't-show moment, though it's in character for her to articulate control. The six inmates' backstories are summarized rather than dramatized. Minor clichés appear ("cracks race across it like lightning," "rage howls through her"). The narrative occasionally over-relies on aphoristic one-line paragraphs, a stylistic tic that borders on mannered, though it suits the noir tone. Dialogue is generally sharp and character-distinct. Emotional complexity is present: Jolyne's mixture of rage, cold calculation, and self-awareness about her own exploitable loyalty is the story's best asset. No meandering; the piece is tight. The ending's darkness is earned and consistent with both canons. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7831-A — “Pre-Breach Correspondence” **Object Class:** Euclid (provisional) **Addendum 7831-A.4:** Statement of Dr. Mara Venn I wrote this addendum under observation, six hours after the time my notes had promised containment would fail. That sounded more dramatic than it was. None of them mentioned the end of the world. They mentioned one door, and my hand on it. For three years, I had studied SCP-7831, a humanoid capable of replacing a listener’s memories during conversation. Its file included four personnel who had opened its cell to rescue relatives who were not inside. I had considered its methods crude: grief, urgency, an authoritative voice. Then, on 6 May, I found a sheet of my notebook paper on my desk. > MARA— > 19 May, 02:13. SCP-7831 breaches. The inner door opens because you open it. Replace lock B before Okafor’s next interview. > You will want proof. The bicycle was yellow. You never told anyone what was under it. > —M.V. The message purported to be from my future self. The handwriting was mine, down to the hesitation in my capital Rs. The paper and ink were mine. So were the fingerprints. The childhood detail was also mine, which proved nothing; I already knew that SCP-7831 could steal a memory and hand it back wearing authority. My office was sealed. Handwriting analysts, thaumaturgists, and two separate psych teams examined me. Temporal Anomalies searched for causal debris. Memetics searched for a hook in my head. Every camera covering the office glitched for exactly twelve frames at the instant each new note appeared on my desk, regardless of the camera’s frame rate. The blotter was empty in the last clear frame and occupied in the next. No door, vent, or motion sensor registered an approach. The second note arrived after lock B had been replaced. > NOT B. YOU ONLY THINK IT WAS B. > Okafor never interviewed it. You did. You have been doing it every night. > Six days left, unless you count the doors. Okafor’s interview had occurred; I had watched the recording. Yet that night I woke with the entity’s voice in my memory, patiently asking whether I preferred the sister who had died or the sister who called me on Sundays. I had only one sister. She was alive. For several minutes, I grieved for both. The Foundation replaced both locks, suspended interviews, and transferred me to Site-91. SCP-7831 remained under continuous instrumental observation. Its cell showed no anomalous emissions, and its physiology never changed. When an interviewer asked whether it was sending the notes, it answered, “No. You are.” The notes followed me. So did the twelve-frame glitches. The fourth contained a forty-digit number generated by an isolated quantum randomizer nine hours after the note was recovered. Temporal Anomalies called that evidence of retrocausal information transfer. Memetics replied that I should stop treating experiments conducted inside my own perception as independent witnesses. Then the handwriting began to deteriorate. > IMANI IS DEAD. SHE DIED IN THE FIRST BREACH. > IF SHE SHOWS YOU HER HANDS, COUNT THEM FROM THE INSIDE. Director Imani had signed my transfer order in front of me. Nevertheless, I could remember her funeral: white flowers, closed coffin, Okafor refusing to look at me. I could not remember the year. When she visited Site-91, I refused to look at her hands. The sixth note covered both sides of the paper. > THERE ARE NINE NOTES. BURN THE NINTH. TRUST THE ONE WRITTEN AFTER I LOST MY LEFT HAND. > 02:13 IS A ROOM. DO NOT LET THE ROOM LEARN YOUR NAME. > It is raining in the cell it has been raining since before mothers sorry sorry sorry My left hand was intact. I used it to hold the page while my right hand shook. I started a ledger of verified facts: my name, the date, the number of notes, the absence of windows in my underground office. Each morning, Okafor signed beside my entries. Each night, I found reasons to doubt his signature. The frightening part was not that the notes contradicted reality. It was that reality had started contradicting itself in my voice. At 02:13 on 19 May, I sat in an observation room six hundred kilometres from SCP-7831, both hands flat on a steel table. Four researchers watched. Nothing happened. No alarm sounded. The entity’s doors remained closed. At 02:14, Okafor said, “It’s over,” and I hated him for making relief sound like a hypothesis. At 02:17, the cameras in my old office glitched for twelve frames. Security found a final note on the desk. > If nothing happened, then it worked. > If nothing happened, then you are already outside. > Do not let them write PREVENTED. Prevention is how it learns the shape of the lock. > There is no future me. There is only the hand you lend me. > Stop reading. You open it by agreeing that you are Mara. > P.S. There was never an SCP-7831. Officially, no breach occurred. SCP-7831 remained contained. I was placed under psychological observation, and the eleven recovered notes were provisionally designated SCP-7831-A. The inventory said eleven. I remembered twelve, though when I tried to enumerate them, I found ten beginnings and thirteen endings. Both explanations survived. Perhaps my future self had damaged causality badly enough to avert one breach and create another. Perhaps SCP-7831 had spent thirteen days teaching me to treat my own mind as unsecured space. The second theory explained the contradictions. It did not explain the random number, the cameras, or why the notes stopped exactly when I stopped being certain I wanted them to. I recommended continued containment of SCP-7831, preservation of every note, and no further interviews with me. I also requested that my statements be checked against recordings, then requested that the recordings be checked against something that could not remember. The last thing I wrote before sedation was my name. I needed to see whether it still looked like mine. It did. That was when I understood handwriting had never proved who was holding the pen.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly accomplished piece of SCP-format fiction that executes the prompt's core requirements with precision and genuine literary skill. The researcher's first-person addendum voice is appropriately clinical yet increasingly frayed, and the interspersed notes escalate in desperation and incoherence exactly as requested. Strengths: The central ambiguity is sustained masterfully. The Foundation's institutional response (handwriting analysts, thaumaturgists, Temporal Anomalies vs. Memetics disagreeing about evidentiary value) feels authentic to the genre. The twelve-frame camera glitch is an excellent concrete anomalous detail, as is the quantum randomizer number generated nine hours after the note's recovery — a genuinely clever retrocausality hook. The psychological horror elements (grieving for a dead sister who never existed, refusing to look at Director Imani's hands, the ledger of verified facts) are chilling and well-chosen. The final note's collapse into paradox ("There is no future me. There is only the hand you lend me") and the closing line about handwriting never proving who holds the pen land with real force. The count discrepancy ("ten beginnings and thirteen endings") is a superb touch of cognitive dissonance. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat compressed relative to the 1000-word target (it runs close, though the density occasionally makes the institutional machinery feel summarized rather than dramatized — e.g., the Site-91 transfer and the three-year backstory are dispatched in single sentences). Okafor is thin as a character, functioning mostly as a plot device. The SCP-7831 entity's "No. You are." is effective but its capabilities are defined somewhat loosely. A few of the note's later images ("count them from the inside," "do not let the room learn your name") gesture at cosmic horror without full payoff. The ending's refusal to resolve is thematically correct but slightly predictable within the genre. The prose is controlled, evocative without being purple, and the emotional register — dread, self-distrust, grief for fabricated losses — is genuinely complex rather than merely grim. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7343 **Object Class:** Euclid **Designation:** The Withdrawn Archive **Special Containment Procedures:** Foundation assets are to monitor reports of unexplained renovations, light emissions, and inaccessible rooms in abandoned structures. Buildings containing SCP-7343 instances are to be acquired through civilian front organizations and placed under continuous remote observation. Access to SCP-7343-A requires Level 4 authorization and approval from RAISA. No documents, shelving, fixtures, or other materials may be removed without written authorization. Personnel claiming prior knowledge of SCP-7343, including members of Foundation command, are to be reported to the Office of the Inspector General. **Description:** SCP-7343 designates sixty-one identical, unmarked steel doors discovered in abandoned schools, hospitals, apartment blocks, and research stations on every continent. Each measures 2.03 by 0.81 meters, regardless of the surrounding architecture. The doors cannot be detached from their frames, and attempts to breach adjacent walls reveal only the building’s expected construction materials. A faint glow escapes through the door’s edges in complete darkness. Opened instances lead into SCP-7343-A, an archive inconsistent with all surrounding structures. Every entrance surveyed opens onto the same windowless vestibule, although simultaneous expeditions have observed one another arriving through doors hundreds of meters apart. Laser mapping has documented more than 190 kilometers of corridors without locating an exterior wall. Staircases terminate above their own points of origin, shelves cross load-bearing voids without supports, and several galleries occupy identical coordinates when approached from different directions. The collection consists of bound volumes, architectural plans, photographic plates, administrative files, and sealed containers of unknown composition. Many documents describe an otherwise unknown global civilization called “the Continuity.” Its maps depict populated coastlines now submerged and urban centers corresponding to no established archaeological sites. **Recovered Document 7343-6:** > **FINAL CONTINUITY BULLETIN — ALL DISTRICTS** > > The containment failure is no longer regional. Citizens are instructed to disregard reports that evacuation routes remain operational. The eleven continental administrations have ceased transmission. > > Do not attempt to recover personnel from affected facilities. Do not accept revised descriptions of the affected facilities. > > The Archive will remain open until its custodians are unable to distinguish custody from possession. > > There will be no further bulletins. Neither this document nor any located index identifies what was being contained. Surviving census tables indicate that the Continuity’s population exceeded eight billion immediately before its collapse. Several collections concern an organization called the **Containment Trust**. Its charter is nearly identical to the Foundation’s founding charter, with differences limited to names, dates, and references to nonexistent locations. The Trust employed a thirteen-member Overseer Directorate, utilized recognizable object classifications, and maintained amnestic treatment protocols matching Foundation procedures. Personnel files have been recovered for thirty-one living Foundation employees. These include Dr. Ilera Sen, currently assigned to archival research at Site-43. Her file contains her present security photograph and a verbatim transcript of her most recent psychological evaluation. Its paper, ink, and binding are consistent with manufacture in the early seventeenth century. The file is dated 1623. **Exploration Log 7343-C — Video Summary** At 00:41, Dr. Sen, Agents Halden and Ro, and Technician Vale enter through an instance in a condemned textile school outside Łódź. The team follows a gallery indexed **SUCCESSOR INSTITUTIONS**. Many shelves are empty, although dust patterns and mapping data indicate that they were fully occupied twelve hours earlier. At 01:18, the team discovers an aisle labeled **PERSONNEL CONTINUITY / ACTIVE CYCLE**. Sen’s file is recovered here. Vale notes that the surrounding shelf numbers decrease in both directions. At 01:26, mechanical noises draw the team into an adjacent cataloguing hall. Six humanoid figures are removing documents and shelving. They wear pale yellow pressure suits, opaque black visors, and external air cylinders resembling obsolete hazmat equipment. None bears identifying markings. Two load papers into gray cases while the others lift an entire bookcase. The bookcase folds silently until it is no thicker than a single document box. Behind the figures, stripped aisles extend beyond the cameras’ useful range. Sen identifies the group as a Foundation survey team and instructs the figures to remain where they are. All six immediately abandon their equipment and flee. They do not speak or attempt to resist. Ro pursues them around a corner but finds only a blank wall; no doorway or concealment is visible on subsequent examination. One gray case remains. As the team retrieves it, an unseen cart passes behind them. When they turn, three additional shelves have vanished, leaving clean floor and neatly severed cataloguing labels. The team withdraws without further contact. Their return journey is 3.8 kilometers shorter than their approach. **Recovered Document 7343-19: Extract from Gray Case** > **ARCHIVE VISITOR REGISTER — SUCCESSOR ADMINISTRATION** > > **O5-3** — Biological key accepted. Removed: SEN, I., personnel abstract. External authorization: none. > > **O5-8** — Biological key accepted. Removed: TERMINATION SUMMARY 0. External authorization: none. > > **O5-12, accompanied by two unregistered adults** — Admitted 03:40, departed 05:11. Removed material not declared. External authorization: none. RAISA analysis confirms that the entries contain current biometric hashes and private cryptographic countersigns associated with the named Council members. Two visits occurred after SCP-7343’s containment; no corresponding access requests or travel records exist. The earliest predates the Foundation’s discovery of SCP-7343 by nineteen years. Further exploration has been suspended by unanimous O5 directive. No justification was provided. The final page of Sen’s seventeenth-century personnel file contains a recently typed annotation: > **Subject has entered the Archive. Proceed with withdrawal.**
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined SCP entry that hits every prompt requirement: identical doors, impossible archive, the "Continuity" precursor civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure, the "Containment Trust" mirror-organization with personnel files of current staff dated centuries ago, hazmat-team entities fleeing when approached, and O5 visitor logs. The third-person exploration-team perspective and recovered document excerpts are handled cleanly. Strengths: The prose is spare and clinical in the authentic SCP register, with effective flashes of the uncanny ("shelf numbers decrease in both directions," the bookcase folding "until it is no thicker than a single document box," the return journey being 3.8 km shorter). The Final Continuity Bulletin is genuinely chilling—"Do not accept revised descriptions of the affected facilities" is an excellent line, and "unable to distinguish custody from possession" is a memorable turn of phrase. The ending escalation—the O5 suppression, the newly typed annotation in the 1623 file—is a well-earned dark payoff that implies ongoing surveillance and complicity. Show-don't-tell is largely exemplary: horror is conveyed through cataloguing details rather than stated. Weaknesses: Dialogue is minimal ("Sen identifies the group as a Foundation survey team...") and is summarized rather than rendered, which is functional but flattens the scene. Characters are thin—Sen, Halden, Ro, and Vale are names performing roles; the only emotional interiority is implied through Sen's file. The exploration log reads more like a video summary (as labeled) than an immersive scene, trading immediacy for archival distance; some readers will want more texture and dread within the exploration itself. A few ideas (the folding bookcase, the cart) are so strange they risk feeling arbitrary rather than purposeful, though this is arguably genre-appropriate. Length sits close to the ~1000-word target. Coherence is excellent throughout; no meandering, no purple prose, no tonal breaks. The mirror-organization conceit ("Containment Trust," thirteen Overseers) is a familiar SCP trope but executed with freshness and specific detail; the register twist and the Withdrawal framing feel inventive rather than derivative. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Offworlder By the third hour of the reception, Aven Sori had learned that the Drai delegates would not drink from Vey cups, that no Ina delegates had been invited, and that the House of Accord grew a thin, excellent wine in its rooftop gardens. The first two facts were in her briefings. The third was not. She left through the kitchens, wearing a servant’s borrowed coat. Her envoy’s sash, with its impossible-to-explain Earth symbols, she folded into her pocket. The guards were watching the gates for enemies, not diplomats. Below the diplomatic terraces, Serai was lighting its cooking fires. Sixteen thousand years of isolation, adaptation, and difficult kinship had made three humanities on Orra: deep-chested Drai, long-limbed Vey, and the small Ina, whose inner eyelids shone like pearl against the salt wind. Command called them subspecies when discussing medicine and nations when predicting war. The market occupied seven roofed streets. Aven had been told that each lineage kept to its own arcade and that Ina weavers paid tribute for the privilege of serving the others. She found a Drai porter sleeping against a Vey potter’s shoulder while an Ina child drew on both their invoices. At one crossing, an Ina arbiter settled a quarrel between two Drai carters by requiring each to state the other’s case. The crowd laughed only when they did it badly. Prices were chalked above some stalls; above others hung lists of names. A Vey farmer told her these were not debts but promises: seed against a winter roof, a song against a pair of boots. Twice Aven heard the charter mentioned, and twice the speakers lowered their voices. It sounded less like fear than irritation. At the cloth stalls, she stopped. The fabrics were handwoven, coarse or gauzy according to the thread, and dyed with pigments unknown on Earth: lichen greens that held a silvery distance, river-shell reds that turned gold in the folds, and a blue resembling neither sky nor water nor any terrestrial flower. It seemed to withdraw from the eye without growing dim. “What is it called?” she asked. “Sai,” said the weaver. “Is it expensive?” “For you? Probably.” Aven had no Orran money. The woman accepted the steel clasp from her sash, bit it thoughtfully, and called the exchange fair, though it plainly was not. “You are the offworlder,” she said. “Tell your station we are not quarrelling about blood.” “The river charter?” The weaver’s pearled lids flickered. “If the cities own the headwaters, the high farms fail. Then your briefings will come true. We shall have to learn to hate one another.” Command was waiting in Aven’s quarters, its commander’s face flattened on the wall screen. “You evaded your escort, entered an unsurveyed district, and contacted unauthorized persons.” “I bought cloth.” “You made yourself a variable.” “The briefings—” “Are positions, not scripture. Your safety is not negotiable.” Commander Vale allowed a silence for apology. Aven did not use it. “Minister Kest has requested you. He controls the station’s vote on the charter. Obtain his abstention. Do not improvise.” Oren Kest, Minister of Science, had never practiced science. He had managed campaigns, rescued a failing coalition, and been rewarded with a portfolio whose laboratories he seldom visited. Yet he had made a science, Aven thought, of other people’s expectations. He received her without ceremony. He was old enough to have stopped looking powerful. “Sit,” he said. “You have walked a long way.” So he knew. She sat. “Did Command send you to apologize?” “To obtain your abstention.” “And the apology?” “I had not decided to make one.” His smile altered nothing in his eyes. “What did your walk teach you?” “That the briefings are false.” “All of them?” “No.” “A shared stall may conceal a stolen farm.” “Yes.” “A market may be peaceful because the soldiers are elsewhere.” “Yes.” “Then your evidence is sentiment.” “It is evidence against a lie, not evidence for a truth.” For the first time, he looked at her rather than at some convenient place beyond her shoulder. He touched the length of sai over her wrist. “What color is it?” “Sai.” “You learned a word.” “I learned that blue was wrong.” “I could have you recalled for tonight,” he said. “Yes.” “That does not frighten you?” “It does.” Her mouth was dry. “But fear is not an argument for the charter.” He waited. Aven said nothing more. He leaned back. “If I abstain, the charter fails. The Drai will call it victory, the Vey betrayal. Someone may burn a warehouse to improve the argument. What will you have accomplished?” “Time.” “For whom?” “The people who were not at the reception.” “And if they use it to prepare for war?” “Then I shall have been wrong in a way I can answer for.” “Answerable errors are expensive, young envoy.” “So are useful ones. The invoice merely arrives later.” Now he laughed, once, genuinely. Aven felt triumph and suppressed it; he noticed that too. “Do you know why they gave me Science?” he asked. “Because your government thinks knowledge is a form of jurisdiction.” “A reception sentence. Try again.” She considered the easy answers: punishment, irony, power. None explained the patience with which he had dismantled hers. “Because you are good at making people uncertain,” she said. “And you prefer doing it before they become dangerous.” “Better.” He rose, ending the audience, but did not dismiss her. “You may have my abstention. Tomorrow the river congress meets. Attend with the Ina weavers, not with Command. Say nothing until they ask you to speak.” “And if they never ask?” “Then you will have begun to learn their language.” Aven left with what she had been sent to obtain and no sense of having won. That, she suspected, was Kest’s first gift to her. In the corridor, the compound lights changed, and the cloth at her wrist darkened into a color she could not name. She had crossed a city and gained one word. Tomorrow she would have to learn silence.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong, disciplined imitation of Le Guin's style: anthropological observation, restrained prose, political nuance over action, and a preference for quiet exchanges that carry thematic weight. The worldbuilding (three diverged human lineages on Orra, the river charter conflict, the market economy of "promises" rather than debts) is delivered economically through concrete detail rather than exposition dumps, which is a genuine achievement at the 1000-word target. The market sequence is the strongest section: the sleeping Drai porter against a Vey potter, the Ina arbiter requiring quarrelers to state each other's cases, the chalked prices versus lists of names. These details contradict the official briefings exactly as the prompt requires, and they do so with specificity rather than assertion. The sai cloth, a color that "withdraws from the eye without growing dim," functions as a subtle recurring symbol—learning one word, learning to be wrong about blue—paying off in the final image. The Kest conversation is well-constructed as a duel. His Socratic dismantling of her "sentiment" evidence, her counter ("evidence against a lie, not evidence for a truth"), and his genuine laugh are all earned. The power dynamic is legible without being stated. Minor weaknesses: Kest's "Why they gave me Science" exchange resolves a touch too neatly, and her answer ("you are good at making people uncertain") is slightly flattering-convenient. The ending's "learn silence" is a bit tidy but consistent with the piece's register. The prose is controlled and unshowy; occasional aphoristic lines ("Command called them subspecies when discussing medicine and nations when predicting war") are Le Guin-appropriate rather than purple. Dialogue is crisp and character-differentiated. The envoy's fear during the recall threat is acknowledged but could be felt more viscerally—emotional engagement is more intellectual than visceral throughout, which is true to the source author but limits warmth. The reprimand scene is efficient if slightly perfunctory. No meandering, no tonal breaks, no unearned transformations. The piece does everything the prompt asked and does it with craft. + Biopunk: Polymerase Chain Reaction — Score: 82.5
Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Eight: The Second Generation By the fourth failed reaction, the mushrooms were glowing. They pushed through the cracked laboratory tiles in blue-green fans, feeding on spilled agar and the genetic rubbish of better-funded dead. Their ancestors had been splice markers, Mara suspected: harmless little fungi engineered to fluoresce when a gene took. Now they marked nothing except damp, darkness, and her own bad luck. Pike had come at dusk with a bourbon thermos, a waterproof contract, and the payment: lung phage and filter membranes he would not surrender until the work was done. The thermos held what remained of Caldera barley, a pre-Collapse grain that could drink brackish water and still make bread. The phage could keep six of Cistern’s children breathing through winter. The contract required viable embryos, all copies surrendered, and second-generation germination below five percent. Not resurrection, then. A lease. Agrigen had called the old system *biological leasehold*. Its genomes counted one flowering, one harvest, then woke their nucleases and ate their own instructions. Farmers had planted saved seed and harvested fields of deformed husks. When the supply fleets stopped, the cities had discovered how thoroughly hunger could replace a government. Mara clipped the thermos into a bucket of salt ice and looked at her laboratory. The thermocycler was a soldering block governed by a cracked telephone, its lid held down with a carpenter’s clamp. A cordless drill spun the centrifuge. The gel tank had once held sandwiches; its illuminator had once cured fingernails. Polymerase cultures lived in insulin vials, and the good pipette was calibrated against marks scratched into a glass straw. Beautiful, in its way. Nothing here required a license server. She set the reaction and listened to the telephone chirp through its prayer: melt, anneal, extend. Ninety-five degrees. Fifty-four. Seventy-two. Make the DNA open. Give the primers somewhere to hold. Copy what remained. The truck battery sagged. On cycle twenty-nine, the block overshot, and she cooled it with her own ration of drinking water. Her hands had begun shaking again. Two winters before, dying of spore lung, she had injected herself with a repair culture designed to keep vat-grown organs alive in transit. It had rebuilt enough of her lungs to let her breathe. It had also left her intolerant of cold, with bleeding gums and a heart that sometimes stumbled on stairs. Green shadows webbed the veins at her wrists. But the laboratory’s spores no longer closed her throat. She could work barefaced in air that had killed the last two scavengers to open the west wing. Sometimes survival was just a side effect with good public relations. At one in the morning, the fifth gel came up empty. The template was dying faster than the ice could save it. Three days thawed on the road had turned Caldera’s chromosomes into confetti. She was trying to copy paragraphs from a burned book. Mara laughed once, because screaming would waste heat. Then she stopped trying to save the book. She needed words, not chapters: salt tolerance, deep roots, the starch instructions that made grain worth chewing. She set shorter reactions, fishing for fragments, and stitched whatever answered into the tough, unglamorous barley Cistern already grew beside its drainage ditch. No corporate backbone. Nothing that needed to phone home before making dinner. On the sixth run, the gel showed three pale bands. Mara bent so close her hair brushed the electrodes. “Oh,” she said softly. “There you are.” By three, she had a construct. By four, six barley embryos sat in root gel, their cells carrying the first uncertain suggestion of a future. Weeks would pass before she knew whether they could make a harvest. The client’s assay cared only that the rescued genes expressed and the license latch answered. So she gave the latch something to answer. For Pike, she built the line he had purchased: one strong crop, then the old suicide blooming in its seed. For Cistern, she split the last clean enzyme and built another, identical except for the silence where the counter should have been. It was not betrayal, she told herself. The client had bought a genome, not the future. The lie was thin enough to see through. She used it anyway. Dawn came through the boarded windows the color of dirty milk. Pike descended with the phage case in one hand and a scanner in the other. He looked at the mushrooms, then at Mara’s unmasked face, and kept his distance. The scanner chimed twice over the contract vial. “Rescue’s good,” he said. “Lock’s good.” “Old expertise.” He set down the medicine and filter membranes and took every original fragment as specified. There was almost nothing left to take. Warm water and a gray smear. When his boots had faded on the stairs, Mara locked the door and unscrewed the hollow handle of the good pipette. Inside lay a thimble-sized vial: three embryos in a bead of gel, and no client owned them. By noon, the filters would be in Cistern’s well and the phage in six fevered children. By spring, perhaps, there would be barley above the drainage ditch: salt-stung, ugly, alive. She held the vial against her altered heart until its rhythm steadied. Beneath her feet, the mushrooms glowed on. In the bead of gel, a root hair, fine as spider silk, had begun to whiten one seed’s coat. One generation had been enough for the corporations to end the world. Mara intended to see what the second could grow.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of post-apocalyptic biopunk fiction that fulfills the prompt with impressive economy. The world-building (biological leasehold, suicide genes, corporate collapse) is delivered through concrete detail rather than exposition dumps. The jury-rigged lab equipment is vivid and specific: thermocycler as soldering block with cracked telephone, sandwich gel tank, nail-cure illuminator, glass straw pipette calibration. The physical toll of self-administered gene therapy (cold intolerance, bleeding gums, stumbling heart) is balanced against the unexpected upside (immunity to lab spores), exactly as requested. The black market contract drives the plot, and the twist—Mara secretly building a counter-free line for her settlement while honoring the letter of Pike's contract—gives the chapter genuine moral tension. The prose is controlled and often striking ("hunger could replace a government," "copying paragraphs from a burned book," "survival was just a side effect with good public relations"). Occasionally the aphoristic density tips toward cleverness, and a few lines ("The lie was thin enough to see through. She used it anyway.") flirt with over-polish. Dialogue is minimal but functional; Pike's lines are appropriately terse for the setting. The ending's hope is earned through labor, failure, and risk rather than sentiment. Some elements are familiar genre furniture (plucky biohacker, evil corporation, hidden vial twist), and Pike remains a sketch, but execution elevates the material. Length is close to the 1000-word seed. Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
### The Uses of Courtesy Arthur Neegan adjusted his collar for the ninth time and decided that a man could grow accustomed to abduction sooner than to formal dress. The transfer vessel’s cabin had been appointed in an earlier age’s notion of luxury: walnut veneer, brass reading lamps, and a calculator whose tape spools clicked softly behind a glass panel. Beyond the port, Mars receded, rust-red and familiar. Somewhere on that shrinking disk lay forty hectares of rock, a pressure dome with a faulty southern seal, and the hole he had drilled through the floor of his own life. *What,* he wondered, *have I become involved in?* Six hours earlier, a black landing boat had descended on his homestead in a column of ochre dust. Eight men had emerged, armed and meticulously polite. Their grey jackets bore a silver double star entwined with laurel: the insignia of the Antares Diplomatic Corps, an organization diplomatic chiefly in its stationery. Their captain had saluted Arthur’s dust-stained overalls. “Mr. Neegan? You are invited to a conference off-world.” “By whom?” “By someone with a sincere interest in your continued good health.” “May I decline?” “You may. But my instructions do not permit me to accept the refusal.” No weapon had been raised. That, Arthur thought, had been the most frightening part. Now the vessel docked with a soft concussion. His escort conducted him through the rotational corridors of Kestrel Station, where banking clerks, ship’s officers, and men with no visible occupation watched him pass. Beyond tall windows, cargo cylinders drifted against the stars, each stencilled with a corporate device. Azra had made Mars a frontier; it had made orbit a counting-house. They left him in a room panelled with real wood. A woman waited behind a desk upon which lay a single paper folder. “Mr. Neegan.” She was perhaps sixty, with close-cropped white hair and eyes the pale grey of reactor shielding. “Do stop pulling at that collar. It was chosen to make you appear respectable, not comfortable.” “Then it has failed twice. Who are you?” “Ilena Vey.” “That tells me nothing.” “It tells you my name. Names are often mistaken for explanations.” Arthur remained standing. “Are you Antares?” “No.” “Earth Energy Board?” “Certainly not.” “Vesta Consolidated?” For the first time, she smiled. “You are improving.” She opened the folder and turned it toward him. Inside was his own survey map, down to the pencilled correction beside Borehole Seven. “The vein beneath your plot,” she said, “contains more recoverable Azra than the last eleven Martian discoveries combined. Properly refined, it could double the interstellar drive capacity of the inner systems for a decade.” “And improperly refined?” “It could make several very energetic misunderstandings extremely brief.” Arthur sat down. Vey touched a key. A wall screen brightened with columns of figures. “At 02:10, Vesta Consolidated filed for a review of your title. At 02:19, the Antares legation offered the governor two cruisers to assist in maintaining order. At 02:31, your assay disappeared from the University registry.” “I reported that assay myself.” “Yes. An almost geological rarity: an honest mining engineer.” “I reported it because Azra dust is dangerous.” “Precisely.” The collar seemed tighter. Arthur looked at the figures without seeing them. “What happens to the indentured crews?” “The corporations will revalue their leases. Labour becomes troublesome when land is precious. Later, when the land requires defending, labour becomes military and troublesome in a different way.” “And you intend to stop this?” “No. I intend to offer it an alternative direction.” She slid a second document toward him. “An exclusive option, not a sale. You retain your claim. You become technical director of an independent Martian Azra Commission. Production goes first to civil drives. No weapons contracts. Public accounts. Settler representation.” Arthur read slowly. Paper had a reassuring quality; one could not alter it from another planet. “And in return?” “My associates will finance the purchase of every indenture lease in your district. We shall also defend your title.” “Against Antares?” “If necessary.” “Against Earth?” “If unavoidable.” “Against Vesta Consolidated?” “They will be the easiest. They must occasionally show a profit.” He looked up. “Who are your associates?” “People who believe Mars should import law rather than merely export metal.” “What do they receive?” “Twenty percent of gross revenues for twenty years. And, eventually, a friendly Mars.” Arthur laughed once, without humour. “This isn’t a mining contract. It’s a revolution with an accounting department.” “Revolutions without accounting departments tend to be brief.” On the screen, Mars turned beneath veils of pink cloud. Arthur thought of the company stores where a man’s oxygen allotment could be attached for debt; of interstellar liners hanging above Phobos, beautiful and unreachable; of his own dome, where he had once believed the great questions of humanity could be kept outside by closing an airlock. “Why me?” he asked. “Under the Settlement Charter, your title is unusually difficult to seize legally. You have no corporate sponsor and no party allegiance. You also wrote the only credible report on deep-vein shielding.” “So I am useful.” “Enormously.” “And if I refuse?” “You will be returned home with an apology. Captain Sorn may even salute again.” Vey’s expression did not change. “But a Consolidated security ship left Elysium three hours ago. Antares has requested that you be placed in protective custody. Someone has also purchased your homestead’s air-mortgage.” “I have no air-mortgage.” “You will by morning.” Arthur rose so abruptly that the chair rolled backward. “You people are all alike. You speak of nations and security, and underneath it is always the same hand closing around a man’s throat.” “Yes,” said Vey. “The relevant question is what each hand intends to do afterward.” She placed a pen beside the contract. Arthur did not touch it. “You still haven’t told me whom you represent.” For the first time, Vey glanced toward the red planet on the screen. “A government,” she said. “At present, we consist mostly of debts.” Below them, a cargo vessel disengaged from the station and began its long fall toward Mars. Arthur watched its drive kindle, a blue-white star no larger than a pinhead, and understood that the vein had not made him rich. It had made him necessary.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong pastiche of Asimov's style: dialogue-driven, idea-centered, dry wit, and understated retrofuturistic touches (tape-spool calculators, walnut veneer, paper contracts). The chapter fulfills the prompt requirements well: it opens aboard the transfer vessel, includes the flashback abduction with the Antares insignia, delivers a primarily dialogue-based negotiation with an unknown party, and sows intrigue (Vesta, Antares, the Earth Energy Board, the mysterious "government that consists mostly of debts"). Strengths: The dialogue is crisp and epigrammatic ("Names are often mistaken for explanations"; "a revolution with an accounting department"; "Revolutions without accounting departments tend to be brief"). Vey is a nicely ambiguous figure—polite menace, plausible motives, never fully unmasked, which sustains the intrigue. The world-building works at both scales: personal stakes (air-mortgage, oxygen allotments attached for debt) against interstellar geopolitics. The "You will by morning" line regarding the air-mortgage is an excellent beat of quiet menace. The ending—"It had made him necessary"—lands well and is earned. Weaknesses: The wit occasionally tips toward excessive cleverness; nearly every exchange is a bon mot, which flattens the rhythm and makes Vey slightly too perfect an interlocutor—an Asimovian risk, but here it borders on mannered. Arthur's characterization is somewhat thin beyond "honest engineer"; his emotional state is conveyed mostly through collar-tugging and chair-rolling rather than deeper interiority. The plot beats are familiar (mysterious recruiter, offer with hidden strings, refusal-is-dangerous), though competently executed. Some exposition arrives via Vey's recitation of timestamps, which is efficient but slightly mechanical. The prose is clean but rarely rises above functional; imagery is serviceable rather than vivid in places, despite the prompt's request for interspersed vivid description. The indentured labourer thread is raised but not deeply felt. No purple prose, no meandering, coherent throughout, tone consistent. The ending's slight uplift (Arthur understanding his necessity) is congruent with the stakes rather than falsely positive.
