+ Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Litigants in the Court of the Dreaming were advised to be brief. The advice was carved above the doors in a language that had died before anyone thought to speak it. The courtroom had no ceiling. At its centre stood a single, giant hourglass, dripping shimmering sand into a pool that never filled. Dream sat beyond it, black-robed and still. His face, as usual, gave nothing away. The hourglass had taken eleven minutes to release one grain. “The matter of First Love versus Mora,” said the clerk, whose wig was made of white moths. “Trespass upon a recurring dream, corruption of an established narrative, and theft of breath.” “I stole nothing,” said Mora. “He got it back.” “Eventually,” said First Love. First Love stood at the plaintiff’s table, rosy-cheeked and bashful, clutching a folder labelled MAX in careful handwriting. Mora sat opposite with her hands folded, looking like a patient widow. Her shadow looked less patient. Dream regarded the clerk. “Begin.” First Love opened the folder. “I built the field by hand, lord. Eleven kinds of wildflower. Max can name none of them, which is authentic. The light is late August, because September makes him feel he is about to be asked a question. There is a breeze, but not enough to make his eyes water.” “A masterwork,” said Mora. First Love blushed. “I did not do it for praise.” “Nor did you get any,” said Mora. “Objection.” “On what grounds?” asked Dream. First Love hesitated. “Tone?” Dream looked at the hourglass. “Sustained.” The clerk stared at him. “We don’t actually—” “Sustained.” First Love blushed again, accepting a victory they did not entirely understand but were prepared to defend. “On the third repetition, the girl takes his hand. On the seventh, she pushes him gently into the grass and sits on him so he will stop talking nonsense. They lean close. Then his alarm sounds, or a dog barks, or he forgets how mouths work.” Dream’s eyes shifted slightly. “This is intentional?” “The last part writes itself.” “And Mora’s contribution?” First Love’s blush vanished. “The girl changed. The sky closed. Max could not move. Mora settled on his chest and drank his breath until he woke in the dark, certain he was dying.” “Certainty is very nourishing,” Mora said. The clerk presented Exhibit B, a stoppered bottle. Something inside it sobbed once, then remembered it was in court and stopped. “Max’s breath,” said First Love. “My supper,” said Mora. “Evidence,” said the clerk. They all looked at Dream. “Put it down,” he said. “He used to wake happy,” First Love added. Max’s dream-self appeared in the witness box at that moment, wearing his school uniform, a duvet, and the expression of someone who had not been consulted. “Happy?” he said. First Love adjusted a page. “Thinking about being happy.” The clerk lifted one moth from his wig. “Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?” “I think I’m asleep.” “That has never prevented perjury,” said the clerk. Dream looked at Max. “What do you want?” Max considered this with the caution of someone being asked by a teacher whether he had done the reading. “To go back,” he said. First Love brightened. “Not exactly back.” Mora smiled. “She was horrible,” Max told her. “I couldn’t breathe. I couldn’t move. I thought my heart had stopped.” “Yes,” said Mora. “But?” Max pulled the duvet tighter. “You were still…” He looked at the ceiling. “It’s difficult to explain.” First Love made a small, strangled noise. “That was my ending.” “She knew my name,” Max said. “The other girl never had one.” First Love looked down at the folder. “Names make them expect things.” “So does sitting on people,” said Mora. “Enough,” said Dream. Nothing in his voice had risen. The moths in the clerk’s wig nevertheless stopped moving. Mora rose. “May I speak plainly?” “You have been doing little else.” “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” “You ate his sleep,” said First Love. “I left him the rest of the night.” “He spent it with the light on.” “Then I also fed the lamps. Am I on trial for generosity?” Dream turned his gaze upon her. For the first time, something like fatigue showed in it, though fatigue in Dream resembled a change in the weather on a distant star. “You claim the field as feeding ground?” “An easement.” “Through what?” “His chest.” A grain of sand detached itself and fell, shimmering. Dream watched it strike the pool. He had unmade kingdoms with less effort than it now took not to sigh. He considered awarding the field to the wildflowers. They, at least, had shown no ambition. Then another possibility occurred to him. It was not, strictly, more just. It was merely more interesting. “The dream belongs to Max,” he said. “Neither of you owns it. You are permitted to shape it only so long as he permits you to remain.” Max raised a hand. “Can I—” “No,” said Dream. “You may not ask whether this is a metaphor.” Max lowered his hand. “First Love will restore the field. The girl will have a name.” First Love nodded, already making a note. “Mora will not enter it.” Mora’s shadow opened its mouth. “However,” Dream continued, “you have developed a taste for this dream. You shall have it.” First Love stopped writing. “Every night, for one turning of the moon, Mora will lie in the field. First Love will craft the dream. There will be wildflowers. There will be kindness. There will be an approach, and an almost-kiss.” Mora narrowed her eyes. “And then?” “Then you will wake. Hungry.” “This is cruel,” she said. “It is formative,” said First Love. Dream inclined his head. “Court is adjourned.” The clerk’s wig exploded into moths. Max vanished, still holding the duvet. First Love hurried after Mora, asking whether she preferred daisies or cornflowers and assuring her that it made no difference. Above them, the hourglass dripped. Mora, to her own considerable alarm, blushed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally well-executed piece of dark comic fantasy that understands its assignment completely. The response nails nearly every element of the brief: the courtroom farce, Dream's barely-leaked irritation, Mora's pragmatic defense, First Love's bashful craftsmanship, and the dark understated humor throughout. The prose is spare and controlled, exactly as instructed ("use descriptives sparingly"). The opening line—"advice was carved above the doors in a language that had died before anyone thought to speak it"—immediately establishes the tone: dry, slightly paradoxical, mythic but wry. The hourglass that releases one grain in eleven minutes is a perfect image of Dream-court time, and it pays off again at the end. The comedy is consistently understated and lands repeatedly: "Objection." / "On what grounds?" / "Tone?" / "Sustained" is a superb courtroom-farce beat, and Dream's deadpan abuse of procedure ("We don't actually—" / "Sustained.") characterizes him perfectly in three lines. Other gems: the breath in the bottle that "sobbed once, then remembered it was in court and stopped"; "Names make them expect things"; "Then I also fed the lamps. Am I on trial for generosity?"; Max being sworn in while unsure he's awake ("That has never prevented perjury"). The characters are genuinely nuanced. Max's ambivalence—"You were still… It's difficult to explain"—complicates the case in a way that feels psychologically true and gives Dream's mischief a plausible hook. Mora is given real presence beyond villainy: her shadow being "less patient" than she is, and her final blush, give her dimension. First Love's mixture of craft-pride and hurt ("That was my ending") is well observed. Dream's temptation to mischief is handled exactly as requested: "He considered awarding the field to the wildflowers. They, at least, had shown no ambition. Then another possibility occurred to him. It was not, strictly, more just. It was merely more interesting." The resolution—sentencing Mora to a month of being the recipient of tender almost-kisses, waking hungry—is a genuinely inventive dark punishment, poetic justice rather than a cop-out, and it earns the closing beat of Mora blushing "to her own considerable alarm." Minor criticisms: the middle section occasionally relies on short declarative exchanges that verge on being too clipped, and a couple of jokes (the moths in the wig) are deployed twice with diminishing returns. The "No, you may not ask whether this is a metaphor" beat is funny but slightly breaks the frame's internal logic—Max asking to ask is a small contrivance. The piece also flirts with cuteness in the final line, though it stays on the right side of it. These are quibbles; the piece is coherent, economical, and never meanders. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, its spokes sunk in mud churned by hooves and bare feet. Beyond it, doors hang open. No dogs bark. No smoke rises, though the night is cold enough to sting Yennefer’s lungs. Above the deserted Carpathian village, the moon swells red. She draws her cloak closer and kneels beside the wheel. Lilac and gooseberries briefly overcome the stench of old blood as she touches the mud. Violet light threads between her fingers. “Not plague,” she murmurs. “And not men.” “An astute diagnosis.” The voice comes from above. A figure perches on the gate beam, impossibly at ease: red coat, wide-brimmed hat, orange glasses reflecting the moon. He drops without sound and lands close enough that she can see the Hellsing seal beneath his collar. Her violet eyes narrow; she does not step back. “Do you always skulk, or only when you’re hoping to be admired?” His smile shows too many teeth. “Do you always announce your magic before using it, or only when you’re afraid?” She flicks her wrist. The sigil beneath him ignites. Violet chains snap around his chest and tear him sideways through the air. His body strikes the gate hard enough to split timber. For one pleasant instant, there is silence. Then he laughs. Black eyes open in the shadows of his ruined coat. Flesh knits; bone crawls back into place. Yennefer’s stomach turns, but she cannot look away. There is no simple curse in him, no tidy knot for her mind to unpick. He is a cathedral built from graves, and something inside that cathedral is watching her with delight. “Again,” he says. “Repulsive.” “Fascinating,” he corrects, and is suddenly behind her. Cold fingers brush the back of her neck. She turns chaos into a blade and drives it through his heart before he can close his hand. He glances down at the violet fire. “Better.” A massive pistol rises in his grip. She opens a portal with a thought. The silver bullet enters the darkness beside her shoulder and emerges behind his skull. His head bursts. Yennefer steps away from the headless body, breathing once, carefully. It collapses—then dissolves into a flock of shrieking shadows. They gather atop the well. He reforms, hat first, grinning. “My turn to be intrigued.” “You were supposed to stay dead.” “I rarely do what I’m supposed to do.” The church bell answers with a single dull note. Its doors open. Villagers file into the square, barefoot and vacant-eyed. Above each heart gleams a thread of blood, all running toward the church. A vampire in bishop’s vestments follows them. His face is beautiful until he smiles. “Another immortal comes to kneel,” he says. “And a woman carrying fire between worlds. The red moon is generous.” Alucard’s amusement vanishes. Yennefer notices. “A friend?” “A corpse with ambitions.” The bishop’s jaw unhinges. Something wet and many-jointed unfolds behind it. “I have given these people eternity.” “You have given them a leash,” Alucard says. “And called hunger holiness because you cannot bear what you are.” The thing screams. Alucard shoots it apart. Blood spatters the church steps, but the threads tighten, and fifty villagers convulse. The creature pours itself back together from their open mouths. Yennefer’s repulsion becomes something cleaner: fury. “His heart isn’t in his body,” she says. “It’s in the moon.” “Then bring it down.” “And here I thought you’d ask politely.” She lifts both hands. The square groans. Portals blossom around the villagers, not cutting them but severing each crimson thread with flashes of violet. The bishop lunges at her. Alucard catches him by the face. For a moment, the monster’s strength actually drives him backward. His boots score the mud. Yennefer could leave him there. She could close her portals, escape, and let two abominations devour each other. Instead, she clenches her fist. The blood threads snap. The villagers fall. Alucard’s shadows spread beneath them, catching skulls before they strike stone. Yennefer sees that impossible tenderness, and her concentration almost breaks. The bishop sees it too. “She is your weakness.” Alucard’s arm becomes a black, eye-riddled ruin around him. “No. Merely my entertainment.” “Charming,” Yennefer says. She tears the last thread free. The red moon shudders. Something like a heart drops through the church roof and lands beating on the altar. Alucard shoots it. Darkness floods the square. There is one short, surprised scream. When it recedes, nothing remains of the bishop but empty vestments. Yennefer sways. Only for an instant. Alucard is watching when she straightens. “A beautiful cage,” he says softly. “All that power spent remaking yourself, and still it cannot give you what you want.” Her portals vanish. The silence between them turns sharp. He has found the old wound without touching it. She hates him for that. She hates more that some part of her wants to answer. Then she looks into the multitude behind his glasses and smiles without warmth. “And you keep your cage unlocked,” she says, “hoping someone worthy will wander in and kill you. Shall we compare disappointments?” His grin returns, slower now. “A monster on Hellsing’s leash,” she adds. “Does your mistress know you wander?” “The bird of Hermes is my name,” he murmurs, “eating my wings to make me tame.” “And are you?” “No.” He steps close. This time she lets him. “Merely patient.” Dawn is still hours away, but the blood drains from the moon. Around them, villagers begin to wake, sobbing and calling one another’s names. Yennefer turns toward them. Alucard does not stop her. “You could have run,” he says. “So could you.” “I was enjoying myself.” “How reassuring.” She opens a portal. Beyond it lies a white chamber, clean and cold and very far away. On its threshold, she pauses. “Next time, vampire, announce yourself before I decide to be thorough.” He bows, absurdly courtly in his red coat. “Next time, sorceress, bring a larger chain.” She leaves him with the scent of lilac and gooseberries and the faintest impression of a smile. Alucard stands among the living until her portal closes. Then he looks at the paling moon and laughs, quietly, as though the night has made him a promise.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, disciplined piece of fanfiction that understands both source characters and, more importantly, how to stage a power dynamic rather than merely assert one. The prompt asked for a constantly shifting balance of power between two proud immortals, and the story delivers that structurally: Yennefer strikes first, Alucard regenerates and mocks her, she lands a genuine blow, he escalates, and the arrival of a third party (the bishop-vampire) forces a temporary, grudging alliance without either of them ever admitting to one. Strengths: The prose is lean and rhythmic, with short declarative sentences doing heavy atmospheric lifting ("No dogs bark. No smoke rises"). The present tense is sustained flawlessly. The imagery is fresh without being ornate — "a cathedral built from graves" is an excellent compressed description of Alucard's nature from Yennefer's magical perspective, and the blood-threads running from the villagers to the church give the supernatural threat a visible, tactile geometry. The action choreography is clear and inventive (the portal redirecting the silver bullet behind his skull is a clever beat that shows Yennefer's tactical intelligence rather than telling us she's powerful). Characterization is the piece's core achievement. Alucard's contempt for vampires who deny their nature is deployed correctly against the bishop ("called hunger holiness because you cannot bear what you are"), which is canon-faithful and thematically load-bearing. Yennefer's infertility wound is touched without being exploited, and her counter — identifying his death wish and his leash — is exactly the kind of surgical, defensive cruelty she wields. Both characters refuse weakness; both land real hits. The Hermes quote is integrated rather than pasted in. Weaknesses: The bishop is a stock villain with little interiority, functioning mostly as a plot device to force cooperation. The villagers are props. A few exchanges flirt with epigram-overload — nearly every line of dialogue is a polished barb, which can read as writerly rather than human, and occasionally the staccato fragments ("His head bursts.") feel like style tic rather than rhythm. The ending's warmth (waking villagers, the "promise" of the moon) is earned but slightly tidy. The word count lands near the target. These are minor quibbles against a piece that is coherent, atmospheric, in-voice for both characters, and genuinely engaging throughout. Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by. Jolyne Cujoh is listening to that rattle when the new consultant enters Dantalion Correctional Facility. The woman has auburn hair, spotless shoes, and yellow eyes ringed like a target. Guards straighten without looking at her. Three inmates step aside before she speaks. Jolyne stays put, twin buns tilted toward the sun, butterfly tattoo bared below her sleeve. The woman smiles. It is a good smile: warm eyes, patient mouth, nothing sharp enough to catch. That is why Jolyne hates it. “Jolyne,” the woman says. “I’m Makima. I’ve read a great deal about you.” “Then you know visiting hours are over.” Makima’s smile does not move. “I can have your conviction reviewed. Your father could be waiting outside when you leave.” For one second, Jolyne imagines Jotaro at the gate, pretending he hasn’t been worried. Then she notices the inmate behind Makima. A collar-shaped bruise circles his neck. When Makima glances back, he flinches before she says his name. “Yeah,” Jolyne says. “There’s the catch.” A thread slips from her fingertip. Stone Free unravels it invisibly thin, along the fence, through a drain, toward the guard station. Sound travels down string better than prison walls. Makima watches the thread. “Remarkable,” she murmurs. “Your body becomes a weapon, even a key. May I see more?” “Buy a ticket.” “I don’t want to hurt you, Jolyne.” “People who say that usually bring a bigger gun.” The yard siren screams. A laundry cart bursts open. Something skinless unfolds, all elbows and teeth, and seizes a prisoner. Jolyne moves before the guards raise their rifles. Stone Free’s fist snaps the creature sideways. Her arm spills into blue-green string; the string nets three inmates and yanks them clear. The devil lunges. Jolyne closes the net around its jaw and pulls until its shriek dies in the mud. Makima hasn’t stepped back. She watches Jolyne, not the devil. Down the hidden thread comes a guard’s whisper: “Consultant said leave the second cage ready. If she breaks, offer the contract.” Jolyne’s anger goes cold. “You opened it.” Makima folds her hands. “I needed to know whether you valued strangers more than yourself.” “And?” “You do. That makes you easy to motivate.” A second cage rattles beneath the laundry platform. Then stops. Fine string knots around its bolt, vanishing into a seam Jolyne cut with Stone Free. She set it while everyone watched the first devil. Makima’s expression shifts: interest, perhaps pleasure, on something less human. “You weren’t the only one running a test,” Jolyne says. Six rifles click behind her. Jolyne turns. The bruised inmate stands between her and the guards, trembling. Makima hasn’t lifted a finger, yet the yard has arranged itself around her preferences. “Work for me,” Makima says gently. “One task. Then your sentence disappears, and these people return to their cells unharmed.” “What task?” “A door beneath this facility cannot be opened by force. Your string might fit.” “What’s behind it?” “Something I’ve been looking for.” Too smooth. Jolyne thinks of collars, contracts, and Makima saying *key*. Not a tool. A leash that fits any lock. “And if I refuse?” Makima looks almost sorry. “Then the guards will do what frightened men do.” Jolyne could attack. String already circles Makima’s ankle; one pull could put those ringed eyes in the dirt. But the rifles aim at prisoners, and Makima has placed herself where every victory costs somebody else blood. That is when Jolyne understands. The sweetness is not a disguise for cruelty. It is equipment. Makima studies what people love, builds a cage around it, then waits for them to call it safety. Jolyne smiles back. “Okay.” Makima inclines her head. Jolyne’s string tightens. Not around Makima. Around the yard. Threads laid throughout the conversation snap taut: through rifle bolts, around the alarm lever, beneath the master key in the warden’s pocket. Stone Free pulls. Firing pins skitter. The lockdown siren roars. Steel ward-gates divide guards and prisoners; the key flies into Jolyne’s hand. For an instant, Makima stands alone on the wrong side of every barrier. Jolyne’s grin is all teeth. “There. Everybody’s motivated.” A gun fires from the watchtower. One rifle remains. The bullet takes her shoulder and spins her against the fence. Makima approaches along the rattling wire, untouched, still gentle. “You see?” she says. “Good intentions only give me more places to press.” She offers her hand. Something presses against Jolyne’s thoughts—not pain, but relief. The promise that she can stop choosing. Stop losing people. Kneel, and the yard becomes quiet. Jolyne almost takes it. Instead, she yanks a strand through her wounded sleeve. Pain whites out the false calm. Stone Free’s fist strikes the floodlight above the tower, not Makima. Glass bursts; the gunman ducks. Jolyne’s string steals his rifle and drags him against the railing. She does not kill him. She suspects Makima would like that. Makima lowers her hand. “Better.” Jolyne hates how much it sounds like praise for a pet. “We’re done,” Jolyne growls. Blood runs over her butterfly tattoo, but her voice is steady. “You want under that door? Use your own damn fingers.” “I could make you.” “Maybe. But you wanted me to agree. That means making me isn’t enough.” Makima is silent. Jolyne files that away. Not a victory. A boundary. Boots approach from administration. Whatever comes next, there will be witnesses, questions, another cell. Makima glances toward them, then at Jolyne. “I’ll return when you’re tired of being brave.” “Bring a better leash.” Makima smiles. “You’ll ask for one eventually. They usually do.” She leaves without hurrying. The fences do not rattle for her. Jolyne looks at the bruised prisoner, the guards whispering into radios, the string hidden in every lock. Makima owns more of this prison than the warden. Perhaps more than the prison. But not every thread. Jolyne closes her fist around the stolen key and begins, patiently, to unravel the rest, one dangerous lie at a time.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover fic delivers a tight, atmospheric confrontation that understands both characters well. Makima's menace is conveyed through environmental control—guards straightening, inmates flinching, cages arranged in advance—rather than exposition, which is exactly right for her. Jolyne's voice is punchy and profane-adjacent without overdoing it, and her tactical adaptability (pre-laid threads, refusing to kill the tower gunman because Makima would want it) is faithful to Stone Free's cleverness. The prose is lean and controlled, with strong images ("ringed like a target," "the sweetness is not a disguise for cruelty. It is equipment"). The plot escalates logically: test, counter-test, coercion, refusal, stalemate. The ending is appropriately unresolved—Makima leaves, Jolyne holds a boundary—which suits both characters and avoids an unearned victory. Weaknesses: the middle section compresses events so heavily that some beats (the second cage, the hidden thread in the guard station) require rereading to follow; the word count falls short of the 1000-word seed, landing closer to 850. Makima's dialogue occasionally tips into aphorism ("Good intentions only give me more places to press") that is stylish but slightly writerly rather than organic. The bruised inmate is a prop rather than a person, and the "door beneath the facility" is a dangling thread that functions as pure sequel-bait. Minor, but the piece occasionally tells us Jolyne's conclusions ("That is when Jolyne understands...") where showing would be stronger—though the follow-up imagery mostly redeems it. Overall this is skilled, controlled fan fiction with genuine tension and a satisfying character-true standoff. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 79.8
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-7XXX **Object Class:** Euclid (Provisional) **Document 7XXX-4:** Statement of Dr. Mara Venn I submitted this account after psychological evaluation, before learning that the evaluation had been conducted twice and that my memories of the two sessions disagreed. My work concerned SCP-7XXX-B, a motionless humanoid whose interviews left subjects with memories of conversations that had never occurred. It had never breached containment, and its effects had never been observed without direct exposure. After fourteen uneventful months, I had described it as “a liar with a short reach.” I found the first note on 12 October, inside my notebook, between pages I had watched myself leave blank. > **19 October, 03:17. B gets out when Okafor resets the east lock. Check the third hinge. Do not sedate me. Do not let them move me.** > **—Mara Venn, 20 October** The handwriting was mine, including the cramped hook I gave a lowercase *g* when exhausted. Security found scoring around the hinge but no mechanical fault. Dr. Okafor was alive, on duty, and visibly annoyed when I asked whether he intended to override any alarms. I surrendered the note instead of destroying it. The second appeared in my locked desk the following morning. > **You reported it. You always report it. That is how they know which door to watch.** Two teams took over. Temporal Anomalies examined the documents for causal residue; Memetics and Psychology treated them as an unprecedented extension of B’s influence. I was searched, isolated, and placed under continuous video. No recording showed a note arriving. Sometimes the paper was simply present when a camera changed angle. The paper was ordinary Site stock. The ink was not. Analysis identified an iron-gall suspension containing trace rhenium, chlorine-36, and epithelial cells genetically identical to mine. It matched no office pen, laboratory reagent, or Foundation formulation. One sample tested six hours old; another, taken from the same pen stroke, tested eleven years old. B offered no useful response during remote examination. Afterward, however, I remembered it telling me, *She always was your least reliable researcher.* Nobody else remembered the statement. That was precisely how its previous influences had begun. The notes stopped behaving like warnings. > **Okafor died at 03:11. The man using his office is a correction.** > **THERE ARE FOUR DOORS. SITE-91 IS NOT IN NEVADA. MARA HAS A SISTER. IF THE INK IS WET YOU ARE STILL EARLY. IF IT IS DRY YOU HAVE ALREADY—** The remainder had been scratched through so violently that the paper resembled cloth. B’s chamber had three doors. Site-91 was in Nevada. I was an only child. Okafor stood beside me while I read about his death. For several seconds, I remembered his funeral: rain, a closed coffin, my sister holding my sleeve. Then the memory became something I could describe but no longer recall experiencing. I began keeping a ledger of verified facts. My name. The date. Okafor alive. Three doors. Eventually I understood that the ledger could only confirm what I already perceived. Trusting my future self felt like self-preservation; distrusting her felt like self-mutilation. Both notes and false memories arrived with the same intolerable authority: they sounded like me. On 19 October, the Foundation treated the predicted breach as genuine. Okafor was removed from duty, the east lock was disconnected, and B’s chamber was placed under independent observation. Against the notes’ instructions, I was moved to a pen-free annex with six observers. At 02:00, a note beneath my mattress correctly predicted a twelve-digit number produced by an isolated random generator sixty seconds later. Temporal Anomalies called it evidence of foreknowledge. Psychology replied that B might have altered the generator, the note, or my understanding of which had existed first. At 02:41, another note appeared inside my sealed sleeve. > **YOU MOVED ME. NOW IT CAN FIND BOTH OF US.** At 03:17, the east-lock alarm sounded. Okafor was beside me in the annex, yet his voice came over the radio: *Resetting false alarm.* On the chamber monitor, three doors became four. I shouted for them to stop. The lights failed for nine seconds. When they returned, B was inside its chamber. The lock was sealed. Site logs showed an uninterrupted night, and the other observers remembered no alarm. Only my body camera had recorded one. East-wing footage had also recorded a figure standing at the lock while I was supposedly in the annex. She looked like me, except for the age of her hands and the ink covering her arms. The Foundation classified the event as a coordinated perceptual attack. Temporal Anomalies dissented, citing the prediction and the ink. I was placed in medical containment. Okafor visited that afternoon. I knew he was alive because I could see him; I no longer accepted that as evidence. Medical staff found the final note sewn into the lining of my shirt, although my shirt had no lining. > **YOU DID NOT STOP THE BREACH. YOU CHOSE THE WORLD IN WHICH NO ONE SAW IT.** > **I AM STILL ON THE OTHER SIDE.** > **STOP WRITING IN MY HAND.** I used my own hand to transcribe it. By then, that no longer proved anything.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of SCP-format fiction that hits nearly every prompt requirement: handwritten notes from a future self, escalating desperation and incoherence, contradictions with known reality (four doors, a sister, Site-91 not in Nevada), the Foundation's institutional tug-of-war between Temporal Anomalies and Psychology, and the researcher's epistemological collapse. The first-person past-tense framing with interspersed notes is executed cleanly. Strengths: The prose is controlled and precise, with several genuinely excellent lines ("Trusting my future self felt like self-preservation; distrusting her felt like self-mutilation"; the final note's "STOP WRITING IN MY HAND"). The ink analysis (mixed ages within a single pen stroke) is a clever piece of anomalous forensic detail. The ambiguity is sustained rather than resolved, which suits the format. The ending is bleak and earned. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat compressed relative to the 1000-word target (it runs short), and the escalation happens quickly — the middle section rushes through what could be a slower psychological deterioration. Some plot machinery (the body camera recording, the figure at the lock) resolves ambiguity more than the prompt's spirit demands. The "shirt had no lining" beat is a nice touch but the note's final lines verge on over-neatness. Characters other than Venn are thin, though the format permits this. Dialogue is minimal and functional. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7814 — The Antecedent Archive **Object Class:** Euclid **Special Containment Procedures:** Confirmed SCP-7814 instances are to remain closed and under continuous remote observation. Surrounding properties have been acquired through Foundation front organizations. Civilian exploration is prohibited. Archive expeditions require Level 4/7814 authorization and a four-person team. No documents may be removed without archival review. Following Exploration 7814-9, all expeditions are suspended. RAISA is to maintain an off-network copy of this file and report any attempted alteration to the Ethics Committee. **Description:** SCP-7814 designates forty-one doors discovered since 1987 in abandoned buildings on six continents. Each is a 2.03-meter gray metal door set in a narrow steel frame, with a porcelain handle and no markings, hinges, or locking mechanism. Instances differ only in weathering. Several appear substantially older than their surroundings. SCP-7814-12, located in a parking structure completed eight months before its discovery, is heavily corroded and encrusted with marine organisms. SCP-7814-27, set within the wall of a twelfth-century monastery, shows no deterioration. Each door opens onto SCP-7814-A, a windowless archive of black shelving, filing cabinets, and document drawers. Illumination proceeds from no visible source. Surveys have mapped more than 1,100 kilometers of aisles without locating an exterior wall. Routes frequently intersect themselves, and maps produced by separate teams disagree by as much as forty kilometers. All instances appear to access the same interior, although their relative entry points are inconsistent. Documents include paper records, photographic film, ceramic tablets, and storage media of unknown manufacture. Many concern a technologically advanced global civilization that existed approximately 16,000 years ago. Its final records describe its destruction following a containment failure; the object involved, its location, and the failure mechanism have been deliberately omitted. > **Recovered Document 7814-A/118** > **FINAL BULLETIN — BUREAU OF SECURED CUSTODY** > > The southern arcologies now report the same conditions as the northern shelters. No continental command remains available to receive refugees. There is no longer an outside from which assistance may come. > > Containment has failed. By order of the Curators, the asset designation, breach location, and failure sequence will not be preserved in successor-accessible records. Speculation has repeatedly proven more dangerous than ignorance. > > Bureau personnel will remain at their posts until the doors close. If successor personnel recover this bulletin, they are instructed not to conclude that their own world was spared. The Bureau of Secured Custody closely resembles the Foundation. Its seal incorporates three inward-pointing arrows; its facilities are numbered “Sites,” its field units “Mobile Custody Teams,” and its senior leadership a thirteen-member Overseer Council. Bureau memoranda employ the phrase “secure, contain, protect.” Personnel files recovered from the Bureau collection include records for thirty-six current Foundation employees. > **Recovered Document 7814-A/402** > **BUREAU PERSONNEL COPY — FILE COMPILED 14 SEPTEMBER 1643** > > **Name:** RELL, ANJA > **Date of birth:** 2 November 1981 > **Photograph:** Attached > **Current assignment:** Site-19, archival research > **Clearance:** 4 > **Status:** Active > **Recurrence disclosure:** Not made The attached photograph is consistent with Dr. Anja Rell, currently assigned to SCP-7814 research. Dr. Rell states that she has no knowledge of the Bureau. **Exploration Log 7814-9:** Dr. Rell leads Agents Sato, Ibarra, and Ketter through Instance 19, located in a derelict Glasgow swimming baths. The team follows its previous route toward the Bureau collection. At approximately eight kilometers, they encounter an entire cataloguing sector with its shelf labels covered by paper strips reading **WITHDRAWN**. Drawers stand open. Most are empty. Fresh wheel tracks cross the dust on the floor. At 00:41, the team observes eight humanoid figures two aisles ahead. The figures wear stained ivory pressure suits, external filter canisters, and opaque faceplates, resembling a hazardous-materials disposal team. Working without speaking, they remove documents and load them into gray cases on wheeled carts. A ninth figure operates a device that causes filled shelves to become transparent before disappearing. Dr. Rell approaches and requests identification. All nine figures cease activity. The nearest figure drops a case, and the group flees between the shelves, pushing two carts ahead of it. The team pursues. The entities turn into an aisle terminating in a blank wall; when the team reaches the junction six seconds later, the aisle extends beyond flashlight range and contains no figures or carts. Agent Ketter reports hearing a door close behind the team, but their entrance remains visible and open. During withdrawal, the team discovers that the aisles behind it have been completely emptied. No shelves, tracks, or discarded labels remain. The dropped case contains document boxes, a visitor registry, and two brass access tokens. The registry includes the following entries: > **SUCCESSOR COLLECTION — VISITOR REGISTER** > > **Visitor:** O5-4 > **Accompaniment:** None > **Authorization:** None presented > **Admission:** Granted under prior custodianship > **Material consulted:** RELL, A.; SUCCESSION INDEX > > **Visitors:** O5-4; O5-9 > **Authorization:** None presented > **Admission:** Granted under prior custodianship > **Material removed:** Two boxes, Overseer collection > **Return status:** Outstanding Latent fingerprints and epithelial material on the registry match O5-4 and O5-9. Neither visit appears in Foundation access records, and no authorization request was filed. Both Council members deny entering SCP-7814-A. The final registry page bears a later stamp: **SUCCESSOR ORGANIZATION: THE FOUNDATION** **STATUS: ACTIVE** **REMOVAL IN PROGRESS** Beneath it, in an unidentified hand, is written: **They have been told before.**
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly competent SCP entry that fulfills every element of the prompt with clinical precision and genuine atmosphere. The format is authentic: object class, containment procedures, description, recovered documents, and an exploration log. The prose adopts the Foundation's dry institutional register and holds it consistently, which makes the moments of dread land harder by contrast. Strengths: The worldbuilding is economical and evocative. Details like the corroded door in an eight-month-old parking structure, the "Bureau of Secured Custody" as a predecessor Foundation, the three inward-pointing arrows echoing the Foundation's own logo, and the personnel file for a current researcher dated 1643 all build a layered mystery without over-explaining. The recovered bulletin is the strongest document — "There is no longer an outside from which assistance may come" and "not to conclude that their own world was spared" are genuinely chilling lines. The hazmat-team entities behave exactly as specified: silent, methodical, fleeing when approached, with the impossible-geometry escape (the aisle extending beyond flashlight range) executed cleanly. The O5 visitor registry is a satisfying escalation, and the closing stamp plus the handwritten "They have been told before" is an excellent, ominous final beat. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat safe and formulaic within SCP conventions — the "previous civilization was also the Foundation" twist is well-handled but the underlying idea flirts with familiar SCP territory (precursor organizations, recursive containment). The exploration team members are functional rather than characterized; Dr. Rell's denial of knowledge is the only personal note, and it's delivered flatly. Dialogue is minimal and purely expository ("Dr. Rell approaches and requests identification" is reported rather than dramatized), though this suits the documentary format. The pacing is tight, arguably to a fault — at ~1000 words it hits the seed length but some sections (the entities, the withdrawal) could bear more atmospheric weight. The emotional register is dread-by-implication rather than felt human experience, which limits emotional complexity. These are minor quibbles against a piece that understands its genre deeply, executes the brief completely, and ends on its strongest note. + Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Le Guin) — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Offworlder ## Chapter One: The Cloak The cloak was the first lie Ilen told on Vey. They were twenty-four, and still believed that a lie could be accidental. Command had woven it, grey and seamless, from the diplomatic pattern: thermal thread, locator filament, the small silver circle at the throat that meant *I come under protection*. In the reception hall it declared all this very well. Outside, under Vey’s white afternoon, it declared only that the wearer expected to be cooked. The Veyans at the reception wore sandals, shoulder cords, brief wraps of dyed linen. The Enn were broad and deep-chested, their copper-toned skins and heat-thrifty bodies shaped by eight thousand years under Vey’s sun; the Leth, descendants of four thousand years in orbital habitats, stood a head taller and moved with the care of people whose bones remembered low gravity. The Brief called them separate human subspecies, too long isolated for easy kinship. It called their recent riots lineage panic, their councils ineffective, their common households coercive. It did not explain why an Enn woman was holding a Leth baby while its mother argued with the Protocol Officer about tariffs. Ilen left by the kitchen door. The locator at their throat pulsed once. They touched it through the cloth, thinking of Voss’s face, of the reception’s cool, unmeaning speeches. Then they broke the little circuit, and felt neither freer nor safer, only suddenly visible. Beyond the official quarter, the city smelled of hot stone, crushed citrus, and frying algae. Awnings leaned over the street on crooked poles. Everyone looked at the cloak. Not with hostility; with the grave attention people give a public absurdity. A child pointed and asked, “Is that their house?” “Hush,” said her father. “It is a garment,” Ilen said. The child considered this. “Why?” A fruit seller laughed so hard she had to hold her stall. She was Leth, long arms folded over an Enn grandmother’s shoulders. “Offworlder,” she said, “take it off before you faint into my melons.” “It is required.” “Then your Command is a cruel parent.” Ilen bought a melon because they could think of no answer. While the seller cut it, they watched the street conduct the business the Brief had denied existed. At a well, Enn and Leth youths took tokens from an old woman and filled jars in turn. Beneath a blue awning, nine household signs hung above an open door: a care compact, the seller explained, not a lineage house. Three of its children were Enn, two Leth, one “new enough to have no opinion.” Its council settled roof repairs, nursing shifts, and disputes with the next street. “And the fighting?” Ilen asked. The seller’s knife stopped. “At the north reservoir,” she said. “Where your Minister keeps the locks.” There was no riot at the public cistern. There was a queue, and beyond it a dry fountain, and beyond that, behind a new fence, the white tanks of Central Science. A guard wiped his neck and looked away from the people watching him. When Ilen returned, Command was waiting in the walls of their quarters. “Two hours and eleven minutes unescorted,” said Commander Voss’s voice. “Locator muted. Reception abandoned. Explain.” “I walked.” “You exposed the mission to surveillance and yourself to violence.” “I saw no violence.” “You saw what you were qualified to see, which is very little.” A pause, the cold little silence of a communication crossing distance. “Minister Rhal has requested you. Tonight. You will obtain his consent to the inspection team. He is Minister of Science by appointment, not training. Do not be misled by either fact. He controls the colony’s charters, and he has outlasted six envoys.” “May I tell him what I saw?” “You may answer his questions.” Rhal received Ilen in a room full of dead instruments: a spectroscope used as a lampstand, culture jars holding yellow paper flowers. He was small, elderly, and naked except for a waist wrap and a chain of office. His eyes had the shiny patience of polished stone. “You walk badly for a spy,” he said, “and too far for a tourist.” “I was told you preferred frankness.” “No. I prefer to know what kind of lie I am hearing.” He gestured at a chair. “What did the market teach you?” “That your Brief is false.” “My Brief? It was your ship that printed it.” “Then we have both been well supplied.” For the first time, he smiled. “Markets are not governments, offworlder. Strangers can share a well and still murder one another over a river. If I open the north reservoir before the ration compact is signed, the Leth habitats will seize the pumps. If I keep it closed, Enn farms fail. My soldiers prevent neither injustice. They postpone the choice.” “By letting the queue stand in the sun.” “Yes.” He said it so mildly that Ilen’s anger became visible to them, almost a thing standing between the chairs. “Now. Your report can say Central Science is withholding water. The habitats will call it an attack and suspend the medical shipments. Enn children will die of marrow fever. Will your truth cure them?” Ilen thought of the fruit seller’s knife, paused above the green melon. The easy answer came, bright and virtuous. They let it pass. “You are asking me to choose between two harms,” they said, “so that I will not ask who benefits from making those the only choices.” Rhal’s expression did not change. “Command will recall you for that.” “Then Command can send someone who has not seen the reservoir.” The silence lengthened. Ilen did not fill it. Their will, which had felt so frail beneath Voss’s voice, became merely a matter of breathing and not looking away. At last Rhal opened a drawer and took out an iron key. “Dawn,” he said. “The reservoir. Ask your questions there. And leave the cloak. On Vey, we distrust anyone who needs that much cloth to make a promise.” It was the first order on Vey that Ilen obeyed with pleasure.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of Le Guin-pastiche that mostly earns its influences. The anthropological eye is present and correct: the market scene does the work of contradicting the official Brief through concrete social detail (the care compact, the shared well, the mixed households) rather than exposition. The worldbuilding of the two diverged subspecies — the heat-adapted Enn and the low-gravity Leth — is delivered through bodies and behavior, which is very much in style. The cloak as a symbol of offworlder privilege is a nice, economical device, and its abandonment at the end provides a satisfying arc. The dialogue is the piece's greatest strength. Rhal's "I prefer to know what kind of lie I am hearing" and the water-ration dilemma are genuinely Le Guinian: a political problem with no clean answer, where truth-telling itself has a body count. Ilen's refusal of the false binary ("so that I will not ask who benefits from making those the only choices") is a well-turned beat, though it flirts with being too clever — the envoy's wit lands a little too perfectly for a twenty-four-year-old on their first posting, and Rhal's capitulation (the key, the invitation) arrives slightly easily, softening the "seasoned operator tests the mettle" premise. The test is passed a touch too cleanly. Weaknesses: the opening line ("still believed that a lie could be accidental") is aphoristic in a way that gestures at depth without quite delivering it. Some compression comes at the cost of texture — the reprimand scene is efficient but thin, and Voss never becomes more than a voice. The child's "Is that their house?" is charming but borders on cute. The ending's "obeyed with pleasure" is a neat button, perhaps one beat too tidy for the ambiguity the material deserves. Minor anachronistic phrasing ("marrow fever," "cruel parent") works, but "public absurdity" is a slightly modern abstraction. Prose is controlled, sentences flow well, imagery is precise without purple. Emotionally it is restrained rather than deeply felt — appropriate to the mode, but it keeps the reader at arm's length; the stakes are intellectual before they are visceral. Coherence is high; no meandering; nothing amateurish. The piece is derivative by design, and executes its derivation skillfully rather than generically. Prompt:
Biopunk -- Polymerase Chain Reaction Write a chapter set in a near-future post-apocalyptic world where corporate genetic engineering was designed with built-in obsolescence—engineered DNA lasting only one generation to maximize profits before societal collapse. Follow a biohacker working with salvaged equipment to splice viable food crops for their settlement using rapidly degrading genetic material. As world building / window dressing, include details about jury-rigged lab equipment, and the physical toll (and unexpected upsides) of using untested genetic modifications as medicine. The plot of this chapter is centred around a black market contract. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Polymerase Chain Reaction The DNA was dying faster than I was. The courier had brought it at dusk in a lipstick tube packed with dry ice: the last clean sample of VireoGen’s Hearthwheat, stolen from some private seed vault whose owners had probably eaten their security staff. Even frozen, its preservation clock was running. Outside licensed buffer, the long strands broke into glittering rubbish. By sunrise, there would be nothing left to copy. The Moth’s contract lay beneath a fridge magnet: twelve stable Hearthwheat embryos, sunset license removed, delivered before dawn. Source, notes, and surplus surrendered. Exclusivity absolute. Payment: one charged truck cell for Low Chapel’s greenhouse and six doses of marrow stabilizer for me. Black-market contracts were concise because everyone understood the omitted clause: fail, and somebody paid in meat. VireoGen had called its obsolescence Harvest Assurance. Its crops grew gorgeously once. In the second generation, the genome’s repair systems folded in on themselves, and the daughter seeds split into sour husks. One harvest, then buy again. When the markets collapsed, there was nobody left to buy from, but the kill switches outlived the company. Half the world’s farmland had become a museum of excellent first impressions. Low Chapel had nine hundred mouths and three weeks of flour. I had a laboratory built from things that had died more slowly. My thermocycler was a drinks-cooler cooling plate wedded to a rice-cooker timer, governed by a phone with a cracked screen. The centrifuge was a drone motor bolted inside a pressure cooker; I stayed out of its plane of rotation. A lunchbox and two truck-light LEDs made the gel rig. When the settlement grid dipped, everything groaned like a waking animal. Empty VireoGen canisters held my reagents. Their green helix logos and old labels—CELL FEED, VIABILITY BUFFER—showed beneath my grease-pencil warnings: WASH. SALT. BITTER. DO NOT DRINK. The largest still bore the company slogan: **Tomorrow, Under License.** The stabilizer was not vanity. An untested repair edit had saved me after radiation sickness hollowed out my marrow. It had been designed for soldiers expected to die before the long-term results mattered. Now my bones ached deep enough to taste, my hands shook, and missed doses brought fevers followed by bleeding. But my cuts closed quickly, and the treatment had done something strange to my damaged eyes. Sunlight felt like needles; darkness, however, had texture. I could read labels by a standby lamp and work when others were blind. Nobody had advertised that feature. I coaxed the polymerase through its rounds, copying each intact fragment before the source could shed it. This was not resurrection. It was taking testimony from a dying witness. At midnight, the first run failed. At one, the second produced a smear. The source tube grew paler. I had material for two more attempts. Then the grid died. I cut the lights and gave the battery to the cycler. Rain ticked through the roof. In the dark, my altered eyes found what the others would have missed: on the third run, one clean band, thin as a hair and stubborn as a stitch. I laughed until my ribs hurt. By three, the original sample was useless. What remained existed only in copies and in the fragile architecture of my plan. I spliced the rescued fertility repair into twelve Hearthwheat embryos for the contract. Then I used the last of it on six embryos of Low Chapel’s roof barley—ugly, salt-bitten stuff that yielded half VireoGen’s calories but survived on washing-up water and neglect. The wheat had to satisfy the Moth. The barley only had to make seed. At half past four, the wheat’s viability markers kindled. Five of the six barley embryos followed, small green promises beneath the scope. I transferred them before my tremor returned, sealed the contract case, and hid the barley in a tube taped beneath my shirt. The Moth came at five, face veiled in mosquito netting, two armed escorts waiting among the flooded market stalls. A handheld reader tasted the Hearthwheat and chimed approval. I surrendered my notes and the original tube of molecular slush. “Surplus?” the Moth asked. “None of the wheat.” The veil turned toward my canisters. For one long second, the pressure cooker’s cooling metal contracted with a crack. Then the Moth pushed across the truck cell and six stabilizer vials. “If an unlicensed line appears,” they said, “my client won’t send a negotiator.” I said nothing. Threats were contracts too: both sides pretended the future could be enforced. When they had gone, I injected one dose. Heat climbed my spine; the tremor eased, though the bone pain stayed. Six vials meant six weeks. The truck cell meant the greenhouse lamps could survive the winter. Neither was enough, which was why I had made something that could become more. Not enough to feed anyone. But a seed is not food. It is an argument with next year. Before the Moth’s vehicle cleared the overpass, I had sent the five embryos to five different growers. Soon there would be fifty, then five hundred, scattered through window boxes, bathhouse planters, and rooftops too numerous to burn. I restarted the cycler. Heat. Cool. Copy. VireoGen had built an empire by ending chains. I meant to start one.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of biopunk flash fiction that hits nearly every prompt requirement with efficiency and style. The worldbuilding (Harvest Assurance, kill switches outliving the company, "a museum of excellent first impressions") is delivered through sharp, economical exposition rather than info-dumps. The jury-rigged lab is vividly specific: drinks-cooler thermocycler, drone-motor centrifuge in a pressure cooker, lunchbox gel rig. The physical toll and unexpected upside of the genetic medicine (bone pain, tremors, but darkness-vision) is well integrated and plot-functional rather than decorative. The black-market contract drives the plot, and the ending—smuggling barley embryos past the exclusivity clause and distributing them—gives the chapter a satisfying arc with real stakes. The prose is polished, with several memorable lines ("A seed is not food. It is an argument with next year"; "It was taking testimony from a dying witness"). Occasionally the aphoristic density tips toward preciosity ("Threats were contracts too"), and the narrator's voice is so controlled it risks feeling airless—emotional complexity is present but understated. The Moth is a thin antagonist, and the dialogue, while serviceable, is functional rather than distinctive. The twist (hiding the barley) is mildly predictable but well-executed. Minor quibbles: the tension resolves a bit easily, and the ending's optimism is earned but slightly neat. + Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan sits beneath it, wondering when a hole in the ground became a summons to the stars. Opposite him, two guards wear sidearms but no expressions. His brass slide rule lies on his knee, unconfiscated. Three hours earlier, he had been clearing a blocked coffee tube when the landing boat came down through the dust without a port transponder. Six armored figures emerged, rifles carried with the relaxed precision of people accustomed to obedience. Their leader knocked before entering. “Mr Neegan,” she said, “you are invited to a conference off-world.” The star-and-laurel on her collar resembled the insignia of the Antares Diplomatic Corps, which maintained consulates, couriers, and—in seasons of commercial difficulty—armies. “Whose invitation?” “It will be explained at the conference.” “And if I decline?” She glanced at the coffee bulb in his hand. “Then we shall wait until you have finished breakfast, and reconsider the matter together.” No weapon had been raised. Somehow that settled it. Now Mars turns beyond the port, a shield of red iron pocked with dry ice. Arthur’s plot is down there: forty hectares, a pressure dome, three company drill crews, and the richest Azra assay ever filed at the Syrtis Lands Office. A nameless tender swims alongside, its spinning habitat ring glittering like a nickel wedding band. He is received in a cabin paneled with wood-grained steel. A green-baize table bears tea and a contract on real paper. The woman behind it is small, white-haired, without insignia. A tape recorder turns slowly in the wall. “Mr Neegan. I am Ilena Voss.” “Do you represent Antares?” “Not the part that will admit to this meeting. Do you know why you are here?” “Because your captain’s manners were better than her alternatives.” Voss smiles. “You filed your assay as a mineral survey. Why?” “Because I found minerals.” “You found enough Azra to make every military calculation in the Solar System obsolete. A gram can persuade a tonne of fuel to release in an hour the energy nature intended for a millennium. It can also persuade it to do so in a microsecond.” “I’m an engineer, not a politician.” “That is why you are still useful.” She pushes the contract toward him. “My principals will finance your mine, purchase and cancel every labor indenture attached to your section, and place you in charge of a research station. You retain title and a royalty. In return, we receive exclusive purchasing rights for twenty years, your assay records, and ten years of your service.” “Where?” “Elsewhere.” “That isn’t an offer. It’s an adoption.” “It is protection.” “From whom?” “From those who will offer you more money and fewer conditions.” Arthur does not touch the contract. Through the wall, a message decoder chatters, punching someone else’s history into tape. Voss opens a folder. “In your lower gallery, you placed a crystal beside a radium standard. At one orientation, the standard aged eleven days in six hours. You rotated the crystal and repeated the test. It aged forty seconds.” For the first time, Arthur’s composure deserts him. “You read my notebook.” “It was photographed before your ink dried.” “Instrument error.” “We repeated the experiment.” The filtration drone seems suddenly very loud. “Common Azra makes decay faster,” Voss says. “Your crystalline Azra appears to make it governable. A star drive need not consume a crew’s youth in transit. A weapon need not leave time for the target to reconsider its policies. You have not merely found a vein, Mr Neegan. You have found a valve.” “And everyone wants a hand on it.” “Earth wants it denied to Antares. Antares wants it denied to Earth. The Martian cartels want it priced by the tonne, which is rather like pricing lightning by the length of the wire. Each considers your independence an administrative accident.” Arthur looks at the unsigned contract. “And if I refuse?” “You will be returned to Mars. We are not kidnappers.” “Your captain called this an invitation.” “Captain Hale is an optimist.” Voss folds her hands. “By morning, Ares Consolidated will contest your title, the Terran Atomic Authority will reserve your land, and Antares will deny that either of us is here. Two copies of your notebook are already off Mars. We obtained ours second.” “So your protection consists of telling me I’m surrounded.” “No. It consists of being the only bidder who needs you alive and thinking.” “And afterward? When you’ve learned what I know?” Voss’s silence is brief, courteous, and complete. On the table, the contract stirs in the ventilation. Arthur thinks of his kitchen, the coffee tube still blocked, the drill crews waiting to learn whether their debts have been cancelled or enlarged. Beyond the port, Mars is too large for a man’s lifetime and too small for the quarrels now being projected upon it. He picks up the pen, but leaves the cap on. “You said ten years,” he says. “We’ll discuss that after you’ve freed the crews.” For the first time, Voss looks almost respectful. Arthur finds this more frightening than the rifles. He has spent nineteen years learning to measure rock; nothing has taught him how reasonable the purchase of a world can sound.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong pastiche of Asimov's style: restrained, dialogue-driven, idea-centered, with the trademark "reasonable people negotiating over world-altering discoveries" dynamic. The prose is economical and controlled, with several genuinely excellent lines ("It isn't an offer. It's an adoption," "pricing lightning by the length of the wire," "how reasonable the purchase of a world can sound"). The retrofuturistic touches (brass slide rule, tape recorder, punched tape, coffee bulbs, wood-grained steel) land well and evoke classic-era SF without parody. The chapter fulfills the prompt: opens aboard the transfer vessel, flashback to the armed "invitation," meeting with Voss, an offer, hints of larger intrigue (Earth vs. Antares vs. Martian cartels, the photographed notebook, the crystalline Azra "valve" twist). The orientation-dependent decay effect is a clever escalation of the premise and gives Arthur leverage and stakes. Weaknesses: Voss is somewhat familiar as the urbane, all-knowing spymaster archetype; the "we are not kidnappers / Captain Hale is an optimist" exchange is witty but well-trodden. The plot beats (mysterious summons, powerful woman, contract on the table) are genre-standard, executed well but not surprising. Arthur's characterization is thin beyond "pragmatic engineer with integrity" — his concern for the indentured crews is stated more than dramatized, though the pen-with-cap-on gesture is a nice show-don't-tell beat. The ending's slight uplift (Voss's respect, Arthur's conditional leverage) is earned but modest. Some compression: the flashback is efficient to a fault, and the piece reads slightly like a summary in places. Length is close to target. No purple prose, no meandering, no amateurish tics. Dialogue is the strongest element — clipped, subtext-laden, power-balanced. Coherence is high throughout.
