+ Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations By midnight, the darkroom smelled of vinegar and warm dust. Under the safelight, everything was the color of a held breath. Elliot stood over the developer in a shredded black sweater, silver chain slipping from his collar. Thrift-store ghost, my friends called him. They meant it as praise. Our project was an exchange of portraits. I had photographed Elliot; he had photographed me. We had three nights to make the prints agree. It was going badly in the interesting way. He lifted my portrait of him from the tray. On paper, he was all cheekbone and shadow, looking away from the camera. “Is that what I look like to you?” “Annoyingly photogenic?” “Dani.” “You look like you,” I said. He made a small sound, not quite a laugh. “That’s the problem.” All semester, I’d been fascinated by him: the soft voice that dismantled an artist’s statement, lace cuffs under a combat jacket, the apologies preceding ferociously good questions. Wanting him had seemed simple until I noticed how carefully I was noticing him. My taste usually ran toward definition: men with decisive shoulders, women who made femininity look like architecture. I wore shaved sides and red lipstick like a thesis statement. I liked knowing what desire said about me, and being the one who decided when conversation became flirting, and flirting became something else. Elliot set the print in the stop bath. “I’ve been thinking about gender,” he said. “Which makes me sound more informed than I am.” “Okay.” “It isn’t just the clothes. I like the clothes. That’s part of what’s confusing. Sometimes being a man feels fine. Sometimes it feels like a coat everyone keeps handing me after I’ve said I’m not cold. I don’t know if that means I’m not one, or not only one, or if I just hate coats.” “Coats are structurally suspicious,” I offered. He smiled, startled. “There it is.” “There what is?” “You not making me finish the thought.” My first impulse was to finish it for him: offer labels, campus resources, a reading list; make tenderness indistinguishable from management. Beneath that was a less noble wish that he would become legible quickly, so I could decide what my attraction meant and whether I was still who I thought. He had not handed me a puzzle. He had trusted me with a pause. And there was exhilaration too, bright and frightening: not at his uncertainty, but at being present when he risked a true sentence and remained himself. I wanted to protect that. I also wanted, with embarrassing clarity, to touch his wrist where his pulse showed. “What do you need tonight?” I asked. “For this not to become a seminar.” “I can be extremely ignorant.” “I’ve seen your critiques. I doubt it.” He nudged my shoulder with his. “Just let it be unfinished.” Unfinished was not my natural habitat. When feeling outpaced me, I tried to be useful. Our last good print needed checking, so I reached for the white light. Elliot said, “Wait—” The room flashed ordinary white. On the counter sat the paper box, open, its black bag folded back around the fresh stack I had meant to close. I snapped the switch off. The whole stack was done for. Too late is a very short time in a darkroom. “Well,” Elliot said. “Those are going to be expressive.” “Twenty-five sheets.” “Twenty-six, if we count my dignity.” I groaned. “I’m sorry. I’ll replace them. I know they’re expensive, and we needed—” “Dani. It’s paper.” “It’s our final-project paper.” “Then it’s our very prestigious mistake.” Being six years older had not made me wiser, only better at looking competent. I stood there, furious, until his fingers closed lightly around my wrist. Not restraining. Just there. “You can mess things up in front of me,” he said. “That is a terrible thing to permit.” “I thought so too.” The safelight hummed. His hand stayed. I could feel where helpfulness might become an excuse to hold on. “Can I ask you something without it becoming a thing?” he said. “Statistically, no.” He laughed, nervous. “I like how you look at me. Even when I don’t know what you’re seeing.” “I’m seeing you. Unfortunately, I’m also trying not to be strange about it.” “You’re being a little strange.” “I’m being extremely strange.” My attraction had not vanished when he spoke; it had lost its explanation. That should have cooled it. Instead, I felt more curious than certain, and more alive than curious. I didn’t want to make his self-discovery into my liberation narrative, or become one more person asking him to resolve so I could relax. “I want to kiss you,” I said, because evasion seemed worse. “But I don’t want to take over.” His breath caught. “Those aren’t the same thing.” “No?” “You could tell me what you want and still let me decide.” Quiet, not passive. I had been so busy giving him room that I had nearly decided where it ended. “Then yes,” I said. “I want to. Do you?” He nodded, then seemed annoyed at the inadequacy of nodding. “Yes. Slowly. I might be bad at it.” “I’m not grading you.” He leaned in and stopped an inch away. I did not close the distance. He did. The first kiss was cautious and ended when he laughed against my mouth. The second was warmer. My hand found the back of his chair instead of his neck. It took effort not to steer, but he curled his fingers into my sweater, and effort became astonishment. When we parted, my portrait of him floated in the wash. Nothing about him had been answered. Nothing about me had either. Wanting without a category was not the same as wanting without care. “Tomorrow,” I said, “we buy paper.” “Together?” “If you want.” “And dinner after? Not project dinner.” I smiled. “You’re getting assertive.” “Exposure,” he said. “It changes things.” I rolled my eyes, because otherwise I might tell him he was wonderful. We cleaned up, shoulders touching, the ruined stack useless on the counter. Nothing about us had resolved. The last print would look different dry, anyway. I turned off the safelight. Elliot found my hand before I found the door.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, controlled piece of literary short fiction. The prose is economical and precise, with a distinctive voice for Dani—wry, clipped, self-aware. The darkroom setting is used thematically (exposure, development, ruined paper) rather than just decoratively, and the ruined photo paper incident is a genuinely well-crafted beat: it gives Dani a flaw (carelessness under stress), gives Elliot a chance to show quiet strength, and grounds the emotional shift in a concrete event rather than pure conversation. The dialogue is the strongest element—naturalistic, funny without being stand-up, and character-revealing ("Twenty-six, if we count my dignity"; "Exposure. It changes things"). The gender-questioning conversation avoids both after-school-special earnestness and glibness; the "coat everyone keeps handing me" metaphor is fresh. The central tension—Dani's assertiveness vs. giving Elliot agency—is dramatized rather than stated, particularly in the kiss scene where she deliberately doesn't close the distance. Minor criticisms: the aphoristic density occasionally tips toward preciosity ("Too late is a very short time in a darkroom"; "Wanting without a category was not the same as wanting without care")—a few too many polished epigrams for a 25-year-old narrator, edging toward the overworked. The ending is tidy and slightly warm for the ambiguity it claims, though the final line ("Elliot found my hand before I found the door") earns its tenderness. The word count is under the 1000-word seed, though the seed is loose guidance. Some emotional beats resolve a touch quickly—Elliot's shift from tentative to "getting assertive" is fast but plausible given the established rapport. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Stolen Moments in Roma At eight on a bright September morning, Ben stepped backward from the Trevi Fountain, trying to reconcile his guidebook with the Baroque riot above him, and nearly died beneath a motorcycle. Alessandra braked with a shriek. Her front wheel stopped an inch from his knees. “Madonna, guarda!” she snapped. “Cammini, leggi, respiri—scegli due!” “I beg your—sorry. *Mi scusi.* Non… vedere… lei.” “Clearly. I was only the large, noisy thing.” Coins glittered beneath the water. Tourists raised their phones, disappointed to find no blood. Ben closed his guidebook on one finger. “I was looking for the correct viewing position.” “For a fountain?” “It’s rather complicated.” “It squirts water, Professor.” “How did you know I was—” “You apologize like a lecturer.” She was all black leather, dark curls and amusement. A courier’s box was strapped behind her. On the motorcycle’s red fuel tank, a deep dent wore flamboyant streaks of turquoise and yellow, as though it had once lost an argument with a parrot. Alessandra took the guidebook from his hands. “Trevi. Pantheon. Lunch, moderately priced. Colosseum.” She turned a page. “You have scheduled *wandering* at four.” “It seemed efficient.” Something in her expression changed. She produced a spare helmet and tossed it to him. He caught it with his stomach. “Come.” “I’m sorry?” “Again? Already?” *** At Piazza Venezia she leaned into a gap in the traffic so narrow that Ben glimpsed his own obituary. He initially held the courier box; after the second roundabout, he held Alessandra. “Better,” she called over her shoulder. “I wasn’t aware there was a correct technique!” “There isn’t. I just like your face.” He could not see it, but suspected she was smiling. They delivered a wax-sealed envelope to a palazzo near Campo de’ Fiori, where Alessandra told the porter that Ben was an English inspector. “Of what?” Ben whispered. “Look serious.” “I *am* serious.” “Perfect.” Five minutes later they emerged onto a private rooftop among chimneys, television aerials and sheets snapping in the sun. Rome spread around them: domes, ochre walls, swallows stitching the sky. Ben forgot to speak. Alessandra watched him instead of the view. “My father repaired motorcycles in Garbatella,” she said. “My mother says I was born in the wrong gear.” “What do you deliver?” “Documents. Medicine. Divorce papers. Once, a cake shaped like an archbishop.” “Was that legal?” “The cake?” A key rattled in the rooftop door. “Custode,” she murmured. They fled down six flights of service stairs, past an astonished woman carrying artichokes, and burst into the street laughing. Ben’s guidebook fell open; Alessandra’s hand closed around his wrist before he could retrieve his dignity as well. Outside a café, he bent double, breathless. “That was—” “Illegal?” “Exhilarating.” She looked at him then, less amused and more curious. Over espresso, Ben explained that he was on sabbatical, writing about monastic silence. “You came to Rome for silence?” “It has been a disappointment.” She laughed so suddenly that the barista glanced over. While Ben attempted to apologize to him too, a tiny silver spoon slid beneath Alessandra’s cuff. By the time Ben looked back, she was stirring her coffee with her finger. “Hot,” she said, and sucked the coffee from it. Ben knocked over his cup. *** At noon she bought them fried artichokes in the Jewish Ghetto and refused to tell him which parts were edible. At three she made him climb a chained stairway down to the Tiber, where he tore his trousers and pretended not to mind. At four—the hour appointed for wandering—she took his pencil and crossed out the rest of his itinerary. “That was library time.” “Tragic.” “I have a book to write.” “So write: *Today I was kidnapped by a beautiful criminal.*” “You’re not—” She raised an eyebrow. Ben discovered he could no longer finish sentences reliably. By sunset they were on the Pincio terrace, Rome turning rose-gold below them. Alessandra stood close enough to adjust the collar of his shirt, though it did not need adjusting. “You do this often?” he asked. “Ruin British academics?” “Abduct strangers.” “Only the polite ones. They’re easier to carry.” Her delivery phone chimed. As she reached for it, her jacket fell open. Ben glimpsed the café spoon, the porter’s scarlet visitor badge, and the pencil he had lost at the fountain. “Did you steal my pencil?” She considered this gravely. “You stole my whole day.” “That seems disproportionate.” “Wait until tomorrow.” Something passed between them—challenge, invitation, warning. Ben had spent thirty-eight years avoiding unattended luggage, unmarked stairways and women who looked at him like that. Now he stepped closer. He kissed her. Clumsily, at first. For one second Alessandra was perfectly still, the first stillness she had permitted all day. Then her hand tightened in his shirt, and she kissed him back: quick, warm, decisive. When she pulled away, she looked almost annoyed. “Finally,” she said, though whether she meant the kiss or something else, Ben could not tell. Her phone chimed again. “Work?” he asked. “Trouble.” “Is there a difference?” She smiled and held out the helmet. Beyond the balustrade, Rome glittered without chapters, opening times or sensible advice. Ben put the guidebook in his pocket and took the helmet. For once, he did not ask where they were going.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, confident piece of commercial literary romance. The opening near-collision is handled with economy and wit; the Italian rapid-fire and Ben's flustered apologies establish the culture-clash dynamic immediately. Alessandra's kleptomania is shown subtly (the spoon, the visitor badge, the pencil) without being explained, exactly as the prompt requested. The pacing through a single day is tight — fountain, rooftop, café, ghetto, Tiber, Pincio — with scene breaks keeping it episodic as requested. Strengths: the dialogue is consistently sharp and character-revealing ("Cammini, leggi, respiri—scegli due!"; "It squirts water, Professor"). The prose is lean and image-driven ("swallows stitching the sky," the fuel tank that "had once lost an argument with a parrot"). Ben's transformation from itinerary-bound academic to willing participant is gradual and earned through small increments rather than a sudden switch. The kiss at sunset is a payoff, and Alessandra's enigmatic "Finally" preserves her ambiguity. The closing line lands well. Weaknesses: some beats are familiar from the genre — the manic-pixie-courier who teaches a repressed academic to live is a well-worn trope, and the story embraces it without subversion. The "You stole my whole day" exchange is clever but borders on rom-com formula. Alessandra's interiority remains thin; she is all surface charm, which the prompt partly licenses ("enigmatic") but limits emotional complexity. The middle montage (noon, three o'clock, four o'clock) compresses events the prompt asked to be shown "in some specific instances," slightly shortchanging the "far outside his comfort zone" escalation — the rooftop trespass is the only genuinely daring act dramatized. The word count is roughly on target. The transformation of Ben, while earned, is still a fairly predictable arc; nothing surprises structurally. Overall, this is skilled, professional writing with excellent dialogue and imagery, held back from masterpiece level by its reliance on genre convention and limited emotional depth for Alessandra. Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter One: Vega, Neat “If you love someone,” Peb says, “do you tell her she has soup on her shirt?” “Before or after you ask her out?” “During.” I set down the glass I’m polishing. “There’s your problem.” Peb frowns into his beer. Rock dust still silvering his eyebrows, he looks like a worried statue of himself. “She laughed.” “At you or with you?” “Does it matter?” “Not to the soup.” Second shift has just ended, and The Last Outpost is settling into its usual evening orbit. Miners occupy the tables nearest the heaters. Merchants occupy the tables nearest the miners, close enough to sell things and far enough to deny it. Beyond the window, our asteroid turns slowly against the dark, towing the whole bar with it. I can mix a drink, mend a pump, and talk a union representative out of a wrestling hold. Minding my own business remains a work in progress. At the back of the bar, Kipp sneezes while carrying a tray. A glass slides off and bursts against the floor. “I’m fine!” Kipp calls. “The glass is less fine,” I call back. “Sweep, don’t sympathize.” The outer door sighs open. The stranger who enters looks as though someone has packed him in a hurry. His coat is inside out at one shoulder, there’s engine frost on his cuffs, and his tentacled dreads hang askew. One has twisted itself around his collar. Another keeps tapping anxiously at his jaw. He crosses the room without looking at anyone and quietly plops down at the bar. “Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double.” “Bad docking?” “Bad decade.” “Those usually require a reservation.” I pour anyway. Vega is too expensive for most bad evenings, but he has the look of someone who has already spent everything else. He turns the glass once between his palms. “You’re Nets?” “Tonight.” “Nettle Sorn?” My hand stops on the bottle. Peb leans sideways from his stool. “Who’s Nettle Sorn?” “A woman who never gave you romantic advice,” I say. “Go sit with Otra.” “Otra thinks ore grades are a personality.” “You’ll get along.” He goes, reluctantly. I lower my voice. “That’s a dangerous name to bring into my bar.” “I know.” “People usually only know that afterward.” The stranger reaches into his coat. Every tentacle in his hair goes still. What he places on the bar is smaller than my thumb: a black survey wafer in a tarnished brass frame. A silver nettle leaf is stamped into one corner. I know the frame. I know the three crooked lines scratched beneath the leaf. Mostly, I know better than to touch it. “Where did you get this?” “Your old crew.” “My old crew thinks I’m dead.” “No. They think you’re difficult.” “Both can be true.” Six years ago, I worked Deep Survey for Meridian. I learned which numbers could turn a village into an empty coordinate and a settlement into an accounting error. Eventually, I stopped filing their numbers. Then I stopped being findable. The wafer on my bar holds the last survey I ever filed. Hearth-9. Permanent settlement. Independent charter. The rock beneath The Last Outpost. “I watched Meridian burn that survey,” I say. “You watched them burn a copy.” “You’re very well informed.” “I’m very tired.” He finally takes a sip and closes his eyes. For half a second, he looks less like a messenger and more like somebody’s exhausted cousin. “What do you want?” I ask. “Page four.” “Why?” “Because page four keeps this station yours.” “Osto’s.” “Yours too, I think.” I glance toward the office, where Osto is almost certainly losing at cards against his own inventory system. “Explain.” “At oh-six-hundred, Meridian attaches a claim to Hearth-9. The station charter goes into review. Residents get relocated.” “There’s nothing here worth relocating.” “They don’t want the rock. They want the dock. A compliant port this far out means tolls, fuel contracts, customs rights.” “A front door,” I say. “With your bar in the doorway.” “And you brought this to me because you enjoy whisky?” “I brought it because your biometric cipher is on the original filing. Open it, authenticate it, and the settlement record predates Meridian’s claim.” “If I open it, they’ll know where I am.” He looks at me. “They already know,” he says. The bar seems to become very quiet, though nobody else has stopped talking. “You led them here.” “No. They were coming at dawn. I moved up the timetable.” “That’s supposed to comfort me?” “It was supposed to give you time to be angry before you have to be useful.” “I can be both at once.” “Your crew mentioned that.” The station speakers chime. A pleasant voice rolls through the bar. “All berths are temporarily closed for routine administrative inspection. Meridian Assurance thanks you for your cooperation. There is no cause for alarm.” Peb raises his beer. “I don’t cooperate before breakfast.” “It’s evening,” Otra tells him. “Then I’m consistent.” A few people laugh. Most don’t. Merchants are already checking their manifests. One of the miners gets up and starts toward the dock noticeboard. I think of Kipp’s battered tray. Of Dr. Imani’s soup. Of the basil Osto grows above the bar because fresh leaves are, in his words, “the difference between civilization and camping.” Home is not a large word until somebody tries to invoice it. “What happens if I refuse?” I ask. “They take the wafer. At six, they take the dock.” “And me?” “You get to keep being Nets until they decide Nettle Sorn is more useful.” “And if you’re lying?” “Then don’t open it for me. Open it for Osto.” “You never gave me a name.” “Ilo.” “Well, Ilo, you have a talent for making a double feel insufficient.” The office door opens. Osto stands there with his cards still in one hand. His face has gone carefully blank, which is how he looks when the still catches fire or someone mentions taxes. “Nets,” he says. “There are two Meridian officers here. They have a copy of your face.” On the bar, the wafer wakes. A thin blue line travels around its edge. **BIOMETRIC KEY REQUIRED: N. SORN.** Ilo wraps both hands around his glass but doesn’t drink. “Last chance to be just a bartender,” he says. Behind Osto, boots click softly against the office floor. Then a pleasant voice calls, “Nettle Sorn? There you are.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted chapter that fulfills nearly all of the prompt's requirements. The first-person present-tense voice is established immediately and sustained without wobble; the prose is lean, dryly funny, and consistent with the "cozy sci-fi" register — warmth and menace in careful balance. Dialogue sits comfortably around the requested proportion, and it is genuinely good dialogue: Peb's soup-on-shirt opener is an efficient, charming way to establish Nets' bartender-as-therapist role, and the stranger's exchanges ("Bad docking?" / "Bad decade") have rhythm and personality. The conflict is established cleanly and, as instructed, left unresolved: Nets' buried identity as Nettle Sorn, the Meridian claim on Hearth-9, the biometric wafer dilemma (authenticate and expose herself, or refuse and lose the station), and the cliffhanger arrival of the officers. The stakes are concrete and personal — home, belonging, the found-family details (Kipp's tray, Osto's basil, Dr. Imani's soup) that make the threat land emotionally. Weaknesses are modest. The "bartender with a secret past" premise is a familiar trope, and the twist is telegraphed early ("Nettle Sorn?" stops the hand on the bottle — a beat the genre has worn smooth). Some of the quips are a touch too polished; everyone, including minor characters like Otra and Peb, speaks in the same wry register, which flattens differentiation. The exposition of the Meridian conspiracy is delivered efficiently but somewhat conveniently — Ilo is a well-informed messenger whose motivations remain opaque (deliberately, perhaps, but it risks feeling like a plot device). A few lines ("Home is not a large word until somebody tries to invoice it") flirt with preciosity, though they mostly earn their keep. The ending is a genuine hook rather than a cheat: the wafer waking, the pleasant voice finding her — menace rendered through corporate politeness, which suits the world. No unearned transformations, no tonal betrayal, no purple excess. This is skilled, professional genre work with real charm. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
## Chapter Two: People Who Were New Once The ride spits me out downtown just after midnight, but the day doesn’t officially begin until sunrise finds me on Canal Street with eighteen dollars, a phone at four percent, and a backpack containing everything I own except a plan. I have been awake twenty-six hours. Every time I close my eyes, truck-stop lights slide beneath my eyelids and Mom says, from two days and one universe ago, *I just need time.* Time is something I can give her by disappearing. At 6:13, I turn on my phone long enough for her text to arrive: *Please come home. We’ll figure this out.* I type *I’m safe.* Delete it. Type *I love you.* Delete that too; it looks too much like goodbye. My thumb aches from not calling her. A man in a clean white shirt crouches beside me. “You look like you could use breakfast,” he says. “I run a hostel. I can get you a shower.” I am so tired my body leans toward him before my brain catches up. A shower. A door that locks. He puts one hand on my backpack, and something inside me goes very quiet. “There you are,” somebody says. “You get lost buying coffee?” The person dropping into the chair across from me has a shaved head, a split eyebrow, and a duffel bag held together with blue tape. Seventeen, maybe. They grin at the man. “My cousin’s with me.” He looks at us, decides whatever this is isn’t worth it, and leaves. “Cousin?” I say. “You want to discuss genealogy or keep your stuff?” Wren, they tell me. No last name. When they offer breakfast, I follow because hunger makes hypocrites of us all. I keep both backpack straps on. On Royal Street, the crowd swallows us: tourists with pink drinks, delivery carts, a bride already sweating through her veil at ten in the morning. Beside a painted balcony, a street musician sends saxophone notes unspooling over the sidewalk. The song is too tired to be joyful and too stubborn to be sad. It makes my loneliness sound almost intentional. I hate it. I want to stand there forever. The sax player lowers the instrument as we pass. Silver glints at her temples. “Who’s your shadow, Wren?” “Taylor,” I say, before Wren can invent another relative. My name in my own mouth. Not an argument across a dinner table. “You new?” she asks. “That obvious?” “Only to people who were new once.” She hands me a bottle of water from behind her case. “Drop-in on St. Claude. Tell Mara Odette sent you. Eat something that isn’t sugar.” A look at Wren. “You too, liar.” Then the saxophone is back at her lips, and we walk on with the music behind us. I want home badly enough to vomit. I would also rather sleep on this sidewalk than sit at my family’s table and become reasonable again. Both things are true. Nobody tells you how much space truth needs. Mara has silver hoops and no interest in my tragic backstory. “Food’s there,” she says. “Outlets by the window. Showers down the hall. You don’t have to tell me anything to use them.” “What’s the catch?” “We close at eight.” I laugh once, ugly and surprised. Wren looks almost proud. In the shower, I cry while I wash my hair. Then I get dressed, because grief has no respect for logistics. My clean shirt smells like Mom’s detergent. For one second that is comfort; the next, it’s a hand around my throat. I leave it on. By afternoon, Wren and I have negotiated a treaty. I watch their duffel while they sleep. They don’t ask why I flinch when my phone lights up, and they save me half a sandwich without ceremony. Trust is not a door. It’s a window you crack to see whether somebody tries to force it. At sunset, we sit on the river steps with fries Wren bought with coins and alarming confidence. “How long have you been gone?” I ask. “Sixteen months.” Their phone, resurrected by my charger, buzzes. MOM. The lock screen shows Wren holding a little boy’s hand at a fair. “Four days,” they say. I stare. “You looked like you needed an expert.” I nod at the screen. “And him?” “He thinks I’m at camp.” Wren’s smile goes somewhere and doesn’t come back. “My stepdad put his fist through the wall beside my head. Mom said he was stressed. I said next time it would be my head, and she told me to stop being dramatic.” The word lands between us. I could push it off the steps. “She texts that she believes me now,” Wren adds. “Isn’t that good?” “Now isn’t a place you can live.” I think of Mom asking for time, Dad leaving the room, the sick, bright relief when my ride crossed the state line. I want to hand Wren the whole story. Instead I say, “I came out. It went bad.” They nod. No questions about my body. No speech about parents coming around. They just push the fries toward me. “You Taylor everywhere, or only here?” “Everywhere,” I say. “I’m working on everywhere.” At eight, Mara finds two beds at a youth shelter across town. Wren agrees to take one only if nobody calls it a fresh start. “I was going to call it Tuesday,” Mara says. Before we leave, I turn on my phone. Eleven missed calls. One new text: *I love you. I am trying.* I read it until the words stop being a key and become only words. Then I answer: *I’m safe tonight. I can’t come home. Please don’t make me.* The reply dots appear, vanish, appear again. I put the phone away. Wren holds the door. “You coming, cousin?” “For tonight.” It isn’t trust or forgiveness. It’s a bed and one person who knows my name. Behind us, a saxophone stitches one blue note into the dark. It sounds nothing like home. I keep walking.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This chapter is a confident, controlled piece of YA writing. Taylor's voice is distinct: sardonic, guarded, hyper-aware, with a self-protective wit ("hunger makes hypocrites of us all") that never tips into preciosity. The mixed-tense, first-person instruction is honored throughout, with internal monologue woven in naturally rather than dumped. The New Orleans setting is rendered economically but vividly — the tired saxophone, the sweating bride, the river steps — and the city functions as more than backdrop; it shapes the emotional register. Wren is a well-drawn counterpart: their intervention in the opening predator scene is both plot and characterization, and their backstory (the wall, the little brother, "now isn't a place you can live") is delivered with restraint. The dialogue is the piece's strongest element — clipped, oblique, character-revealing, avoiding both exposition and sentimentality. Lines like "You want to discuss genealogy or keep your stuff?" and "I was going to call it Tuesday" do real work. The emotional complexity is genuine: Taylor simultaneously wants home and dreads it, and the piece holds both truths without resolving them prematurely. The mother's texts escalate believably. The ending resists false redemption — "It isn't trust or forgiveness. It's a bed and one person who knows my name" — earning its small, provisional hope. Minor weaknesses: a few aphorisms strain slightly ("Trust is not a door. It's a window you crack..."), the Mara Odette drop-in referral resolves a bit too smoothly, and the predator scene resolves with almost cinematic convenience. The prose occasionally leans on its own cleverness. But these are small complaints against a chapter that is coherent, moving, disciplined in length, and stylistically consistent. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy “The situation,” said Midas, “is that we have half a bucket of water, no food worth interrogating, and a roof that has become a second, less reliable bucket.” Chewy blinked one glass eye. The other had been blinkless since the business with the magnet. “Your mission planning has improved,” he said. “You’ve included the weather.” They lived in the remains of a garden centre, behind a sign reading EVERYTHING MUST GO. Most of it had. Home base consisted of two shelves, a stove, three defiant tomato plants and a bed made from potting-compost bags. It was dry, provided one did not count the bed. Chewy was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from the Before Time, when people built machines to love their children so they could get on with building machines to replace one another. His fur was grey, his left ear was held on by wire, and his solar panel was cracked. He ran on sunlight, spite and, he maintained, a warranty. “The pumping station,” said Midas. “A washer for the filter. Food if we see any. Back before dark. No detours.” “Define detour.” “Anything you have to define.” At the old flyover they found the graffiti. It was red, chest-high and painted with the care of someone who had survived the end of the world but not the education system. WHEN THE LAST LIGHT FAILS, SEEK HAVEN WHERE THE WILDS BEGIN. THE CROWNED STAG POINTS. KNOCK WHERE THE RIVER CANNOT HEAR. ASK FOR TOMORROW. Underneath, in smaller letters: NO KINGS. NO TOLLS. BRING SEEDS. Midas read it twice. “Hidden refuge.” Chewy’s ear rotated. “Or a trap with good signage.” “Could be people. Water. A bed.” “You have a bed.” “You’ve never slept in it.” “I have standards.” The detour began, as detours often do, with someone insisting it was practically on the way. The Crowned Stag turned out to be a pub sign in a nettle bed. Its painted antlers pointed into the hills. Midas pointed too, slipped, and discovered the pub cellar. Chewy threw him a washing line and offered advice until he climbed out. “You could have used the door,” said Chewy. “I was checking the cellar.” “For refuge?” “Mostly for my knees.” Beyond the pub, the wilds began with brambles and became increasingly sincere. They followed a dry stream uphill. Where the river could not hear turned out, after Chewy explained acoustics and Midas pretended to listen, to mean a concrete culvert above the old riverbed. Behind it stood a green door in the hillside. There was a brass knocker shaped like a hand. Midas knocked three times. “Password?” said the door. They looked at each other. “Tomorrow,” said Midas. A light came on. Both flinched. Civilization had often started that way, and frequently gone downhill from there. The door opened onto white corridors, warm air and rows of plants under glowing panels. There were tanks of water, crates of tools and, on a steel table, a single tin of peaches. There were no people. “HAVEN SIX,” said a voice. “POPULATION: ONE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED AND FOUR.” Chewy looked along the seed racks. “It may be counting optimistically.” Midas picked up the peaches. “UNAUTHORIZED HOARDING,” said the voice. “One tin isn’t hoarding.” “IT IS A BEGINNING.” Doors slammed. Somewhere, something large woke up and began considering its options. “Put them back,” said Chewy. Midas obeyed. “REFUGE IS ABOUT SHARING,” said the voice. “Excellent,” said Chewy. “Share the exit.” “EXIT REQUIRES AUTHORIZATION.” Chewy found a service socket and plugged in the cable he kept for emergencies, which was universal in the sense that it fitted nothing without effort. His eyes dimmed. “What’s it doing?” Midas asked. “Searching for an authorized person.” “How long?” “At the current rate, until your beard achieves sentience.” Midas looked for a manual override. He found a red handle labelled ONLY IN EMERGENCY, which was now merely descriptive. He pulled it. The sprinklers started. Then the seed conveyor. Then a siren, which had been waiting sixty years for this and intended to do it properly. Potatoes rattled from a hopper. Water struck Midas in the face. He skidded into a rack, obtained the filter washer by the ancient method of falling with his hand open, and grabbed the peaches on general principles. Then he disappeared down a compost hatch. Chewy followed, because the alternative was being adopted by a building. The hatch delivered them into a bramble patch above the river, along with its green cover, which Midas had opened with his head. It also delivered four potatoes and a quantity of compost that would later turn up in surprising places. They went home by raft, using the green cover; by wheelbarrow, after the raft met a shopping trolley; and finally by air, when the wheelbarrow hit the usual stone. At the garden centre, Midas was soaked, limping and missing an eyebrow. Chewy had lost his wired ear, gained a dent and developed a tendency to say, “Please cuddle responsibly,” at moments of deep personal regret. Midas fitted the washer. The pump produced clean water. He planted the potatoes, patched the roof with the green cover and put the peaches on the shelf for a special occasion. “A successful mission,” he said. Chewy’s remaining ear twitched. “We went for a washer.” “And found a refuge.” “It evicted us.” “The cellar wasn’t keen on me either. I’m beginning to think the world has a theme.” Rain ticked gently on the new roof. For once, nothing dripped into the bed. Outside, something set off the distant siren again. The garden centre had survived raiders, storms and Midas’s cooking. It was not much of a haven. But it had never asked for authorization, and its population, however optimistically counted, was exactly right. It was also, unlike most of the world, glad to see them. Midas blew out the lamp. “Tomorrow, we stay home.” There was a pause. “Please cuddle responsibly,” said Chewy. Midas sighed and put an arm round him. It was, he reflected, the first thing all day that had gone according to instructions.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's register well: dry asides, anthropomorphized objects with opinions, footnote-like digressions embedded in prose ("when people built machines to love their children so they could get on with building machines to replace one another"), and a plot that escalates through plausible incompetence. The structure follows the brief precisely — deliberation at home base, a mission (a washer) that goes sideways via a detour to a mysterious refuge, and a return home "worse for wear" via raft, wheelbarrow, and air. Strengths: The dialogue is consistently witty and character-differentiated (Chewy's deadpan pedantry vs. Midas's hapless optimism). The graffiti puzzle is a nice mid-story hook, and the HAVEN SIX sequence — an AI sanctuary counting a population that isn't there — is genuinely Pratchett-esque in its satire of bureaucracy and institutional optimism. The running gags (the "Please cuddle responsibly" glitch, the bed that is also a bucket) are set up and paid off cleanly. The ending lands the emotional beat without sentimentality: the garden centre as a haven that "never asked for authorization" mirrors the refuge's failure elegantly. Weaknesses: The plot is somewhat episodic and the middle section (brambles, culvert) is lightly sketched compared to the refuge. The "return in multiple ways" is dispatched almost too briskly — raft/trolley/wheelbarrow in a single sentence, which is funny but slightly rushed. Some jokes are a touch mechanical ("Define detour." / "Anything you have to define." is a good exchange, but the pattern repeats). The emotional depth is modest; this is comedy of situation rather than character, and Midas remains a type rather than a person. The prose occasionally strains for cleverness ("became increasingly sincere" as a joke about brambles works; "civilization had often started that way" is a bit pat). Nothing here is purple, overwrought, or amateurish. The voice is controlled throughout, the word count is appropriate, and the ending's warmth is earned by the established contrast between the false haven and the shabby real one. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell over the door gave a startled clang, and Rhys Maddox fell into Eleri Price’s bookshop, bringing with him half the rain in Hay-on-Wye. “Good afternoon,” he said. “I’d like to hide behind your Russian novels.” “They’re at the back.” “Even better.” Outside, three men with cameras splashed past the window. One stopped, cupped his hands to the glass, and Eleri found herself flattening a famous actor against a shelf of Tolstoy. “Not the face,” he murmured. “Be quiet.” “I was thinking of your livelihood. People come miles to see this face.” “Not in Hay. They come for books.” His smile was the one from the posters: amused, apologetic, faintly wicked. Eleri, who had expected to feel nothing, felt rather a lot and resented him for it. “Blinds,” he said. “Please?” “Please. I am begging, charmingly.” She lowered the blind and turned the sign to CLOSED. “There. You’ve ruined my afternoon trade.” “I’ll buy everything in the window.” “You couldn’t carry it.” “I have people.” “Of course you do.” Rain darkened his hair, and blood beaded on one cheek. “Nice shop.” “You don’t have to do that.” “Do what?” “Like everything.” His smile faltered. “I was being polite.” “You were being liked. There’s a difference.” For a second he said nothing. Then he laughed, not the poster laugh but a short, surprised bark that did something unwise to her stomach. “Eleri,” she said. “Rhys Maddox,” he said, offering his hand. “I know.” “Ah.” He looked pleased. “So you have seen—” “My niece has your face on her bedroom wall.” “Excellent.” “She’s eleven. She also has a picture of a goat.” He lowered his hand. “You’re enjoying this.” “A little.” “Have you seen *The Glass Crown*?” “No.” “*Blackwater*?” “No.” “Anything I’ve been in?” “I read mostly.” He looked so affronted that she took refuge in the till. “You could pretend,” he said. “I could. You could also stop bleeding on the floor.” He touched his cheek, seemed surprised by the blood, and she was annoyed by the impulse to go round the counter and inspect it. “Tea,” she said. “If you’re staying.” “Am I?” “Until your fans lose interest.” “They’re not fans.” “Then until the men with cameras find someone more interesting.” “That could take years.” She filled the kettle. “What would you recommend?” “For hiding or reading?” “Reading. I’ve got the hiding sorted.” She took down a paperback of R. S. Thomas and handed it to him. “Will I like it?” “Probably not.” “Then why—” “You asked what I’d recommend, not what would flatter you.” He turned the book over. “You really don’t like me, do you?” It should have sounded petulant. It didn’t. That was the trouble. “I don’t know you,” she said. “That isn’t usually a requirement.” “For liking you?” “For deciding.” The kettle began to rumble. Eleri busied herself with two mugs, though her hands had become oddly clumsy. “When I was twelve,” he said, “my school in Swansea put me in the eisteddfod. Recitation. I had a stammer you could hear from the car park.” “I got through the first line. Then some boy shouted, ‘Get on with it.’ So I did the rest as a pirate.” “A pirate.” “Very committed pirate. Didn’t win, but everyone laughed, and for about three minutes I wasn’t frightened. I’ve rather been doing the pirate ever since.” The kettle clicked off. Neither of them moved. “And if you stop?” she asked. His eyes met hers. “Haven’t the faintest. That’s the frightening bit.” Eleri imagined him at twelve, all panic and elbows, and felt a disastrous tenderness unfold beneath her ribs. She poured water over the tea bags with great concentration. “You were probably an annoying child,” she said. “Insufferable.” “There we are, then.” “Milk?” “In the jug.” He rose and came around the counter for it. There was not enough room. There was, strictly speaking, plenty of room, but he somehow occupied all of it. As he reached past her, his sleeve brushed hers, and she forgot whether she had put tea in the second mug. “Sorry,” he said. He did not sound charming. He sounded a little breathless. Eleri stepped away. “Your public appears to have gone.” Rhys glanced toward the blind. “Has it?” “You can check.” “I believe you.” “Don’t. I might be keeping you for my niece.” “The goat will be jealous.” She laughed before she could stop herself. His expression changed—not triumph exactly, but pleasure so unguarded that she looked down at once. “There,” he said softly. “I was beginning to think you wouldn’t.” “Don’t become unbearable.” “Too late. Ask anyone.” A car horn sounded outside. He looked at the door, then back at her. “My driver.” “Your people.” “My people,” he agreed. He paid for the poetry, but ignored the change in the paper bag she held out. “Would you have dinner with me?” “No.” The word pleased her for its steadiness. Her pulse was less disciplined. He nodded, absorbing it. Then, instead of producing another smile, he said, “All right. May I come back and tell you what I thought of the poems?” “You won’t like them.” “Then we’ll have something to talk about.” “You could write a letter.” “I could. But I’d be showing off in it, and you’d see through me by the second sentence.” “First.” “First,” he said, and smiled. This one was smaller. Eleri discovered she liked it far more, which was extremely inconvenient. She pushed the paper bag toward him. “Back door’s through the stockroom. It leads to the alley.” “Will you turn the sign over after I’ve gone?” “Yes.” “And if I came back when it said OPEN?” She should have said something final. Instead she said, “Don’t bring the pirate.” For a moment he looked almost shy. “No,” he said. “I’ll try not to.” When he had gone, Eleri turned the sign with great care and made herself a fresh cup of tea. Hers had gone cold. Her hands, absurdly, had not quite stopped shaking.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-controlled scene that fulfills nearly every prompt requirement. The setting (Hay-on-Wye, Welsh names, eisteddfod, R.S. Thomas poetry) grounds it convincingly in Wales. The dialogue carries the scene as instructed, and the voices are distinct: Rhys deploys deflection, charm, and jokes as armor; Eleri responds in clipped, dry deflections. The pirate anecdote is a smart device for revealing the fragile ego beneath the charm without exposition. The chemistry is built through subtext and small physical beats (the tea-making, the sleeve brush, the fumbled tea bags) rather than told outright—mostly. A few lines do tell ("felt rather a lot and resented him for it," "disastrous tenderness unfold"), but these are brief and mostly earned by behavior. The beats of the prompt are all hit: the superficial immunity, the paradoxical attraction, the derailment of the charm offensive, the owner's inner fluster. The prose is lean and elegant, with well-timed paragraph breaks doing comedic work. Weaknesses: the piece is slightly formulaic within the genre (the "one honest confession from the celebrity" beat is familiar), the ending's "come back when it says OPEN" exchange is charming but predictable, and a couple of Eleri's interior lines lean on convenient narration. Rhys's ego-fragility is more implied than fully tested—Eleri never truly wounds him, so his vulnerability arrives a touch easily. The word count target (~1000) is respected. Nothing meanders; the pacing is tight. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door opened on a breath of cold, salt-rotten air. Beyond it, the underhold was a low, barrel-vaulted chamber paved in green stone. Whale-oil lamps burned along the walls, their flames screened in brass, and the scythan artefact stood at the centre upon a block of black basalt: a cage of verdigrised coils around a lens the colour of a drowned eye. It had no business being beautiful. Madam Rask sat beside it in a counting-house chair, a long-barrelled revolver across her black bombazine skirts. Her iron-grey hair was braided close to her skull; a silver harpoon barb gleamed at her throat. Six bodyguards stood in the lamp-shadow with carbines and harpoon-pistols levelled. “You’re late,” Rask said. “I expected ambitious vermin an hour ago.” Aya’s first thought was that the arrest had been bait. Her second was that she had brought Katra and Simeon into the trap. “Your arrest,” Aya said. “The watch exaggerated its industry. They took my housekeeper, my coach and a very good hat. I wished to see who would dance on my grave before the sexton had measured it.” “You might have sent word,” Katra said. “And spoiled the test?” Simeon’s gaze moved over the carbines. “Choke-bores,” he murmured. “At this range there won’t be enough of us to identify.” “Thank you, Sim.” “Hands where steel can see them,” Rask said. Aya felt for the immateria. It was there—an Arctic pressure behind her thoughts—but the instant she touched it, the relic’s black lens seemed to turn towards her. Something vast and attentive leaned against the other side. She withdrew, cold to her teeth. Six guns were a simpler terror. Simeon trusted mechanisms because they failed for reasons one could name. “Wise,” said Rask. “I’ve heard you can whistle devils through a keyhole. I should hate to test my marksmanship on one.” They were searched and bound where they stood. Katra’s knives made a bright little heap; Simeon’s picks followed, then Aya’s chalk, silver filings and three stoppered vials. Sailmaker’s twine bit into her wrists as a guard forced her to her knees. Rask rose and crossed the floor. “Let us see what ambition looks like.” She caught the lower edge of Aya’s mask and tore it free. For a moment, nobody spoke. “Well,” Rask said softly. “Veyl’s daughter.” “Lady?” Simeon said. “Not here,” Aya told him. Katra stared at her. “You said your people were in shipping.” “They are. Among other things.” Rask tilted Aya’s chin towards the lamplight. “I was at Gallows Quay when your mother was hanged. She had that same look. As though the rest of us were a disappointing experiment.” Aya saw, with the clarity of a diagram, what followed now. **VEYL’S DAUGHTER IN THIEVES’ DEN**, the first broadsheet would shriek. The second would add **WITCH**. Her father’s club, her old lecture halls, the servants who had taught her to curtsey—every locked door she had opened in Morska would acquire her face. Her mother had been hanged as a solitary horror. Aya would be hanged as a confirmation. Beyond the guild walls, the harbour foghorn sounded: one long blast, a second, then a third. The final note died slowly in the vault. Rask released her. “Put them in the old blubber drain. It still runs to the sea.” “That would be unbusinesslike,” Aya said. Rask paused. “You came to rob me. Sentiment has its limits.” “I’m not appealing to sentiment. I’m discussing price.” Her mouth was dry. She made her voice into the cool instrument she used in lecture rooms. “A dead Veyl is an inquiry. A living Veyl is credit.” “Your father may decline to invest.” “My father holds the northern whaling charter. He hates waste almost as much as scandal. Send him a letter in my hand. Tell him I was taken outside a lecture, not beneath a thieves’ guild. He’ll pay for my return, and again to keep the story off the Exchange.” “Or he’ll pay me to ensure you never come home. Your mother already cost him one reputation.” “Then sell him silence instead. One daughter, two markets. I should have thought you’d appreciate the economy.” Rask’s eyes narrowed. “You’d auction your own name?” “You’ve already taken everything else.” “And your companions? Are they included in the lot?” “They live, or you get no letter, no names, no performance. A hostage who wants to die is just a corpse with patience.” “She means it,” Katra said. “She’s tedious like that.” “And if I keep them alive merely to encourage you?” Rask asked. “Then encourage me gently. My handwriting suffers when I’m grieving.” Rask studied her for so long that Aya could hear the lamp flames ticking in their brass cages. She had come to the underhold hoping to escape the gilded coffin of her name. Now that name was the only thing between her and a pine one. “A tide,” Rask said at last. “Separate cells. Gently with her ladyship’s face; it’s inventory now.” Aya did not thank her. Gratitude would have made the bargain sound like mercy. As the guards pulled them towards the dark, something within the scythan coils knocked—once, twice, thrice. Aya did not look back. Some doors were opened merely by answering.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of genre fiction that executes the brief with notable skill. The whalepunk/Victorian texture is delivered through concrete, era-appropriate details: bombazine skirts, whale-oil lamps in brass cages, harpoon pistols, sailmaker's twine, the blubber drain running to the sea. The worldbuilding is economical and confident rather than expository. The confrontation is handled well. Rask is a genuinely menacing antagonist whose power comes from wit and composure rather than theatrics — "I expected ambitious vermin an hour ago" is a fine opening line. The unmasking and the reveal of Aya's parentage land with appropriate weight, and the internal monologue about broadsheets and being "hanged as a confirmation" is a sharp, character-true piece of reasoning that deepens the stakes. The negotiation is the strongest section. Aya's "A dead Veyl is an inquiry. A living Veyl is credit" is an excellent line, and the logic of the hostage economy — selling silence, two markets, "a hostage who wants to die is just a corpse with patience" — is genuinely clever and consistent with her established aristocratic/scientific persona. Katra's dry interjection ("She's tedious like that") and Simeon's earlier morgue-humor about choke-bores give the companions distinct voices in few words. Minor criticisms: the ending's knocking from the scythan artefact is a slightly familiar beat, and "Some doors were opened merely by answering" strains for aphorism. The gothic-horror element is present but light — the immateria pressure and the lens "turning towards her" are effective but brief. Rask's capitulation to "a tide" comes a touch easily, though the story sells it as pragmatism. The prose occasionally flirts with preciousness ("a cage of verdigrised coils around a lens the colour of a drowned eye") but stays on the right side of it. Dialogue is consistently period-flavored without tipping into parody. Overall: coherent, atmospheric, well-paced, with authentic voices and a satisfying negotiation scene that fulfills every story beat requested. Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous The jukebox in the corner has a cracked neon lightning bolt and one song left in it. The record is scratched; the same guitar riff stumbles every forty seconds, picks itself up, and charges back toward the chorus. Spike Spiegel has heard it eleven times. He sits at the bar with an empty stomach, a full ashtray, and a whiskey he cannot afford. Beside his elbow lies a photograph: Viktor Sorn, syndicate courier, two hundred thousand alive. Sorn is due here at midnight. It is eleven-fifty. The door opens. Revy comes in with rain on her shoulders and gun oil on her hands. Black crop top, shorts, twin pistols. A dragon climbs her right arm as she slides onto the stool next to Spike and slaps down an identical photograph. “You’ve got to be fucking kidding me.” “Most people start with hello.” “Most people aren’t trying to steal my rent money.” She orders whiskey, tells the bartender to leave the bottle, and lights a cigarette from the one Spike has just forgotten in the ashtray. He watches her do it. She watches him watch. “Spiegel,” she says. “The skinny guy with the big reputation.” “Two Hands,” he says. “The big reputation with the short temper.” Her grin is brief and genuine. That surprises them both. Up close, her reputation makes sense. It lives in the loose readiness of her shoulders, in the way she checks the bar mirror without seeming to. Spike recognizes someone who expects every room to turn hostile. Revy keeps glancing at his hands. They are too still for a drunk’s. “You always dress like you’re going to a funeral?” she asks. “Usually someone else’s.” “Cute. You practice that?” “Only on people who might shoot me.” “Must work great.” She pours two fingers and pushes the glass toward him. He drinks. She drinks from the bottle. The jukebox repeats the riff. They do not compare employers. In their business, a name is just a debt somebody else owns. Revy nods at Sorn’s picture instead. “He comes in breathing. My client was specific.” “Mine wants him able to talk.” “Then try not to shoot him in the mouth.” Spike turns his glass, watching whiskey climb the sides. “And if he doesn’t cooperate?” Revy taps the butt of one pistol against the bar. “Then I get creative.” For the first time, Spike looks less bored. Revy notices and hates that she notices. The jukebox repeats the riff. Revy reaches for her pistol. “If you shoot that thing,” Spike says, “I’m not carrying you out.” “Worried about me?” “Worried about the song. It’s growing on me.” Sorn arrives at midnight with four men and a metal case. He sees Revy stand, sees Spike unfold from his stool, and makes the reasonable decision to run. One bodyguard is faster. Revy’s first pistol comes up before the man’s gun clears his coat. Her shot punches him into a table. Then both Cutlasses are out, and the bar becomes noise: muzzle flashes, breaking glass, the bartender praying underneath the register. Spike moves through it without hurry. He kicks a chair into one gunman’s knees, catches another’s wrist, and turns him just far enough that the man shoots his own reflection. A twist sends the pistol skidding. Neon strobes; distance lies to Spike’s artificial eye. He stops measuring, lets instinct take over, and fires his Jericho once. The last guard drops his weapon and decides the floor is a fine place to live. A bullet hits the jukebox. The neon dies. The song keeps playing. Sorn vanishes through the rear door. Spike and Revy reach it together, shoulder to shoulder, neither yielding. On the threshold, Spike nearly trips over a brass key. PARADISE MOTEL. ROOM 8. Revy looks at the key, then at him. “Temporary partnership.” “How temporary?” “Depends how annoying you get.” The Paradise is across the alley, its sign promising color television in three languages and delivering none. Room 8 smells of mildew. Sorn is stuck halfway through the bathroom window. Spike pulls him back by the belt. Revy zip-ties him to a chair. Then she points one pistol at Spike. Spike’s Jericho is already level with her ribs. “My bounty,” she says. “He doesn’t look grateful.” “Split him and I’ll split your skull.” “That’s not usually how fifty-fifty works.” Rain ticks against the glass. Sorn breathes through his nose. Spike sits on the edge of the bed because standing feels like effort, and because Revy is close enough now that he can see the pulse at her throat. She steps nearer. The muzzle of her pistol touches his shirt, just over his heart. His gun doesn’t move. “You think I won’t shoot?” she asks. “I think you haven’t.” Something flickers behind her eyes—not fear, exactly. Recognition, maybe. Then her mouth hardens, and whatever was there goes back into its cage. Spike knows the trick. He has been doing it for years. “You’re strange,” she says. “You’re pointing a gun at me.” “That usually makes people less strange.” “Whatever happens, happens.” “That’s a shitty way to live.” “It’s worked so far.” “You’re broke.” “It hasn’t worked perfectly.” She laughs before she can stop herself. Spike smiles, and for a moment the room changes shape. Her attention drops to his mouth. His drops to hers. Whiskey, tobacco, rain-damp skin: the distance between them narrows to a dangerous inventory. He lifts his free hand but doesn’t touch her. She doesn’t step back. Behind them, Sorn begins hopping his chair toward the open door. “Fifty-fifty,” Spike says again, quieter. Revy’s finger rests along the trigger guard. “You always negotiate like this?” “Only when I’m interested.” “In the money?” He doesn’t answer. Sorn’s chair scrapes into the hall. “Your bounty’s leaving,” she murmurs. “So catch him.” “After you.” From the bar comes the faint, stubborn beginning of the same riff. Revy’s pistol stays against Spike’s heart. His stays at her ribs. Her smile is all teeth; her eyes are not. The obvious solution—lower the guns and see what happens next—occurs to them both. Neither pulls the trigger. Neither closes the last inch.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted piece that hits every beat of the prompt: the seedy bar, the shared bounty, the drinking, the gunplay, and the motel standoff with unresolved tension left deliberately unresolved. The prose is lean and rhythmic, with a strong noir sensibility that suits both source universes—the scratched jukebox riff recurring like a clock, the neon failing Spike's prosthetic eye, the rain ticking against motel glass. Character work is the standout. Spike's fatalism ("Whatever happens, happens") is deployed at the exact right moment, and his laziness-as-efficiency in the bar fight—kicking a chair, redirecting a gunman's wrist, letting instinct override his faulty depth perception—captures his fighting philosophy without exposition. Revy's volatility, chain-smoking, and guarded vulnerability ("hates that she notices") are all present, and the detail of her lighting a cigarette from his abandoned one is an economical, physical way to establish intimacy and shared habit. Both characters' trust issues are dramatized rather than stated: the mutual gun-pointing at the motel, the refusal to holster, the "I think you haven't" exchange. Dialogue is sharp and in-voice throughout, though it occasionally tips into being a little too polished—every line lands like a screenplay beat, and a few exchanges ("Worried about me?" / "Worried about the song") are clever to the point of self-consciousness. The banter is consistently good but rarely surprising in its rhythm; both characters quip in the same register, which slightly blurs their distinct voices in the middle stretch. The ending is the piece's best structural choice: neither pulling the trigger nor closing the distance, with Sorn comically hopping his zip-tied chair out the door as a deflating counterpoint. It honors the "unresolved" requirement while feeling earned rather than evasive. The recurring song motif ties the bar and motel together nicely. Weaknesses are minor: the plot is thin (Sorn is a MacGuffin who barely exists), some imagery is stock noir (rain, neon, whiskey), and the piece's coolness occasionally keeps the reader at arm's length emotionally. But the restraint is largely intentional and appropriate to these characters. No purple prose, no meandering, no unearned transformations.
