+ Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
Before dawn, Rome smelled of wet ash and bread. Rain had polished the tiles above my cell; beyond the ludus wall, cartwheels banged over basalt and a muleteer cursed his gods with admirable invention. Inside, the air was close with straw, old sweat, and the sharp oil the trainer rubbed into my scars. I set a bean before the little clay Hercules on my shelf. He was no taller than my thumb, his club chipped, his lion’s skin worn smooth by handling. Mars belonged to the men who owned me. I preferred Hercules, who had known servitude and performed impossible tasks for a lesser man. I liked him best not strangling the lion, but holding up the sky while Atlas fetched the apples. Even a hero’s back could be borrowed. “One more day,” I told him, “and keep Comates breathing.” Comates answered from the next cell with a cough like a torn sail. At breakfast he could manage only a few spoonfuls of barley porridge. I ate his beans when the attendant turned away. We were *hordearii*, barley men, fed like oxen and appraised like them. The physician pressed my belly, examined an old seam beneath my ribs, and told Crispus, my lanista, that I would last another season. Seven years earlier, Roman soldiers had brought me out of Dacia in chains. My mother had named me Dapyx. On the programmes, I was Hilarus: the Cheerful One. At the third hour, Crispus took me to be fitted for a new leather manica, with Felix, his house slave, carrying the old one. Rome received me in a rush of noise and stink: frying onions, wet wool, dung, garum, roses browning in a vendor’s basket. A fountain pattered into its trough. Somewhere a flute player practised the same six notes until I wanted to strangle him with the flute. A butcher recognized me and lifted two bloody fingers in salute. Boys argued over whether I had killed twelve men or twenty. At law I was infamous; in the street, strangers mouthed my name. A man could be cheered by fifty thousand people and still be sold with the furniture. Outside a grain office, citizens shuffled in a queue that bent around the corner. One man praised Trajan for keeping Rome fed. Another said the Egyptian ships were late and the emperor’s Dacian gold would not bake bread. A woman spat near my feet and predicted another war, another triumph, and the same empty pot. In the wineshops, men already spoke of Parthia as a nut awaiting the hammer. I did not hate the crowd. That would have been simpler. Most wanted bread, a little courage by proxy, and an hour when their own troubles shrank. But their wonder had a body, and the body was mine. I was one of the things Rome’s wars had brought home, along with the gold, the marble, and the coughing sickness in our cells. In Trajan’s new forum, stone dust dried my tongue. The column rose above me, its carved spiral so fresh it had the pallor of a scar. Romans climbed it in marble: building bridges, raising camps, receiving submission. My own people burned and bled around them. A Dacian woman carried a child from a village. She wore my mother’s dress, though of course she did not. “Fine work,” Crispus said. “Yes,” I answered. It was. Rome had made my country’s defeat into something beautiful, so that citizens could tilt back their heads and admire it. On the coins, Trajan’s face remained lean and serene. Perhaps he believed the column. Perhaps an emperor had to. The armourer’s shop smelled of charcoal, singed leather, and the vinegar he used on bronze. He was a small Syrian with burn constellations on both forearms. While Crispus and the editor’s steward discussed prices in the doorway, he fitted the manica from wrist to shoulder, asking twice whether the straps pinched. They were the first questions anyone had asked that day about my comfort. “The Dacian opens,” the steward said. “The crowd remembers him.” Crispus named a sum. Then, because I was listening, he added that if I pleased the editor at the next games, he would ask for my *rudis*—the wooden sword that meant release. He had promised it before. Freedom, in his mouth, was a morsel held beyond a dog’s teeth. Still, my heart stirred, which shamed me more than despair would have. On the way back, I spent one of my own copper coins on a honey cake. Crispus pretended not to see. By then the Flavian Amphitheatre cast a cold, broad shadow. A woman selling cabbages beneath it called, “Smile, Hilarus!” I did. That, too, was part of my training. Comates’s fever had risen. I fed him half the cake and lied that I had eaten the rest. He would need the remainder before morning. At dusk, the bath furnace roared. Oil and grime ran from my skin beneath the strigil. Around us, men diced, prayed, argued over women, and listened for the cough in Comates’s cell. From the direction of the amphitheatre came the dry rasp of sand being raked. The games were six days away. Comates asked what I would do if the *rudis* truly came. Some men took it and then returned, signing away their freedom for another purse. He thought he might. He knew no trade but the one Rome had taught him. “I would go to Puteoli,” I said. “Your sister?” “If she is there.” “And if she isn’t?” I had no answer spacious enough for that question. After the lamps were extinguished, I took Hercules from his shelf. Beyond the wall, a late reveller sang, stopped to vomit, and resumed in a different key. Rome could be ridiculous even while it devoured me. I thought of Puteoli, which I knew only as blue tile in a mosaic, and of my sister’s face, which became less distinct each year. I thought of Crispus’s promise and let myself hope for exactly three breaths. Then I asked Hercules for nothing glorious: only that Comates might live to hate his breakfast, that my sister might have kept one name Rome had not given her, and that I might remember mine. In the darkness, Comates drew another ragged breath. I listened until the next one came.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong piece of historical fiction. The response fulfills every instruction: first person, past tense, roughly 1000 words, no combat scene, rich sensory detail, interiority, and political/social context woven in organically (Trajan's forum, the grain dole, Dacian wars, Parthia looming, the infamia legal status of gladiators). The sensory work is precise and fresh rather than generic: "Rome smelled of wet ash and bread," the flute player repeating six notes, the armourer's vinegar on bronze, the "dry rasp of sand being raked." The clay Hercules is a superb concrete device — a personal religion of the enslaved, contrasted with Mars who "belonged to the men who owned me." The detail of preferring Hercules holding up the sky rather than strangling the lion is thematically resonant and characterful. The Dacian narrator renamed "Hilarus" carries the piece's central tension: a man whose body is Rome's trophy, staring at his own people's defeat carved into Trajan's column. The moment with the Dacian woman in the frieze ("She wore my mother's dress, though of course she did not") is the emotional peak — restrained, devastating, earned. The social commentary is integrated rather than lectured: the grain queue conversation, the woman spitting about war and "the same empty pot," the observation that "a man could be cheered by fifty thousand people and still be sold with the furniture." These are period-plausible and thematically load-bearing. Minor criticisms: the prose occasionally reaches for aphorism ("Freedom, in his mouth, was a morsel held beyond a dog's teeth"; "Rome could be ridiculous even while it devoured me"), which flirts with preciosity, though it mostly stays controlled. The Comates subplot is somewhat conventional (the sick cellmate, the shared cake, the lie about eating), and the sister-in-Puteoli thread is a familiar longing device. The dialogue is functional and believable but not remarkable. The ending — listening for Comates's next breath — is quiet and appropriate, though the "asked Hercules for nothing glorious" prayer is a touch tidy in its tripartite structure. The piece avoids combat, avoids melodrama, avoids anachronism (rudis, lanista, editor, hordearii, strigil all used correctly), and feels genuinely like a slice of a larger story. The voice is consistent throughout — literate, wry, wounded, observant. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper **Rubha Reidh, Wester Ross — 18 September 1984** Dear Mum, Arrived with both cases and only one of them wet. The light is a fussy old thing, but I like fussy things; they tell you what’s wrong if you listen. From the gallery, when the murk lifts, you can see the Cuillin on Skye. Mr Bain says the view wears off. I’ll let you know. My pay goes in Friday. I’ll send enough for the roof. Ewan **Govan — 25 September 1984** Ewan, Your letter would pass for a report to the Board. Are you eating? Is the bed damp? Did you find the vest with the red stitch? That’s the good one. The roof can wait. It’s waited through two governments. I’m still doing school dinners, so don’t send every penny and live on lint. Mrs Shaw asks after you. I told her you’d joined a monastery with better machinery. Mum **Rubha Reidh — 22 October 1984** Dear Mum, The bed’s dry and the food’s better than yours, which I’d never say if you could reach me. There are three keepers, so don’t picture me on my own. Bain talks engines. Robbie talks football. I clean things that were clean yesterday. The money is for the roof, not for the Post Office book under my name. I know how you work. Ewan **Govan — 4 November 1984** Ewan, I did not picture you on your own. I pictured you lonely, which is a different matter and not one a third man at breakfast can fix. I’ve banked thirty pounds and spent the rest on shoes, so there. Your old room has my sewing machine in it now. You needn’t think that means anything. It means your mother has trousers to alter and no wish to kneel on the kitchen floor. Mum **Rubha Reidh — 30 December 1984** Dear Mum, The supply lorry couldn’t get past Melvaig before Christmas. We had tinned ham and Bain’s emergency whisky, which turned out to be mostly emergency. Robbie went home on the 27th. I’ve not slept right since. I keep finding jobs at two in the morning, then standing in the lamp room wondering what I came up for. The foghorn was tested Tuesday and I still hear it on my nights off. Don’t put that in your next letter to Aunt Jean. Ewan **Govan — 12 January 1985** Ewan, I fell on the ice outside the Co-op and spent two nights in the Western. Bruises, nothing broken. I’m telling you now because Mrs Shaw says I should have told you then, and she’s enjoying being right. I didn’t want you hitchhiking out of Wester Ross over a blue hip. You don’t have to make a punishment of a payslip. If it’s bad, say it’s bad. That’s all. Mum **Rubha Reidh — 3 February 1985** Mum, You should have told me. There. That’s the part I’ve been sitting on for a week. After the yard laid us off, I couldn’t stand you seeing me come back from the Labour with nothing doing. The Board wanted electricians. I thought, here’s a job where nobody can watch me fail. It sounded funny when I said it to Bain, so I never said it again. Last Sunday I couldn’t get up. Not ill. Just couldn’t. Robbie brought me tea and I wanted to throw it at him. I’m frightened when the mail comes and frightened when it doesn’t. I don’t know how to explain that without sounding soft. Don’t write back saying you’re proud of me. Ewan **Telegram — 11 February 1985** PHONE ME SUNDAY SIX AT MRS SHAWS STOP NO SPEECHES STOP JUST PHONE STOP MUM **Rubha Reidh — 19 February 1985** Dear Mum, I phoned. You cried and pretended it was the line, which was considerate of you. Bain sat with me after. His brother had the same trouble on Hyskeir, years back. I thought I was the only keeper who’d ever made a mess of being sensible. I’ve asked for a relief and a medical. Bain made me put it in writing. He said paper is harder to argue with than yourself. I’m eating. The vest with the red stitch had a hole in it, so I binned it. Ewan **Govan — 2 March 1985** Ewan, I did cry. Mrs Shaw had to make her own tea, so there were casualties all round. When you first went, I kept your cup on the draining board for a month. I didn’t write that either. We’re a fine pair at postage and a poor pair at the rest. I’ve started bookkeeping at the community centre on Tuesdays. Your father would have laughed, then asked me to do his pools. You needn’t make me the reason to stay or go. I’m not a roof, and I’m not your excuse. Love, Mum **Rubha Reidh — 21 June 1985** Dear Mum, I’ve been ashore since March. The doctor talks a lot of sense for a man with suede shoes. I’m back for six weeks, then finished. An electrical contractor in Greenock will take me in September. Less money, more buses. Come in August, as threatened. There’s a room above the shop in Gairloch with your name on it. I want you to see this place while I’m still here, before I start improving it in the telling. Bain says I’m not to make a hero of the last six weeks either. Ewan **Govan — 6 November 1985** Ewan, So Greenock has wet floors and a foreman who thinks he’s funny. You’ll be right at home. That’s not a reason to stop writing. The photograph is on the mantel: me with my hat pinned on, you looking straight at the camera, and the Cuillin clear behind us. It was a good week, even allowing for Bain’s porridge. I didn’t say so at the time, but I understood why you wrote about the view. I also understood why you stopped. I’ve paid the roofer from the Post Office book. You can paint the stair when your wages come in, if you must be useful. Your key is cut. I’ll be at bookkeeping till four on Saturday, so let yourself in. There’s no need to stand in the close composing a letter about it. Love, Mum
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished epistolary piece that fulfills the brief with unusual discipline. The correspondence spans just over a year (September 1984 to November 1985), which technically falls short of "several months or years" only marginally — it does span more than a year, so the requirement is met. The two voices are genuinely distinct: Ewan is dry, deflective, prone to understatement and self-deprecation ("a monastery with better machinery" is his mother's joke, but his own lines like "mostly emergency" whisky carry the same wry economy), while Mum is brisk, bossy, affectionate through practicality, and — crucially — the more emotionally fluent of the two while still hiding things. The plot unfolds gradually and organically: Ewan's unemployment shame, his choice of the lighthouse as a place "where nobody can watch me fail," the Christmas isolation, the onset of what reads convincingly as depression ("Last Sunday I couldn't get up. Not ill. Just couldn't."), the mother's concealed fall, and the mutual revelation that both have been withholding. The telegram is a well-judged formal variation — terse, commanding, exactly what a mother would send. The resolution (medical discharge, Greenock job, mother's visit, the photograph on the mantel) is satisfying without being saccharine, and the final letter's "Your key is cut... let yourself in" is a quietly perfect closing gesture of welcome and reconciliation. The prose is restrained and precise. Details do character work: the vest with the red stitch (binned — a small, believable act of self-care/letting go), the cup kept on the draining board, Bain's advice that "paper is harder to argue with than yourself," the suede-shoed doctor. The Scottish working-class texture (Govan, the Co-op, the close, the Post Office book) is authentic without being performative. The mother's "I'm not a roof, and I'm not your excuse" is the emotional thesis of the piece, delivered with force. Minor criticisms: the emotional climax is somewhat muted by design, which is a defensible choice but means the piece never quite soars; the middle letters occasionally compress exposition ("After the yard laid us off" arrives with less buildup than it might); Robbie and Bain remain thin; and the mother's voice occasionally tips into epigram so polished it borders on authorial ("We're a fine pair at postage and a poor pair at the rest"). The ending is warm but earned — the recovery is gradual, mediated by a doctor and a relief posting, not a sudden cure, so the positivity is congruent. Nothing here is purple, overwrought, or amateurish. Dialogue is absent by form, so that criterion is excluded. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The restaurant had two exits, one camera with a dead insect on its lens, and a Wi-Fi password printed on the specials board. I noticed all three before I noticed Mara had arrived. Old habits don’t die. They change employment status. These days I had contracts, scopes, rules of engagement. Companies paid me to test their doors and tell them which ones opened when leaned on. I no longer confused *could* with *should*, at least not professionally. Personally, the distinction still needed occasional maintenance. The hostess responded to confidence; the waiter, to apology. My brain offered this information like a complimentary appetizer. I declined. Mara sat across from me, paint on one cuff, smiling as if she hadn’t just watched me inventory the room. Human being. Dinner. No scope. For ten minutes, I performed the recommended behaviors. I asked questions. I listened to the answers instead of composing better questions during them. Then she said, “You look like you’re deciding whether to counterspell the waiter.” I forgot the exits. “Only if he targets me with another appetizer.” She laughed. “You play?” “Played. Badly, then expensively.” “Commander?” “Sometimes.” “What color?” I hesitated, which was answer enough. “Oh, you’re blue,” she said. “Of course you are.” She played green-black and described her favorite deck with the tenderness other people reserved for childhood homes. I admitted I owned twelve counterspells and considered restraint a deck-building limitation. She called me a monster with such warmth that I nearly knocked over my water. For an hour, the restaurant became background noise. She’d learned Magic from her brother in Cedar Falls, at a library with a broken heater. Her childhood dog, Waffles, had eaten three cards from her first deck. Her first car had been a yellow Civic named Moxie, which sounded charming until she explained that the brakes had also been theoretical. Hometown. First pet. First car. Somewhere behind my eyes, an account-recovery form began completing itself. I closed the window. Not literally. I wished it were literally. She wasn’t answering questions I’d designed. She was telling stories. Offering pieces of herself without checking whether my hands were clean. Then her phone lit up beside her glass. “My sister,” she said. “Sorry.” Her thumb moved across the screen: down, then right. An L. Four points, no hesitation, the same route polished faintly into the glass. “Your unlock pattern is an L,” I said. There are moments when you can hear a sentence leave your mouth and still believe, briefly, that you might catch it. Mara looked at the phone, then at me. “Were you watching me unlock it?” “No. Yes. Not—” “Not on purpose?” That would have been an excellent place to stop talking. “I just noticed. It’s a very visible pattern.” She set the phone face down. The movement was small and precise, like a door closing without a slam. “Do you do this to everyone?” A joke presented itself. Something about only auditing people I liked. I let it die. Humor could lower defenses; that was exactly why I didn’t trust myself with it. “My ex used to go through my phone,” she said. “So I really don’t love being watched.” There it was: context, the thing my habits rarely waited for. I had seen a weak lock and missed the person standing behind it. I wanted to explain that I hadn’t memorized the pattern deliberately, that my attention worked like a stray animal, that noticing wasn’t the same as intending harm. All true. All engineered, however accidentally, to make me feel better. “I’m sorry,” I said. “Your phone isn’t my business. I saw something and treated the observation like permission. It wasn’t. If you want to end the night here, that’s okay.” I didn’t suggest a better pattern. I didn’t demonstrate how easily someone could have seen it. I didn’t turn my own phone face down as a reassuring gesture; gestures could be exploits too. She studied me. For once, I was the system under assessment. Fair enough. “Is that what you do?” she asked. “Look for ways in?” “It used to be. Without asking. Now I get permission first, and I stop when I’m told.” “And with people?” “Apparently I’m still learning.” The waiter arrived with dessert menus, took one look at our table, and retreated. Competent threat detection. Mara stayed. Not forgiveness. Not a reset. Just the next few seconds, offered provisionally. I tried not to grab at them. Eventually she asked, “If I ever agreed to see you again, what deck would you bring?” “Is that a hypothetical?” “It’s a security question.” I looked at her, checking whether the joke had really been an opening or merely a test with severe penalties. Then I decided to stop checking and answer like a person. “The mono-red one. Fewer counterspells.” “Acceptable.” Her smile returned at half power. It was better than any clean report I’d ever written. We split dessert. She told me Waffles had also eaten a library copy of *Where the Red Fern Grows*, which explained both his digestive resilience and her lifelong distrust of sentimental dogs. I laughed without filing anything away. At the door, she said, “Saturday. Bring the red deck.” “No comments on your phone.” “No comments on anything unless I ask.” “Agreed.” She hesitated. “I’m changing the pattern anyway.” “Okay,” I said. I didn’t ask what to. On the walk home, my mind tried anyway. Six points? Something without a visible smudge? I shut the thought down. Her phone could remain unknown territory. So could Saturday, and whatever came after it. Not every locked door was an invitation. Some victories looked exactly like not knowing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly controlled, well-crafted piece that hits nearly every prompt requirement with precision. The first-person internal monologue dominates, the hacker's professional deformation (inventorying exits, cameras, Wi-Fi passwords, and eventually people's security-question answers) is rendered through sharp, specific observation rather than exposition. The Magic: The Gathering fandom is woven in naturally and thematically—the "you're blue" color-pie exchange is a genuinely clever character beat, and the counterspell/mono-red payoff at the end ties the fandom into the emotional resolution rather than leaving it as decoration. The central faux pas is handled well: the L-pattern observation lands with realistic awkwardness, and Mara's reaction (the ex who went through her phone) gives the conflict real stakes rather than making it a throwaway gag. The protagonist's self-awareness—"I saw something and treated the observation like permission"—avoids both self-justification and groveling. The recovery is negotiated rather than magically resolved; Mara's forgiveness is explicitly provisional, which keeps the ending from feeling unearned. Weaknesses are minor. The aphoristic tic ("Old habits don't die. They change employment status." / "Not every locked door was an invitation. Some victories looked exactly like not knowing.") occasionally edges toward overly polished cleverness—a stylistic choice that mostly works but once or twice feels like the author showing off. The waiter's "competent threat detection" beat is funny but slightly sitcom-ish. Mara, while likable, is somewhat idealized—warm, quick, forgiving in exactly the right measure; her characterization is a touch thin compared to the protagonist's. The prose is lean and confident throughout, with strong sentence rhythm and almost no fat. Emotionally, the piece earns its hopeful ending through restraint and demonstrated change rather than sentimentality. Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It The projector squeaks when Mr. Halden advances the slide, a metallic sound like a mouse stepping on a bicycle brake. I focus on it because if I focus on Theo Martin, eighteen inches to my left, he might notice. I am in eighth grade, and my brain still treats being noticed as a potential catastrophe. Our project is on thermal energy. My group is Theo and me, which is either a gift or proof that the universe enjoys cruel variables. “Choose a question, identify your variables, and plan your procedure,” Mr. Halden says. Easy. I like questions. Questions have structure. Unlike the space between Theo’s elbow and mine, which apparently requires its own field of study. I rehearse: Do you have any ideas? Reasonable. Normal. Also pointless, because he will think I have none. Then I’ll have to say I have several, which sounds defensive. I could lead with an idea instead. We could test which material insulates best. Good. Clear. Except “we” might sound too eager, as if I am delighted to be a we. I am delighted, but he does not need evidence. What about insulation? Worse. I sound like I’m discussing attic repairs. The projector squeaks. Slide two: a steaming mug. Theo clicks his pen, and I briefly forget every fact I know, including whether heat rises. Heat does not rise; warm air rises. I know this. I could explain convection, radiation, and conduction through the mug. I could explain it to the whole class if the class were furniture. Theo is not furniture. He is the person who told Ashley her experiment was interesting before suggesting an improvement, instead of just saying it was wrong. He also has a freckle below his right ear, which I should not know the location of so precisely. Perhaps I could say, I liked what you said in the discussion yesterday. No. Too much. He will wonder why I remember. Then I’ll have to explain that I remember many things, including things said by people I do not like, which will require listing people I do not like. There is no non-alarming direction for that conversation. Perhaps: Your pen is cool. It is a black pen. I press my pen against my notebook so I will not click it. My hands are suddenly very noticeable. On the table, they look posed. Under it, secretive. I tuck my hair behind my ear, then wonder if I do that too often, then if wondering has made my face strange. I try neutral. Neutral feels suspiciously like frowning. This is exhausting before I have said anything. “We could test insulation,” Theo says. Inside, I answer immediately: Yes, and we could keep the water temperature, volume, container size, and room conditions constant, wrapping identical cups in foil, felt, or bubble wrap. We should include an unwrapped control and measure temperature at two-minute intervals, comparing rates of heat loss rather than final temperatures, because— “Yeah,” I say. One syllable. A pebble dropped off the roof of a cathedral. He waits half a second, perhaps for the rest of me. My face gets hot, which is scientifically understandable and personally offensive. I could recover. Sorry, I mean yes, that’s a good idea. Now I have apologized for agreeing. I was thinking the same thing. Was I? Yes, but saying so sounds competitive, or like I am trying to create a special mind-connection between us. Do you want to write the materials list? This sounds safe until I imagine him hearing, I have already assigned you a task because I am controlling and possibly in love with stationery. The projector squeaks again. Around us, other groups argue about containers and solar ovens. Maya’s group has written a title. My page contains only THERMAL ENERGY PROJECT, underlined twice, because underlining has become the only action I can trust. Theo sketches three cups, his lines quick and slightly crooked. I want to tell him his idea is good. I want to ask whether foil will work better because it reflects radiation or worse because it conducts heat. I want to say, I like working with you, then travel backward in time and arrest myself at I. “Five minutes,” Mr. Halden says. Fine. A sentence is just particles of air moving. I have survived particles before. We should use the same amount of water in each cup. I practice it silently, checking the we for enthusiasm, the should for bossiness, the water for any possible weirdness. Water is safe. Probably. Theo reaches for the ruler. If I wait until he looks up, I can speak while we are both looking at the diagram, which will make it a project sentence instead of a personal one. Then he looks up. My prepared sentence falls out of order. “We should—” My voice comes out too quietly. I clear my throat, which is somehow worse. “The water. Same amount. In each cup.” Excellent. I have become a laboratory label. But Theo nods. “So insulation’s the only thing changing.” He writes same volume beneath the cups. “And same starting temperature?” “Yeah,” I say, then force the next part out before the committee in my head can revise it. “Otherwise we wouldn’t know what caused the difference.” “Right.” He smiles at the diagram, not at me, which makes it easier to breathe. “Want to do the procedure while I do the materials?” I do. I also want to analyze whether want to sounded friendly, whether right meant he respected my idea, and whether my nod looked like a puppet malfunctioning. Instead, I write Step 1. My letters are too small. I let them stay. The projector squeaks when Mr. Halden flips the slide. Nobody reacts. Apparently, a sound can just be a sound, not an announcement that something has gone wrong. I am testing a similar hypothesis: that a sentence can just be a sentence. My pencil moves. Beside me, Theo clicks his pen. I still notice everything, but for the moment, I keep writing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding brief: nearly all internal monologue, first-person, socially anxious 8th-grade girl, crush on a classmate during a science project, rehearsed-and-rejected conversational approaches, gap between articulate inner voice and stunted speech. The model nails the core dynamic — her internal monologue is hyper-articulate (full experimental design, precise scientific reasoning) while her actual utterances collapse to "Yeah" and fragmented labels ("The water. Same amount. In each cup."). That contrast is the emotional engine of the prompt, and it's delivered with consistency and wit. Voice: The narrator's dry, self-deprecating, slightly clinical humor ("I am delighted, but he does not need evidence"; "I have become a laboratory label"; "a pebble dropped off the roof of a cathedral") is distinctive and sustained. The tone stays believable for a smart 13-year-old without being precocious to the point of implausibility — mostly. A few lines ("arrest myself at I"; "the committee in my head") flirt with being too writerly for an 8th grader, but the prompt explicitly asks for an articulate internal voice, so this is within bounds. Imagery: The recurring projector squeak ("a mouse stepping on a bicycle brake") is a well-chosen ambient anchor that gets a satisfying thematic payoff at the end ("a sound can just be a sound"). Small physical details — pen clicking, hair tucking, hands on/under the table, underlined title — ground the anxiety in body-level self-monitoring, exactly as the prompt requests. Structure: The piece cycles through rehearsed lines and second-guesses with good rhythm; each rejected approach has a distinct comic logic ("There is no non-alarming direction for that conversation"). The pacing is tight, no fat, and the ~1000-word target is respected. The ending — a small, tentative loosening rather than a transformation — is earned and appropriately modest. She doesn't suddenly become confident; she just keeps writing while still noticing everything. This avoids both incongruent positivity and unearned transformation. Weaknesses: The dialogue, while functional and realistic, is thin — Theo is a bit of a blank, though that's arguably the point (she can't read him). A couple of the self-deprecating metaphors stack up quickly and edge toward overwrought in the middle stretch. The science-teacher framing and "gift or proof that the universe enjoys cruel variables" is a touch sitcom-clever. The emotional range, while genuine, stays within a fairly narrow band — anxiety, wit, mild relief — without deeper stakes or backstory; the piece is a well-crafted vignette rather than a story with arc. Overall: A polished, funny, precise piece that fulfills the prompt almost exactly, with only minor over-cleverness and limited emotional depth as deductions. Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
At 6:42, with my phone at eight percent and Lena due at seven, I decide the black sweater says I have expectations. I change into the blue one. The blue one says I own other sweaters. If she says I look tired, she means difficult. If she says I look beautiful, she means she has come from somewhere better. “You’ve been a lot lately,” she’ll say. “No,” I’ll say. “I’ve been honest. You liked honesty when it was convenient.” “I never called you too much.” “You didn’t have to.” Then she’ll look down, and knowing I was right will feel like being abandoned twice. Already I resent her for making me say these things. She has not said any of them. Useful distinction. Useless. Nine years of friendship, three weeks of kissing. Her recent silences lie on the bed while I find my keys: three texts without a kiss, a postponed dinner, *sorry, slammed* where there used to be paragraphs. There was also a voice note at one in the morning, Lena saying she wished I were there. I leave that out. It complicates the case. On the bus, the battery drops to five. At 6:58 she texts: *Back table. Got you the good chair. Can’t wait to see you.* I read it four times. The fourth time, *can’t wait* sounds practiced. But she stands so quickly her knee bumps the table. She has given me the chair facing the room, because she knows I hate people behind me. There is ginger tea and the orange cake I said I liked months ago, in passing. “Hey.” Then, into my hair, “There you are. I missed you.” Something starved in me stands up so fast I feel dizzy. I want to live inside the sentence. I want her to repeat it before it evaporates. Instead I wonder why she spoke where I couldn’t see her face. The cake becomes a way of softening something. “I’m sorry I went quiet,” she says. “Work got bad. It wasn’t about you. I should have told you instead of letting you guess.” Her hand rests palm-up between us. I take it before I can decide whether that looks weak. “I love you. I missed you. I’m really glad you’re here.” The words land with such precise nourishment that I hate how much I need them. Heat, then suspicion. Love how? As in *stay*, or as in *this will make leaving kinder*? People cushion what they are about to drop. *Glad I’m here* could mean only here: this table, this hour, this manageable version of me. At two percent, my phone vibrates. A battery warning, not a message. My body doesn’t know the difference. If it dies, no one can reach me. If no one can reach me, I cannot prove anyone tried. Later, I will need her old messages to check against her face. Lena sees the red icon and takes my charger from her bag. “You left it at mine. I figured we’d need it.” She plugs it in beside the table. *We. Mine.* The ordinary intimacy of my charger in her bag almost undoes me. She coiled it, remembered it, carried it. Then I think: people are often most careful at the end. “Can I cook for you Sunday?” she asks. “I just want time with you.” A future, four days wide. Relief arrives so sharply my eyes burn. Then I see Sunday’s message: *I’m so sorry, something’s come up.* I hear myself answer, *Don’t bother. I knew this would happen.* By the time I have finished not sending it, I am furious with her for making me look pathetic in a conversation she isn’t even in. For one second, I see the actual evening: she came early. She is nervous too; there is ink on her thumb where she has been pressing it. She ordered the cake. She has not taken her hand away. She is not reading from my script. This is the pattern. I am doing the thing. The recognition should interrupt it. Instead I feel briefly clever, as if naming a fire is the same as putting it out. Then the other room returns, better lit, everyone more articulate. In that room she says, *You always do this*, and I finally have the perfect answer. “Are you okay?” she asks. “Fine,” I say. She nods. She doesn’t punish the word by withdrawing. “Okay. We can just sit.” No cross-examination, no demand that I become legible before I can be loved. The kindness is so exact I almost tell her everything: the rehearsal, the verdict, the little court where she is guilty before she arrives. Instead I imagine her face. *There you go. Too much. I was wrong to try.* She asks about my sister, remembers the appointment, listens without checking her phone. When I say it went badly, she doesn’t rush in with a solution. “That sounds horrible,” she says. “Come here.” Her arm goes around my shoulders. For a moment I let myself be held, and the wanting is so naked it frightens me more than any imagined verdict. If this is real, losing it matters. If it isn’t real, wanting it makes me a fool. Either way, she has power now. Either way, I must get it back. The phone lights at one percent, then two. Lena nudges the cake toward me and offers the fork, handle first. Under the table, her knee rests against mine and stays there. For three seconds, there is nothing to answer. Then Sunday darkens. Her train is cancelled, or she is tired, or she has finally understood me. I begin composing my defense, gentle this time, so she cannot call it an attack. Already I am hurt by her response; already I am refusing to need her. Her thumb moves once across my knuckles. It is happening now. I know it is happening now. I hold the real touch like evidence, and quietly begin to cross-examine it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally strong piece that fulfills nearly every demand of a very demanding prompt. The narrator's BPD cognition—preemptive resentment, imagined dialogues, desperate need for validation followed by immediate suspicion—is rendered almost entirely through internal monologue, exactly as instructed. The actual events (Lena's warmth: the good chair, the ginger tea, the remembered cake, the charger in her bag, the palm-up hand) are consistently non-judgmental and loving, and the narrator's reinterpretation of each as evidence of impending abandonment is handled with precision. The cognitive dissonance is vivid: "Heat, then suspicion," "I hold the real touch like evidence, and quietly begin to cross-examine it." The limited self-awareness is captured perfectly: "This is the pattern. I am doing the thing. The recognition should interrupt it. Instead I feel briefly clever, as if naming a fire is the same as putting it out." The selective awareness (leaving out the 1 a.m. voice note because "it complicates the case") is a masterstroke of characterization. The prose is lean, aphoristic, and controlled—"The blue one says I own other sweaters," "A future, four days wide," "the little court where she is guilty before she arrives." The recurring phone-battery motif works as both plot device and metaphor for the narrator's dwindling grip on reality versus the charged, sustaining real moment. The dialogue is minimal but sharp, and Lena's lines ("Okay. We can just sit.") are believable and kind without being saccharine. Minor criticisms: the piece occasionally tips into being almost too polished—every line lands, which risks feeling curated rather than raw. A few aphorisms ("knowing I was right will feel like being abandoned twice") are so compressed they flirt with cleverness over authenticity. The ending, while thematically apt (no resolution, the cycle continuing), is somewhat expected given the premise. The imagined Sunday cancellation scenario is slightly repetitive of earlier rehearsal beats. But these are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, emotionally complex, and stylistically disciplined. Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt By midnight, the abandoned temple had become a court without judges. Rain whispered through the collapsed roof, but no moonlight followed. A single torch on the east pillar provided the only light; when it bowed, shadows swelled across the crumbling walls. The ground lay between the fallen altar and the doorless entrance, six paces of swept flagstone. At the altar end waited Ren Kuroda, Jigen-ryū’s young prodigy, a bokken high in both hands. Opposite him stood Liang Chen, Piguaquan’s quickest fighter, empty-palmed and loose-shouldered. Ren’s companions crowded north; Liang’s people—porters, bodyguards, men with dock tar under their nails—pressed in from the south. Coins clicked into bowls. More than money was at hazard: by dawn, one school would be proclaimed supreme in every wineshop that would listen. Three generations earlier, a Jigen swordsman had killed a Pigua fighter beside the harbor. Ren’s school called it a lawful challenge; Liang’s, murder after surrender. Both had inherited the story before they could read. Their masters forbade this meeting. Ren’s master called it theft of another man’s quarrel. Liang’s said only, “You are not ready to learn what revenge costs.” They had come anyway. “No edged steel,” the old bookmaker croaked. “The bout ends when one man yields or cannot rise. Weapons as agreed.” Liang glanced at the wooden sword. “Keep your stick.” Ren smiled without warmth. “Keep your excuses.” Four paces separated them. Ren erased two in a single explosive step. His bokken dropped in a diagonal cut toward Liang’s left collarbone, fast enough that the torch seemed to stretch after it. Liang did not retreat. He pivoted left, off the cut’s line, and the wood hissed past his right shoulder. Now outside Ren’s right arm, he swung from the waist. His open hand whipped around and cracked into Ren’s ribs. Ren grunted, but did not give back the pace. He turned toward the pain and cut horizontally at Liang’s head. Liang ducked; the bokken stirred his hair. Ren stepped after him, attacking again before the first miss had cost him balance, and drove him westward with a third descending strike. Liang’s heel struck the plinth of a headless guardian. Behind him, spectators scrambled away. Ahead, Ren was already lifting the sword. Liang stepped forward instead of back. He slipped to his right, inside Ren’s left shoulder, as the bokken slammed into the flagstone he had just left. Stone chips jumped. Liang’s near palm snapped upward beneath Ren’s chin. Ren’s head jerked back. Blood brightened his lip, then blackened as he staggered from the torchlight. Liang followed with a backhand that Ren caught on the bokken’s flat. The impact knocked the weapon aside, but Ren’s return swing forced Liang away. They came back to the center more slowly. “Peasant tricks,” Ren said. Liang spat on the stones. “Samurai footwork.” This time Liang advanced. His arms looked careless, swinging low, but each arc began in his hips and ended at an unexpected height. A palm flashed toward Ren’s eyes. Ren lifted the bokken. The palm never arrived; Liang had changed direction around Ren’s lead foot, and his other hand struck the same ribs. Ren answered by stepping into him. The hilt thudded against Liang’s breastbone and drove him back. Ren pursued, cutting at neck, knee, neck again. Liang gave ground in a curve, never where the next cut expected him. Their path carried them toward the altar, Liang always just beyond the wooden edge, Ren one step behind. His supporters roared for him to move. Ren’s shouted for the finish. Ren had stopped watching Liang’s hands. When Liang next shifted outward, Ren cut not at his body but across the space his lead foot was entering. Wood struck the outside of Liang’s left thigh with a flat, ugly crack. His knee buckled. Ren reversed the blade and clipped his left shoulder, sending him stumbling. Three backward steps put Liang against the altar’s lowest tier. Ren stood between him and the open floor, breathing hard, blood threading from his lip. Liang’s left leg would barely take weight. With stone behind him and no speed for a long circle, he was cornered. Ren raised the bokken overhead. His shadow jumped on the western wall like an executioner. He surged forward with a cry, hips and shoulders committing behind the cut—the terrible first principle of Jigen-ryū: overwhelm, decide, end. Liang’s eyes flicked toward the torch, to his left. He leaned that way. Ren corrected to seal the escape. It was a feint. Liang turned the other way, injured leg dragging, and swung from his hips. Ren could not stop, but he could answer. He dragged the bokken back across his body, intercepting the pivot. Both blows landed. The wooden sword crushed into Liang’s side and tore the breath from him. Liang’s palm, whipping around on the same rotation, struck Ren across the jaw. Ren’s head snapped sideways; the bokken flew from his hands and skidded into the center of the ring. He fell backward onto the flagstones. Liang collapsed against the altar step, one arm clamped around his ribs. For several heartbeats there was only the torch, fluttering and hissing. Ren rolled onto one elbow. He tried to rise, swayed, and went down again. Liang planted his right foot and pushed; his left leg folded beneath him. Across the length of the fallen bokken, the two young men glared at each other, each waiting for the other to yield. Neither did. The bookmaker’s bowls overturned as supporters surged inward. Some shouted that Ren’s cut had landed first; others, that Liang’s palm had. Wagers were demanded and refused. Faction pride, briefly compressed into silence, returned twice as loud. Hands dragged the fighters apart. Liang caught Ren’s gaze through the forest of legs. There was no triumph in it, only pain and the bewilderment of someone who had expected an ending. Above them, the torch flared. Their separated shadows sprang together on the ruined wall, vast and tangled. The old debt had not been paid. It had merely found two younger names.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, well-crafted fight narrative that hits nearly all of the prompt's requirements. The physical choreography is unusually coherent: positions, distances (four paces, six paces), directional movement (westward, toward the altar, cornered against the tier), and momentum shifts are all tracked with precision. The styles are accurately characterized—Jigen-ryū's explosive first-strike philosophy ("overwhelm, decide, end") and Piguaquan's whipping, hip-driven circularity are not just named but mechanically demonstrated in the action. The setting (ruined temple, torch, rain, spectators, wagers) is established economically, and the generational feud is given a concrete historical anchor (the harbor killing) rather than vague abstraction. Strengths: The prose is lean and controlled, with strong verb choices ("the bokken stirred his hair," "shadows swelled"). The mid-fight tactical intelligence—Ren cutting across the space Liang's lead foot was entering rather than at his body—is a genuinely sophisticated beat that rewards attentive reading. The double-knockdown ending, with neither yielding, is thematically apt: the debt isn't paid, it's inherited. The final image of the shadows "springing together" on the wall is a graceful closing note. Weaknesses: The character interiority is thin; both fighters are defined by style and grievance rather than distinct psychology, and the crowd remains an undifferentiated mass. Dialogue is functional but slight ("Keep your stick" / "Keep your excuses" is serviceable, not memorable). The narrative is more admirable than emotionally involving—there's little visceral dread or personal stake beyond the abstract feud. Some phrasing edges toward the formulaic ("fast enough that the torch seemed to stretch after it"). The ending, while thematically sound, is also the expected ending for this kind of piece—a draw that indicts the feud itself is the conventional move in rivalry fiction. Still, the piece avoids overwriting, maintains coherence flawlessly, and delivers a satisfying, well-structured bout. It's a very good genre execution that falls short of masterpiece only in emotional depth and character nuance. # Breaking Formation At 00:19:58, Master Kwon put me at front left, my left sneaker on a blue tape cross. Seven trainees took the other marks: two rows of four, all facing the mirror. Hana stood two metres to my right; the back row waited two and a half metres behind me. To my left lay empty grey floor, then the wall. Above the mirror, red digits ate rehearsal: 00:19:57, 00:19:56. Kwon had built three generations of K-pop idols. Dormitory legend said he broke students to remake them; he called it removing what couldn’t survive a stage. I believed him. His gaze snagged on my glued soles, then my too-new academy shirt. My scholarship had gotten me through the elite academy’s glass doors, not made me belong behind them. Five weeks in Seoul, I still caught pieces of his Korean and assembled the rest from his hands. I bowed late. At meals, I converted prices into shifts my mother had worked. Back home, my studio was a cracked court, my music bass leaking from a parked car. In a cypher, you didn’t obey the beat. You argued with it. Kwon stood between my row and the mirror, his back to me. The phrase was commercial geometry: square shoulders, clean blocking, synchronized levels, every head angled for an invisible camera. “One through eight,” he said. “No interpretation.” The track started. On one, I stepped my right foot sideways and opened both arms into a T. On two, I closed my left foot to my right and crossed my forearms over my sternum. Simple—except my knees bounced on the *and* of one, my right shoulder rolled, and my hips drew a circle inside his straight lines. Hana’s arms sliced the mirror at shoulder height. Mine looked like they were searching for someone. Kwon killed the music. “No bounce. No decoration.” I reset. On the next attempt, three sent my left foot into a forward lunge while my right arm punched toward the mirror, left hand at my hip. The punch was supposed to arrive as one event. Muscle memory divided it into shoulder, elbow, wrist—a wave, smooth as smoke. Four returned my left foot beside my right and snapped both arms down, but I added a chest isolation on the way up. “Again.” For six minutes, he rewound us. Sweat darkened my collar; my thighs burned. My body, which could freestyle for twenty minutes without repeating itself, could not remember to be empty. At 00:12:46, I finally reached five with the others. Arms pinned straight, I stepped my right foot back. On six, my left was meant to join it, leaving me thirty centimetres behind my cross. Instead, it stepped back through a heel-toe—heel out, toe in—dragging my weight west before settling beside my right. I ended forty centimetres left of my lane while everyone else held their spacing. On seven, the others pivoted right on the balls of their feet, turning east together. On eight, they dropped to their right knees, left feet planted, arms at their sides. I was still correcting my drift. I finished the pivot half a beat late and remained standing while Hana settled without a wasted movement. Kwon walked into the empty lane and stopped an arm’s length away. “You feel accents before they happen,” he said. “Your isolations are excellent. I cannot teach that quickly.” His voice lowered. “But you treat every correction like theft.” I thought of home: somebody biting your move, everybody laughing until you transformed it and threw it back. Here, individuality wasn’t a conversation. It was a spacing error. “Where I come from,” I said, “copying gets you laughed out.” “You are not there.” His eyes flicked to my sneakers. “And potential is not a place to hide.” The clock dropped below 00:08:00. I wanted to tell him what obedience cost when you had paid with a plane ticket, your mother’s savings, and the last voice on the block that sounded like yours. Instead, I returned to my mark. Kwon walked back toward the mirror. The others rose and reset. Hana didn’t look at me. He ran me through seven more minutes of starts and stops. At 00:00:41, he said, “Last time.” One: right foot out, arms T. No bounce. Two: left foot closed, forearms crossed. Three: left lunge, right punch, the line so hard my elbow stung. Four: recover, arms down. Five: right foot back. Six: left foot joined it. I stopped thirty centimetres behind my cross, feet together, arms pinned, facing my reflection. For six counts, I was perfect. I had never looked less like myself. Seven arrived. The others pivoted east. I did not. I stepped my left foot fifty centimetres into the empty lane, keeping my face to the mirror. On eight, as the others lowered, I kept my right foot planted and dropped my weight left, knees soft. The empty space caught my groove. On the next beat, I hit Kwon’s T exactly, wrists level, fingers rigid. Then a wave travelled from my right shoulder through elbow and wrist, breaking the angle without lowering the arm. My weight poured farther left; my right heel lifted and turned out. I answered the next snare with two chest pops, then sank into a bounce no tape could measure. The formation had a torn edge. I was the tear. Kwon stopped the track. In the mirror: seven kneeling bodies facing east in two precise rows; me upright at the far left, off my mark; Kwon motionless beside the glass. The digits kept falling. “That is not the choreography,” he said. “No, sir.” My lungs burned. It was the only true thing I had breath for. Perhaps he would send me home. Perhaps there would be no second ticket. I could still step right and forward onto my cross, kneel, and keep my place. The clock reached 00:00:00. I stayed where I was, shoulders keeping a beat now ticking only in my head. If Kwon wanted to remake me, he would have to build around the pulse. I was done amputating it to fit.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, disciplined piece of writing that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with precision. The narrative tracks spatial relationships meticulously—blue tape crosses, two rows of four, distances in metres and centimetres, the countdown clock as a structural device. The choreography is described count-by-count (one through eight), and the narrator's deviations (heel-toe drift, late pivot, the final refusal on seven and eight) are physically legible. The contrast between street improvisation and commercial precision is dramatized through specific technical vocabulary: isolations, chest pops, heel-toe, blocking, cypher, groove, wave. The internal monologue effectively conveys class anxiety (converting prices into mother's shifts, the plane ticket, "the last voice on the block that sounded like yours") and the central threat of losing one's authentic movement voice. The decision point—conforming for six perfect counts, then breaking formation—is well-earned and lands with genuine weight. The line "I had never looked less like myself" is the emotional pivot, and it's earned. Strengths: the countdown clock gives the piece tension and structure; the prose is lean and controlled; the ending is ambiguous but resolute without being falsely triumphant. Kwon is a credible, economical character; his dialogue ("potential is not a place to hide") is sharp. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat schematic—the beats arrive exactly as the prompt ordered them, which slightly reduces surprise. The narrator's background remains generic (no specific neighborhood, city, or cultural texture beyond "the block"). Hana is a name with no function. The dialogue, while competent, is sparse and occasionally aphoristic in a way that feels written rather than spoken. The final image ("build around the pulse") flirts with a neat, quotable ending. The clock conceit, while effective, is also a bit mechanical—fitting for the theme, but it risks flattening emotional texture. Some may find the piece emotionally cool rather than viscerally engaging; the narrator's fear is stated more than felt in the body at times. Still, this is professional-grade work: coherent, controlled, vivid, and thematically unified. It shows rather than tells for the most part, avoids purple prose, and earns its ending. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The case was called just before the hour when dentists dream of being pursued by their own teeth. “First Love versus Mora,” said the clerk. “In the matter of one wildflower meadow, one almost-kiss, and alleged wrongful occupancy of the thorax.” Dream looked down from his throne. His face, as usual, gave away nothing. The way he held the summons gave away rather a lot. “This,” he said, “is why the night is too long.” A hush followed. It was not reverence; the court had simply learnt that when Dream sounded tired, someone was usually about to become a story with a moral. Mora’s chair scraped backwards by itself. First Love pretended not to notice that his own had moved closer to the exit. Neither movement improved his opinion of furniture. Mora occupied the defendant’s chair in several incompatible postures. First Love stood opposite, rosy-cheeked and trying not to be. He clutched a roll of drawings and blushed whenever addressed directly, which had made the preliminaries mercifully brief. “Show me the dream,” said Dream. Above the evidence table, a meadow opened. Max lay in it with a girl whose name he knew perfectly well until anyone asked him. Bees stumbled among clover. She had grass in her hair. He had a daisy behind one ear and no idea how it had got there. They talked. They laughed. They leaned closer. At the last possible moment, Max said something about the weather, though there was none, and the kiss dissolved into a pleasant bewilderment. “Fourteen revisions,” said First Love. “The breeze alone took a month. Three petals a minute. Any more looks like an accusation.” “It ends with nothing happening,” said Mora. “It ends with everything being possible.” “So does an open grave.” Dream looked at her. Mora became interested in her nails. “Show me the intrusion,” he said. The meadow returned. This time, when the girl laughingly clambered onto Max, her laughter continued after her mouth had stopped. Her shadow lengthened. Her face became a beautiful lesson in why beauty should not always be trusted. She settled on his chest. Max tried to move. His arms declined. She bent as if to kiss him and drank his breath instead. It left him in a thin silver thread. The wildflowers turned their faces away. The clerk stopped the exhibit. “Three nights,” said First Love. “Three. He now associates romantic promise with respiratory failure.” “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” said Mora. Her faint cackles echoed through the vaulted ceilings and came down somewhere less comfortable. “Objection,” said First Love. “On what grounds?” asked Dream. “Taste.” “Overruled. Taste has no standing in this court.” Mora spread her hands. “I left the meadow. I left the girl. More or less. I even left the almost-kiss. If anything, I improved the tension.” “He could not breathe.” “Anticipation.” “He could not move.” “Commitment.” First Love made a small, strangled noise. Mora looked almost maternal. Max was then called, asleep and wearing one sock. He stood beside the clerk’s desk, carefully not looking at Mora. “Do you wish either party to continue visiting your dream?” Dream asked him. “Could I just have a dream about missing the bus?” “No,” said Dream. “You have several of those already.” Max glanced at Mora despite himself, blushed, and appeared to hate the entire human condition. “She’s horrible,” he said. Then, with the courage of the condemned: “Also…” “Witness excused,” said Dream. Mora smiled after him. First Love did not. When Max had gone, Mora presented her defence. It consisted of an ancient easement over sleepers’ chests, a claim of title by artistic improvement, and the practical observation, repeated with minor variations, that girls must eat. She submitted that fear and desire were substantially the same thing, since both made people clutch the bedclothes. “The court will pretend that last argument was not made,” said Dream. He took the drawings from First Love and turned them over once. Something like impatience crossed the stillness around him, though not his face. “Enough. The meadow belongs to Max.” First Love’s mouth opened. “You crafted a gift,” Dream said. “You did not acquire the recipient. A dreamer is not a garden to be fenced by whoever brings the best flowers.” Mora cackled. “Nor,” Dream added, “by whoever brings a chair.” “I did not bring a chair.” “You became one. The distinction does not assist you.” He pronounced Mora evicted. She was to return Max’s breath, restore his nights, and make no further claim upon his chest. “With interest,” he said. “Interest?” “He is a growing boy.” First Love was permitted to repair the dream if Max wished it repaired. Dream advised him not to improve the almost-kiss. “It was perfect,” First Love said. “It was fourteen minutes long.” “He has a great deal to process.” Dream then considered the question of Mora’s hunger. He considered making the two parties exchange dreams for a night. He considered giving them joint custody on alternate Wednesdays. The temptation to mischief passed. Mostly. “For seven nights,” he said, “Mora will assist First Love. She will learn to quicken a heart without obstructing it. She will practise anticipation, restraint, and the breeze.” Mora’s cackle stopped halfway up. “With her?” said First Love. “With him?” said Mora. “You both depend upon poor judgement,” said Dream. “You may as well compare methods.” “And on the eighth night?” Mora asked. “When I’m hungry?” Dream regarded her. “You may come to me and plead hunger again.” Mora looked into his eyes. Whatever she found there appeared to contain no supper and several excellent reasons not to ask. “I expect something will turn up,” she said. “Very likely,” said Dream. They left arguing about whether daisies could be made unsettling. First Love was saying they could not. Mora was explaining that he lacked vision. The clerk dipped his pen. “Shall I file the judgment under trespass or digestion?” “Under romance,” said Dream. He looked almost pleased. The vaulted ceiling, wisely, said nothing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, controlled piece of dark comic fantasy that executes the brief with unusual precision. The courtroom farce is grounded in dry, deadpan narration that suits Dream's irritation without ever spelling it out. The opening line ("the hour when dentists dream of being pursued by their own teeth") immediately establishes tone and world. Strengths: The dialogue is the engine of the comedy. Mora's one-word rebuttals ("Anticipation." / "Commitment.") are a masterclass in economical comic timing, and Dream's rulings carry genuine wit ("You became one. The distinction does not assist you."). The legalistic language colliding with dream logic ("alleged wrongful occupancy of the thorax") is exactly the requested register. Dream's temptation to mischief is handled as instructed — considered, then mostly passed, with the "seven nights of community service" resolution feeling both mischievous and thematically apt. The ending ("Shall I file the judgment under trespass or digestion?" / "Under romance.") lands a satisfying final beat. The dream exhibits are shown rather than told — the meadow, the bees, the silver thread of breath — with sparing description as requested. Max's testimony ("She's horrible... Also...") is a lovely understated touch capturing adolescent confusion, and Dream cutting him off before the confession is a well-judged beat. Minor criticisms: The piece occasionally leans on aphorism density that borders on mannered ("a beautiful lesson in why beauty should not always be trusted" is a touch strained). First Love is somewhat thinly characterized compared to Mora and Dream — his function is mostly reactive blushing. The middle section's rhythm of short punchy exchanges, while delightful, is slightly relentless; a little more variation in pace would help. The "interest" joke ("He is a growing boy") is clever but its logic wobbles slightly. These are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, funny, dark, and disciplined throughout.
